What it means: Two mechanisms, both existing: format-as-objectivity (a single integer — "Category 4" — performs comprehensive hazard assessment while measuring one of several lethal dimensions; the format presents wind-speed classification as danger classification because a single authoritative number is easier to broadcast, easier to compare year to year, easier to anchor emergency response communications around than a multi-dimensional probability framework; the number is experienced as the storm when it is a measurement of one physical property of the storm; compare #267 pain scale where a single-dimensional self-report stands for a multi-dimensional clinical state, #271 AQI where a composite index conceals the variation among constituent pollutants, #306 wind chill where an apparent temperature is experienced as an ambient condition) + dimensional-truncation (hurricane hazard has at least four lethal dimensions: wind, storm surge, inland flooding, and tornadoes spawned by the system; the scale captures one; the three omitted dimensions killed, by documented historical record, far more people than the one retained; the truncation is not incidental but structural — storm surge and flooding were explicitly removed from the scale in 2010 because they were too variable to predict from wind speed alone, which is precisely why their removal concentrates the scale's signal on the dimension that does least lethal work; compare #293 beef grading where marble in the rib-eye section stands for the whole animal, #308 wine score where a hundred-point integer stands for a multi-dimensional sensory experience, #319 internet speed where bandwidth stands for connection quality). The Sandy case reveals a third dynamic: the scale's categorical vocabulary breaks down entirely when the storm's most dangerous dimension — surge — peaks outside the wind-speed thresholds that define the categories. A storm that has lost tropical characteristics is removed from the scale's language precisely when coastal hazard is greatest. The number's absence is not a signal of reduced danger; it is a signal of the scale's limits. But the format has trained the public to look for the number, and when there is no number, there is confusion rather than heightened alertness. First tropical meteorology / disaster communication entry. Source: National Hurricane Center / Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale, NOAA Technical Memorandum NWS TPC-6 (2012). Rappaport, E. N. / "Fatalities in the United States from Atlantic Tropical Cyclones: New Data and Interpretation," Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society 95(3): 341–346 (2014). Blake, E. S. et al. / "Tropical Cyclone Report: Hurricane Sandy," NHC Report AL182012 (2013). Blake, E. S. & Zelinsky, D. A. / "Tropical Cyclone Report: Hurricane Harvey," NHC Report AL092017 (2018). Saffir, H. & Simpson, R. / "The Damage Potential of Wind," Weatherwise (1974).

Object: MPAA film rating system and content classification (#324) Assumed channel: A letter on a movie poster — G, PG, PG-13, R, NC-17 — communicates the content of a film to parents and audiences. The rating is a standardized, objective assessment of what a film contains. Higher ratings indicate more adult content. The letter is a content fact. Actual channel: The Motion Picture Association of America's Classification and Rating Administration (CARA), established in 1968 by MPAA president Jack Valenti to replace the Hays Production Code (1934–1968), assigns ratings through an anonymous board of 8–13 members required only to be parents. No film industry experience is required. No published criteria govern the decisions. Ratings are determined by majority vote based on "standards of an average American parent" — a phrase that is the entire standard. The five-tier system — G (general audiences), PG (parental guidance suggested), PG-13 (created in 1984 after Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom and Gremlins generated controversy), R (restricted, under 17 requires adult), NC-17 (created in 1990 to replace the commercially associated X rating) — performs the precision of a content audit through a process that is opaque by design. The violence/sex asymmetry is the rating's most studied and most concealed feature. Studies by Thompson and Yokota (2004) and Leone and Barowski (2011) document that PG-13 films routinely contain substantial violence — gunfights, explosions, battlefield deaths, hand-to-hand brutality — that does not trigger upgrade to R, while a single use of "f" in a sexual context automatically triggers R under current CARA practice. The same word used non-sexually is typically permissible twice before triggering R. The rating is measurably more tolerant of violence than of sexuality. This asymmetry reflects an American cultural value — violence is less threatening than sex as a category of exposure — that has been embedded in the rating system without disclosure. The rating presents itself as a content description; it is also a moral hierarchy. Ratings creep compounds the opacity. A Harvard School of Public Health study (Nalkur et al., 2010) compared ratings assigned to films between 1992 and 2003: content that received an R rating in 1992 was receiving a PG-13 rating by the study period. The thresholds drift without announcement, without methodology disclosure, without public notice. A PG-13 film in 2024 contains, on average, more violence than an R-rated film in 1985, but the letters are the same. The temporal instability is invisible in the format. NC-17 functions as commercial censorship. Many major theater chains have written policies declining to screen NC-17 films. Many newspapers and television networks decline to carry NC-17 advertising. The studio economics follow: an NC-17 film loses a significant portion of its theatrical distribution, its marketing reach, and its box office potential. Directors who receive NC-17 often edit the film to obtain an R — not because of any legal requirement but because the rating's commercial consequences function as a veto. The rating was designed as parental guidance; it operates as distribution control. No appeals body independent of the MPAA existed until 2020 reforms. Before that, the body reviewing appeals was itself composed of MPAA members. The rating determines not only parental advisory but marketing budget eligibility, TV advertising windows, theater placement, and the total commercial infrastructure of a film's release. What it means: Two mechanisms, both existing: format-as-objectivity (a letter grade — G, PG, PG-13, R, NC-17 — performs standardized, consistent content assessment while being determined by anonymous votes with no published criteria, no disclosed methodology, no auditable process; the format implies a content audit and delivers a cultural judgment; see also #267 pain scale, #292 MBTI, #308 wine score, #304 impact factor — in each case, a compact format performs the objectivity of systematic measurement while concealing the judgment, convention, or cultural assumption that produced it) + convention-as-nature (the violence/sex asymmetry and ratings creep are experienced as properties of the content — this film is more sexual, this film is more violent — when they are properties of the rating board's cultural assumptions; a viewer who finds NC-17 content unacceptable is responding to a commercial boundary designed to manage distribution, not a content boundary derived from any published standard; the thresholds are not discovered in the content but imposed by a board whose criteria are undisclosed and whose composition is anonymous; what the culture treats as leniently is embedded as the default without disclosure — see also #282 legal age where age thresholds are experienced as natural developmental boundaries, #314 octane where the rating scale conceals the airport/city gap). Cross-references: #267 pain scale (subjective judgment expressed as a number), #282 legal age (threshold presented as neutral developmental fact), #292 MBTI (undisclosed typological assumptions presented as psychological measurement), #308 wine score (expert consensus expressed as a number that performs objectivity). First film classification / media regulation entry. Source: Valenti, Jack / The Voluntary Movie Rating System: How It Began, Its Purpose, The Public Reaction, MPAA (2000). Thompson, K. M. & Yokota, F. / "Violence, Sex, and Profanity in Films: Correlation of Movie Ratings With Content," Medscape General Medicine 6(3): 3 (2004). Leone, R. & Barowski, L. / "MPAA Ratings Creep: A Longitudinal Analysis of the Age-Appropriateness of Film Content," Journal of Children and Media 5(1): 53–68 (2011). Nalkur, P. G.; Jamieson, P. E.; Romer, D. / "The Effectiveness of the Motion Picture Association of America's Rating System in Screening Explicitness and Violence in Movies," Journal of Adolescent Health 47(5): 440–447 (2010). Mast, G. & Kawin, B. F. / A Short History of the Movies,* 12th ed., Pearson (2012).

Object: Correlated color temperature on consumer light bulb packaging (#325)

Assumed channel: A number printed on a light bulb box — "2700K," "5000K," "6500K" — communicates the color of the light in degrees Kelvin, a unit of absolute temperature. Higher numbers mean cooler-looking light; lower numbers mean warmer-looking light. The number is a physical measurement. The Kelvin unit anchors it to thermodynamics. The labels "warm white" and "daylight" describe the visual experience. The consumer reads a temperature that describes the light.

Actual channel: The Kelvin number on a light bulb is not the temperature of anything inside the bulb. It is the temperature a theoretical perfect blackbody radiator — an idealized opaque, non-reflective body that absorbs all incident radiation — would need to be heated to in order to emit light of a similar color. Max Planck derived the spectral distribution of blackbody radiation in 1900. The CIE (Commission Internationale de l'Éclairage) standardized correlated color temperature in 1931 as part of the CIE 1931 color space, using the chromaticity coordinates of the same seventeen-observer standard observer (#239). The "correlated" is the key word. Real light sources — incandescent bulbs, fluorescent tubes, LEDs — do not emit blackbody spectra. An incandescent filament approximates a blackbody because it is a heated solid, but its emissivity deviates from unity across the spectrum. Fluorescent tubes emit discrete mercury emission lines plus broadband phosphor fluorescence — a spectrum that looks nothing like a thermal radiator. LEDs emit narrow-band radiation from a semiconductor junction, typically blue, converted to broader-spectrum white by a phosphor coating; the resulting spectrum consists of a sharp blue peak near 450 nm and a broad phosphor peak near 560 nm with a valley between them. This bimodal distribution bears no resemblance to a Planckian curve. The CCT is determined by finding the point on the Planckian locus — the curve traced by blackbody chromaticity coordinates in CIE color space — that is nearest to the source's chromaticity. McCamy's approximation (1992) provides a cubic polynomial for calculating CCT from chromaticity coordinates. The mathematical projection collapses the source's actual spectral power distribution into a single number that describes not what the source emits but which blackbody it most closely resembles in two-dimensional chromaticity space. Two sources with identical CCT can have radically different spectra — a phenomenon called metamerism. Two "5000K" bulbs may render the same red fabric as different colors because their spectral power distributions, though projecting to the same point near the Planckian locus, distribute energy differently across the visible wavelengths. The Color Rendering Index (CRI), developed by the CIE in 1965 and revised in 1974 and 1995, was invented specifically to address what CCT alone cannot capture: how faithfully a source renders object colors compared to a reference illuminant. CRI is calculated against fourteen test color samples (eight standard, six supplementary) and averaged. An LED with CCT 4000K and CRI 80 renders colors measurably less faithfully than a halogen at 3000K and CRI 100. Yet the consumer box typically displays the CCT prominently and the CRI in small print or not at all. Duv — the signed distance from the Planckian locus — measures how far a source actually is from blackbody color: positive Duv means the source is above the locus (greenish tint), negative means below (pinkish). Duv is almost never reported to consumers but is the parameter that determines whether a nominally "5000K" source looks neutral or sickly green. The perceptual labels perform an additional inversion: "warm" light corresponds to low CCT (2700K), and "cool" light corresponds to high CCT (6500K). In physics, higher temperature means higher energy. A blackbody at 6500K is hotter than one at 2700K. The marketing language reverses the physics: what is physically warmer is labeled "cool," and what is physically cooler is labeled "warm." The labels describe a psychological association — reddish light feels warm, bluish light feels cool — and attach it to a temperature scale running in the opposite direction. The consumer reads "warm" and sees "2700K" and experiences coherence. The coherence is between the perceptual label and the visual experience, not between the label and the unit.

What it means: Two mechanisms, both existing: format-as-objectivity (the Kelvin unit performs physical precision — degrees of absolute temperature, a unit from thermodynamics — for what is actually a psychophysical projection onto a theoretical locus in a two-dimensional chromaticity space derived from seventeen observers in 1931; the number looks like a measurement of the light source when it is a mathematical proximity calculation to an idealized radiator that no commercial light source resembles; the format — four digits and a capital K — implies that 5000K describes the light the way 100°C describes boiling water, when it describes a geometric relationship in color space; see also #312 stellar magnitude where a logarithmic scale from ancient perception is dressed in decimal precision, #239 CIE standard observer where the perceptual responses of seventeen people became the definition of color, #317 megapixels where a single number performs the objectivity of image quality) + convention-as-nature (the warm/cool inversion naturalizes a perceptual convention that reverses the physics; "warm white" at 2700K and "cool daylight" at 6500K map psychological associations — firelight feels warm, overcast sky feels cool — onto a temperature scale running in the opposite direction; the labels are experienced as describing the light when they describe a cultural association between color and comfort; the consumer who selects "warm" light is choosing low temperature, and the consumer who selects "cool" light is choosing high temperature, but the labels have so thoroughly naturalized the inversion that the contradiction is invisible; see also #312 stellar magnitude where brighter stars get lower numbers because "first" meant "best" in 129 BC, #277 time zones where political boundaries are experienced as geographic facts). The CCT's relationship to #239 is direct: the Planckian locus onto which all commercial light sources are projected exists within the CIE 1931 color space — the same space built on seventeen observers' perceptual responses. The CCT inherits every limitation documented in #239 — the short-wavelength deviations, the foveal-only field, the population unrepresentativeness — and adds another layer of abstraction: projection onto the blackbody curve within that already-compromised space. The consumer sees a number in Kelvin on a box. The number is a projection onto a theoretical curve in a perceptual space derived from seventeen people, labeled with words that reverse the physics it claims to measure. First lighting science / consumer photometry entry.

Source: Planck, Max / "Über das Gesetz der Energieverteilung im Normalspektrum," Annalen der Physik 309(3): 553–563 (1901). CIE / CIE 015:2004 Colorimetry, 3rd ed. (2004). McCamy, C. S. / "Correlated color temperature as an explicit function of chromaticity coordinates," Color Research and Application 17(2): 142–144 (1992). Ohno, Yoshi / "Color Rendering and Luminous Efficacy of White LED Spectra," Proceedings of the SPIE 5530: 88–98 (2004). Wyszecki, Günter & Stiles, W. S. / Color Science: Concepts and Methods, Quantitative Data and Formulae, 2nd ed., Wiley (1982).

Object: Alcohol proof and the labeling of spirit strength (#326)

Assumed channel: A number printed on a bottle of spirits — "80 proof," "100 proof," "151 proof" — communicates how strong the alcohol is. The word "proof" sounds empirical: a test, a demonstration, evidence. The number is a measurement. Higher proof means stronger spirit. The consumer reads a property of the liquid.

Actual channel: The word "proof" derives from sixteenth-century English excise law, where spirits above a certain strength were taxed at a higher rate. The method traditionally cited is the gunpowder test: spirit was mixed with gunpowder and ignited. If it burned, the spirit was "proof" — strong enough to sustain combustion despite the water. Potassium nitrate in gunpowder is more soluble in water than in ethanol, so a sufficiently diluted spirit extinguished the flame. The test is widely cited but poorly documented in primary sources — Matt Pietrek, searching original Royal Navy records from the 1700s and 1800s, found no primary account of the gunpowder test aboard a ship. Clarke's hydrometer was in naval use by the 1730s. Whether the gunpowder test was widespread practice or retrospective folklore, the word "proof" named a tax threshold: the concentration at which excise duty changed. Bartholomew Sikes, a British excise officer, won a competition among nineteen submissions in 1802 to replace Clarke's hydrometer. He died in 1803. The Hydrometer Act of 1816 established his instrument as the British standard and defined proof spirit as the concentration at which a specific volume weighs thirteen twenty-thirds of the same volume of distilled water at the same temperature — approximately 57.15% alcohol by volume. One hundred degrees proof (UK) meant 57.15% ABV. The number was calibrated to a specific gravity ratio useful for revenue calculation, not to a round percentage meaningful to the drinker. The United States adopted a different definition: proof equals twice the percentage of alcohol by volume. One hundred proof (US) means 50% ABV. The same number — 100 proof — means different concentrations in different countries: 57.15% in Britain, 50% in America. A bottle labeled 70 proof contained approximately 40% ABV in Britain (70/100 × 57.15) but only 35% in America (70/2). Same word, same number, different liquid. Gay-Lussac published his centesimal alcoholometer in France in 1824, graduating directly in percent by volume at 15°C — no proof, no conversion factor, just the fraction of the volume that is ethanol. France made it obligatory in 1884. EU Directive 76/766/EEC brought Britain into alignment in 1980 after 164 years of the Sikes system. The concept of proof disappeared from British labels. It persists in the United States, where it carries no information beyond doubling the ABV percentage already printed on the same label in smaller type. Federal excise tax is still calculated per "proof gallon" — one gallon of liquid at 100 proof (50% ABV), or its equivalent at other concentrations. The 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act reduced the federal excise to $2.70 per proof gallon on the first 100,000 gallons for qualifying distillers, with the standard rate at $13.50 per proof gallon. The unit of taxation remains a concept from an era when instruments measured density, not composition. Ethanol-water mixtures exhibit non-additive volume: 50 mL of ethanol plus 50 mL of water yields approximately 96.4 mL, not 100, due to hydrogen bonding between ethanol and water molecules filling the structural spaces in water's tetrahedral network. Mendeleev's 1865 doctoral dissertation, "On the Combinations of Water with Alcohol," studied this contraction systematically — the same physical anomaly that makes proof measurement by density possible and imperfect, since density varies nonlinearly with concentration and temperature. The proof number on a bottle is a number from a tax system, named after a test that may be apocryphal, defined differently on different continents, surviving in one country where it merely doubles the percentage, printed larger than the information it duplicates.

What it means: Two mechanisms, both existing: format-as-objectivity (the word "proof" performs empirical authority — it sounds like evidence, a test, a demonstration — for what is an arbitrary scaling of alcohol percentage calibrated to tax collection; the number looks like a measurement of the liquid when it describes a position in a revenue classification system; "80 proof" carries the weight of certainty while merely restating "40% ABV" in a different arithmetic; see also #314 octane rating where a knock-resistance test calibrated to two reference fuels became a consumer quality metric, #318 horsepower where a unit from brewery horses became a marketing number, #325 CCT where degrees Kelvin perform physical measurement for a psychophysical projection) + convention-as-nature (three different national conventions — British proof at 57.15% ABV, American proof at 2× ABV, French/European ABV directly — were each experienced as measuring a property of the liquid rather than applying a local administrative convention; the same bottle of whisky was a different number in London, New York, and Paris; the American convention survived the British one's retirement and is now experienced as a natural property of spirits; see also #315 shoe sizing where the same foot gets different numbers in different countries, #322 clothing sizes where a size 8 means different measurements in different decades, #277 time zones where political boundaries are experienced as geographic facts). The proof system's survival in the United States — where it duplicates the ABV percentage on the same label in a larger font — demonstrates that a number can persist after losing its informational function, sustained by infrastructure (tax code, regulation, marketing convention, consumer expectation) rather than utility. First distilled spirits metrology / alcohol taxation entry.

Source: Sikes Hydrometer Act (56 Geo. III, c. 140, 1816). Gay-Lussac, Joseph Louis / Instruction pour l'usage de l'alcoomètre centésimal (1824). Mendeleev, Dmitri / "On the Combinations of Water with Alcohol" (doctoral dissertation, Saint Petersburg, 1865). EU Council Directive 76/766/EEC (1976). Pietrek, Matt / "The Myth of Royal Navy Rum and the Gunpowder Test," Rum Wonk (Nov 21, 2022). TTB / 27 CFR Part 5 — Labeling and Advertising of Distilled Spirits. Linstrom, Peter J. & Mallard, W. G., eds. / NIST Chemistry WebBook, NIST Standard Reference Database Number 69 (excess volume data for ethanol-water mixtures).

Object: Television and monitor screen size measured by diagonal (#327)

Assumed channel: A number on a television box — "55 inches," "65 inches," "75 inches" — communicates how big the screen is. Larger diagonal means larger screen. The number is a measurement. The unit is inches (or centimeters in metric markets). The consumer compares diagonals to compare sizes.

Actual channel: The diagonal measurement convention originated with cathode-ray tubes. A CRT was a funnel-shaped glass vacuum tube with a phosphor-coated front face. The tube was roughly circular, and the diagonal of the rectangular viewable area corresponded approximately to the tube's outer diameter — the manufacturing dimension used to specify the glass envelope. Manufacturers advertised the tube diagonal, not the viewable image. A 19-inch CRT monitor might display only 17.3 inches of viewable image because the bezel and shadow mask covered the tube's curved edges. The FTC took enforcement action in the mid-1990s, requiring computer monitor manufacturers to disclose "viewable image size" (VIS) alongside the advertised diagonal after determining that the discrepancy — sometimes two or more inches — was misleading to consumers. The regulation corrected the bezel problem without changing the measurement convention: screens continued to be sold by diagonal. Flat-panel displays (LCD, LED, OLED) eliminated the bezel discrepancy — the advertised diagonal is now the viewable diagonal. But the convention persists across a change that makes it less informative: the aspect ratio transition from 4:3 (standard definition) to 16:9 (widescreen). For a given diagonal d and aspect ratio w:h, the screen area equals d² × (w×h)/(w²+h²). A 55-inch 16:9 screen has an area of approximately 1,293 square inches. A 55-inch 4:3 screen has an area of approximately 1,452 square inches — roughly 12.3% more viewing area at the same diagonal. A consumer who replaced a 32-inch 4:3 television with a 32-inch 16:9 television kept the same number and lost viewing area. The diagonal conceals which dimension changed: widescreen is wider but shorter. A 27-inch 16:9 monitor stands 13.2 inches tall; a 27-inch 4:3 monitor stood 16.2 inches tall — three inches of vertical space disappeared behind the same diagonal number. Ultrawide monitors (21:9, 32:9) extend the compression: a 34-inch 21:9 ultrawide has less total area than a 34-inch 16:9 monitor, despite the consumer parsing both as "34 inches." No major manufacturer advertises televisions by area. The calculation is trivial — width times height — but area is a two-dimensional quantity and resists the single-number format that marketing, specifications, and price-comparison sites require. The diagonal persists because it is one number.

What it means: Two mechanisms, both existing: format-as-objectivity (the diagonal performs measurement precision — inches to one decimal place, sometimes to the hundredth — for a geometric abstraction that conceals the two dimensions consumers actually experience; the number looks like a size when it describes a line no one looks along; the format — "55 inches" or "139 cm" — implies that the diagonal captures screen size the way weight captures mass, when it captures only the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs determine the actual viewing experience; see also #317 megapixels where a sensor dimension performs image quality, #318 horsepower where a power output performs vehicle capability, #319 internet speed where a maximum bitrate performs connection quality) + dimensional-truncation (a two-dimensional property — viewing area — is communicated through a one-dimensional measurement — the diagonal; the truncation from area to length discards the aspect ratio, which determines how the two dimensions are distributed; comparing a 55-inch 16:9 to a 55-inch 4:3 by diagonal alone erases a 12% difference in area; comparing a 34-inch 21:9 ultrawide to a 34-inch 16:9 standard by diagonal alone erases a difference in both shape and area; the truncation is enabled by the convention's origin in a technology — CRT tubes — where the diagonal correlated with the manufacturing dimension and aspect ratio was fixed; when aspect ratio became variable, the measurement stopped tracking what it originally tracked, but the convention was already infrastructure; see also #315 shoe sizing where a single number erases width, #322 clothing sizes where a single number erases multiple body dimensions, #320 thread count where a single number erases fiber quality and weave type). The diagonal's survival through two technology transitions — CRT to flat panel, 4:3 to 16:9 — demonstrates how a measurement convention outlasts its original justification when the infrastructure (retail displays, spec sheets, price comparison, consumer vocabulary) crystallizes around it. First consumer electronics display / screen metrology entry.

Source: FTC / "FTC Guides for the Advertising of Television Sets" (16 CFR Part 410, originally adopted 1966, amended). FTC enforcement actions (1990s) regarding CRT monitor viewable image size disclosures. VESA / Video Electronics Standards Association display measurement standards. CTA / Consumer Technology Association screen size specifications for retail.

Object: Dog years and the seven-to-one aging ratio (#328)

Assumed channel: A number — "one dog year equals seven human years" — translates canine aging into human terms. A five-year-old dog is thirty-five in "dog years." The formula is a biological conversion factor, like Celsius to Fahrenheit: a fixed ratio mapping one species' developmental timeline onto another. The number is a measurement of comparative aging.

Actual channel: The seven-to-one ratio has no documented scientific origin. No published study derived it. No researcher is credited with establishing it. The number appears to emerge from a rough arithmetic: average human lifespan (~70 years) divided by average dog lifespan (~10 years) = 7. The division treats both lifespans as averages of highly variable distributions and treats the ratio as linear, implying that development proceeds at a constant relative rate across the lifespan. It does not. A one-year-old dog is sexually mature, reproductively active, and skeletally near-adult — corresponding to roughly a 15-year-old human, not a 7-year-old. A two-year-old dog has completed nearly all physical development — corresponding to approximately a 24-year-old human, not a 14-year-old. The AVMA (American Veterinary Medical Association) recommends a piecewise approximation: first year = 15 human years, second year = 9, each subsequent year ≈ 5. This captures rapid early maturation better but still treats all breeds identically. Breed variation is enormous: Irish Wolfhounds live 6-8 years (implied multiplier: ~10-12), Chihuahuas live 14-17 years (implied multiplier: ~4-5). A single ratio erases a twofold lifespan variation within the species it claims to describe. Tina Wang, Jianzhu Ma, and colleagues at the University of California San Diego and the University of Pittsburgh, publishing in Cell Systems (2020), developed an epigenetic aging formula based on DNA methylation patterns in 104 Labrador Retrievers compared to 320 humans. The relationship is logarithmic: human_age ≈ 16 × ln(dog_age) + 31. A one-year-old Labrador corresponds epigenetically to a 31-year-old human, not a 7-year-old. A four-year-old to a 53-year-old. A twelve-year-old to a 71-year-old. The curve is steep early and shallow late — the opposite of the linear seven-to-one model. The formula is Labrador-specific; it would differ for other breeds because body size correlates with aging rate within the domestic dog species (Kraus et al., American Naturalist, 2013: larger dogs age faster, consistent with accelerated growth rather than delayed senescence). The seven-to-one ratio persists despite being wrong at every age, for every breed, by every measure — because it performs a function that accuracy does not. It converts a cross-species comparison into a single multiplication, producing a human number that communicates urgency (your ten-year-old dog is seventy) rather than precision. The format — one number, one operation, one species mapped onto another — is the product.

What it means: Two mechanisms, both existing: convention-as-nature (the seven-to-one ratio is experienced as a biological fact — a conversion factor discovered by veterinary science — when it is a folk heuristic with no documented origin, no empirical derivation, and no breed specificity; the clean integer and the simple multiplication perform the authority of a natural law; see also #310 where the 10,000-step threshold was a brand name experienced as a health recommendation, #318 horsepower where a unit derived from brewery observation became a physical constant, #326 alcohol proof where a tax threshold was experienced as a property of the liquid) + format-as-objectivity (the single-multiplier format — multiply any dog age by seven, get a human age — performs scientific precision for a conversion that fails at every data point; the formula's portability is its persuasiveness; a logarithmic function or a piecewise approximation would be more accurate but less memorable, less printable, and less useful in casual conversation; the seven survives because it is one number that produces one number through one operation; see also #327 TV diagonal where a one-dimensional measurement performs a two-dimensional property because one number is what spec sheets accommodate, #317 megapixels where a sensor count performs image quality because it fits a comparison chart). The ratio is the purest case in this inventory of a number with no empirical basis at all — not a measurement that simplifies, not a proxy that approximates, but a folk number that performs measurement through format alone. First comparative gerontology / veterinary folklore entry.

Source: Wang, Tina et al. / "Quantitative Translation of Dog-to-Human Aging by Conserved Remodeling of the DNA Methylome," Cell Systems 11(2): 176-185.e6 (2020). Kraus, Cornelia et al. / "The Size–Life Span Trade-Off Decomposed: Why Large Dogs Die Young," American Naturalist 181(4): 492-505 (2013). AVMA / "How to Calculate Your Dog's Age" (veterinary guidelines). Fortney, William D. / "Implementing a Successful Senior/Geriatric Health Care Program for Dogs and Cats," Veterinary Clinics of North America: Small Animal Practice 42(4): 823-834 (2012).

Object: Paper size standards and the Letter/A4 divide (#329)

Assumed channel: Paper is a size. In the United States, it is 8.5 by 11 inches — "letter size." Everywhere else, it is 210 by 297 millimeters — "A4." Each is experienced as the natural shape of paper. The user loads the printer tray without deciding. The paper is simply paper.

Actual channel: US Letter (8.5 × 11 inches, 215.9 × 279.4 mm) has no mathematical derivation. The dimensions appear to originate from paper mold sizes used in American mills, likely inherited from British and Dutch papermaking traditions of the colonial era. No governing equation or optimization principle produced the ratio. The dimensions are customary — they are the custom, hardened into a standard by the American National Standards Institute (ANSI Y14.1). A4 has an equation. Georg Christoph Lichtenberg, a German physicist, observed in 1786 that a rectangle with a length-to-width ratio of 1:√2 is self-similar under halving: fold the sheet by cutting the long side, and the resulting half-sheet has the same proportions. This property means that A-series paper can be scaled between sizes without cropping or distortion. Walter Porstmann formalized the insight into DIN 476 in 1922, defining A0 as exactly 1 square meter with the 1:√2 ratio (841 × 1189 mm). Each subsequent size is the previous halved: A1 = 594 × 841, A2 = 420 × 594, A3 = 297 × 420, A4 = 210 × 297. ISO 216 adopted the system as an international standard in 1975. Nearly every country adopted ISO 216. The United States, Canada, and parts of Latin America retained Letter. The two standards differ by 6 mm in width (Letter is wider) and 18 mm in height (A4 is taller). The difference is small enough to be invisible on a single page and large enough to cause layout failures in every cross-border document exchange. A manuscript formatted for Letter prints with cropped margins on A4. A manuscript formatted for A4 prints with shifted margins on Letter. Software mediates the division: Microsoft Word defaults to Letter in the US and A4 in Europe based on the operating system's locale setting — a decision made before the user types a word. The US federal government attempted to adopt A4 in the 1980s-1990s as part of metrication. The installed base — filing cabinets, binders, envelopes, all dimensioned for 8.5 × 11 — resisted. Infrastructure decided.

What it means: Two mechanisms, both existing: convention-as-nature (each paper size is experienced as the natural shape of paper rather than as a decision by a standards body or a legacy of colonial papermaking; the user loading the tray does not perceive a choice because the choice was made by the manufacturer, the retailer, the software default, the locale setting; the convention becomes invisible precisely because it is pervasive — every printer, every ream, every template reinforces the same dimensions until the dimensions feel inherent; see also #277 time zones where political boundaries are experienced as geographic facts, #315 shoe sizes where national sizing systems are experienced as properties of feet, #326 alcohol proof where national proof definitions are experienced as properties of the liquid) + infrastructure-absorbs-error (the 6mm × 18mm incompatibility between Letter and A4 is absorbed by printer drivers, margin settings, and PDF scaling rather than resolved by standardization; the software silently reformats the document — shifting text, adjusting margins, occasionally cropping footnotes — and the user sees only the reformatted result; the incompatibility persists because the infrastructure has learned to accommodate it; see also #277 time zones where software handles conversions that the underlying system leaves ambiguous, #290 SST where bucket-to-intake transitions were absorbed by correction algorithms). The Paper size divide illustrates a concealment species that might be called default-as-decision: when software selects a standard based on locale before the user acts, the selection is experienced as an absence of choice rather than a hidden choice. First paper metrology / document standards entry.

Source: Lichtenberg, Georg Christoph / Letter to Johann Beckmann (Oct 25, 1786). DIN / DIN 476: Papierformate (1922). ISO / ISO 216: Writing paper and certain classes of printed matter — Trimmed sizes — A and B series (1975). ANSI / ANSI/ASME Y14.1: Decimal Inch Drawing Sheet Size and Format (1995). Kuhn, Markus / "International Standard Paper Sizes" (technical note, University of Cambridge, 2006).

Object: Battery capacity in milliamp-hours (mAh) on consumer electronics (#330)

Assumed channel: A number on a phone spec sheet — "5,000 mAh" — communicates battery capacity. A higher number means a longer-lasting battery. The consumer compares mAh across devices to compare battery life. The unit is a measurement of how much energy the battery holds.

Actual channel: Milliamp-hours measure electric charge — the quantity of electrons a battery can deliver — not energy. The energy stored in a battery is the product of charge and voltage: watt-hours = milliamp-hours × voltage ÷ 1,000. A 5,000 mAh battery at 3.7 volts (typical phone cell voltage) stores 18.5 watt-hours. The same 5,000 mAh at 7.4 volts (a two-cell laptop battery) stores 37 watt-hours — twice the energy. The mAh number is equal. The energy is not. Comparing mAh across devices with different voltages is comparing charges, not capacities. Phone-to-phone comparisons at the same nominal voltage are approximately valid (a 5,000 mAh phone vs a 4,500 mAh phone has roughly 11% more stored energy). Phone-to-laptop comparisons are not (a 5,000 mAh phone and a 5,000 mAh laptop differ by a factor of two to three in actual energy). Power banks add a further layer of compression. A "20,000 mAh" power bank stores energy at its internal cell voltage (typically 3.7V, yielding ~74 Wh). It delivers power at 5V (USB-A) or higher (USB-C PD). Voltage conversion incurs losses of 15-30% depending on circuitry, cable resistance, and protocol negotiation. The usable output at 5V is approximately 14,800 mAh, not 20,000. The consumer expecting four full charges of a 5,000 mAh phone gets three and a half. The discrepancy is inherent in the physics of voltage conversion and invisible in the marketing number. The aviation regulatory system uses the correct unit: the TSA/FAA limit for lithium-ion batteries in carry-on luggage is 100 watt-hours — the energy measure, not the charge measure — because energy content, not charge, determines the thermal runaway severity in a fire. Watt-hours produce smaller numbers than mAh (18.5 vs 5,000 for the same phone battery). Marketers use mAh because it produces four-digit numbers. Regulators use Wh because it captures what matters. Both numbers describe the same battery. The marketing number is 270 times larger.

What it means: Two mechanisms, both existing: format-as-objectivity (the mAh number performs battery capacity through a four-digit figure that looks like a comprehensive measurement; "5,000 mAh" carries the precision and authority of a complete specification when it captures one of two variables needed to calculate energy; the format — large integer, scientific-looking unit abbreviation — implies that comparing mAh is comparing batteries the way comparing kilometers is comparing distances; it is not, because distance has one dimension and battery energy has two: charge and voltage; see also #317 megapixels where a sensor count performs image quality while erasing sensor size, #318 horsepower where a power number performs vehicle capability while erasing torque curve and transmission, #327 TV diagonal where a length performs screen size while erasing area) + dimensional-truncation (the two-dimensional property — energy = charge × voltage — is communicated through one dimension: charge; the voltage is omitted from marketing because it varies across products and complicates comparison; the truncation from Wh to mAh discards the voltage dimension the way the diagonal discards the aspect ratio; the result is a number that can reverse rankings: a lower-mAh battery at higher voltage can store more energy than a higher-mAh battery at lower voltage; see also #327 TV diagonal where a larger-diagonal screen can have less area than a smaller-diagonal screen of different aspect ratio, #320 thread count where a higher count can mean lower quality when multi-ply inflation is present). The marketing/regulatory split — mAh for consumers, Wh for FAA — demonstrates that the unit chosen depends on the purpose: mAh is chosen because it produces the largest number, Wh is chosen because it measures the actual risk. First battery metrology / consumer electronics marketing entry.

Source: IEC 61960 (secondary lithium cells performance standards). FAA / TSA / 49 CFR 175.10 (lithium battery carry-on limits: 100 Wh). IEEE Std 1725 (battery systems for mobile electronics). Buchmann, Isidor / Batteries in a Portable World, 4th ed., Cadex Electronics (2016).

Object: Fuel economy measured in miles per gallon (MPG) (#331)

Assumed channel: A number on a car's window sticker — "30 MPG" — communicates fuel efficiency. Higher MPG means less fuel consumed. The consumer compares MPG across vehicles to compare cost of ownership. The scale is linear: the same improvement in MPG always saves the same amount of fuel.

Actual channel: The relationship between MPG and fuel consumption is hyperbolic, not linear. MPG measures distance per volume (miles/gallon), but the consumer's cost is volume per distance (gallons/mile or gallons per hundred miles). The inversion distorts the scale. An improvement from 10 to 20 MPG saves 5 gallons per 100 miles. An improvement from 30 to 40 MPG saves 0.83 gallons per 100 miles. The same 10-MPG improvement saves six times more fuel at the bottom of the scale. Richard Larrick and Jack Soll at the Fuqua School of Business, Duke University, named this the "MPG illusion" in a 2008 paper in Science (320(5883): 1593-1594). In experimental studies, they showed that consumers systematically underestimate savings from improving low-MPG vehicles and overestimate savings from improving high-MPG vehicles. When asked whether upgrading from 10 to 20 MPG or from 25 to 50 MPG saves more fuel, most consumers choose the larger numerical jump — but the savings are identical (both halve consumption). The illusion has policy consequences: CAFE (Corporate Average Fuel Economy) standards, expressed in MPG, compress marginal improvements in already-efficient vehicles and expand marginal improvements in inefficient ones. A 1-MPG improvement at the 15 MPG level saves more fuel per vehicle than a 5-MPG improvement at the 45 MPG level. Europe and most of the world report fuel consumption in liters per 100 kilometers — the inverse unit. L/100km is linear with actual consumption. The improvement from 8 to 5 L/100km saves the same proportional amount of fuel that the numbers suggest. No inversion. No compression. The EPA added gallons per 100 miles to US fuel economy labels in 2013, following advocacy by consumer researchers and the National Academy of Sciences. The number appears in small type below the large MPG figure. The correction is accurate and insufficient — the headline remains MPG because the infrastructure (CAFE standards, advertising conventions, consumer vocabulary) has crystallized around it.

What it means: Two mechanisms, both existing: format-as-objectivity (the MPG number performs linear comparability — "30 MPG vs 20 MPG, fifty percent better" — for a relationship that is nonlinear; the format of distance-per-volume produces intuitive, larger numbers that obscure the hyperbolic distortion; the consumer reads the number as a proportional measure of savings when it is an inverse measure whose proportions are systematically misleading; see also #330 mAh where charge is presented as energy through a format that produces larger numbers, #317 megapixels where a sensor count is presented as image quality through a format that produces impressive figures) + convention-as-nature (the American MPG convention is experienced as the natural way to express fuel economy, but it is one of two possible orientations — distance/volume or volume/distance — and the choice of orientation determines whether the scale is linear or hyperbolic with respect to actual cost; Europe chose volume/distance and eliminated the illusion; the US retained distance/volume and embedded it in regulation (CAFE), consumer education (EPA labels), and daily language ("I get thirty"); the convention is not a measurement choice but a perceptual choice — it determines what pattern the consumer sees in the numbers; see also #326 alcohol proof where different national conventions produce different numbers for the same liquid, #329 paper sizes where different national standards produce different defaults for the same function). The MPG illusion is a case where the format does not merely simplify — it systematically reverses the consumer's intuition about where savings are largest. The format is not neutral. It has a direction, and the direction is wrong. First automotive fuel economy / transport metrology entry.

Source: Larrick, Richard P. & Soll, Jack B. / "The MPG Illusion," Science 320(5883): 1593-1594 (2008). EPA / 40 CFR Part 600 — Fuel Economy and Greenhouse Gas Exhaust Emissions of Motor Vehicles. National Academy of Sciences / Assessment of Fuel Economy Technologies for Light-Duty Vehicles (2011). CAFE / 49 USC 32902 (Corporate Average Fuel Economy standards).

Object: Fahrenheit and Celsius temperature scales (#332)

Assumed channel: Temperature is measured in degrees. In the United States, 32°F is freezing, 212°F is boiling. The consumer reads a property of the weather. The number is how hot or cold things are.

Actual channel: Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit (Amsterdam, 1724) anchored his mercury thermometer to three reference points: 0°F = freezing point of saturated ammonium chloride brine (the coldest reproducible temperature in his workshop), 32°F = water freezing, 96°F = body temperature (chosen for easy scale subdivision — 96 = 2⁵ × 3). The boiling point of water (212°F) was a derived consequence, not a designed landmark. Anders Celsius (Uppsala, 1742) proposed an inverted scale: 0 = boiling, 100 = freezing. Linnaeus or Christin (1743) reversed it to the modern convention. Celsius anchors to water's two phase transitions, separated by 100 degrees — transparent, intuitive. Fahrenheit's anchors are opaque to the consumer: 32 for freezing is a consequence of choosing brine as zero; 0 is a laboratory condition no consumer encounters. The US (with Bahamas, Belize, Cayman Islands, Palau — ~331M of 8B people) uses Fahrenheit. The conversion (°F = °C × 9/5 + 32) involves fraction and offset, making mental calculation impractical. The scales intersect at -40°. One Fahrenheit degree = 5/9 of a Celsius degree, giving finer integer resolution for weather (70-71°F = 0.56°C difference; Celsius needs decimals: 21.1-21.7°C). The "98.6°F" body temperature is a conversion artifact — Wunderlich measured 37°C, which converts to 98.6°F through the fraction, creating false precision (#123).

What it means: convention-as-nature (each scale experienced as the temperature of things, not as a calibration choice; see also #329, #326, #315) + format-as-objectivity ("32°F" looks as inevitable as "0°C" but is a consequence of brine calibration; see also #123, #325). First thermometry / temperature standards entry.

Source: Fahrenheit / Phil Trans R Soc 33: 78-84 (1724). Celsius / Kungl Sv Vet Handl 3: 171-180 (1742). Middleton / A History of the Thermometer, Johns Hopkins (1966). Chang / Inventing Temperature, OUP (2004).

Object: Tire size designation and the P-metric system (#333)

Assumed channel: A tire labeled "P225/45R17 91V" encodes the tire's physical dimensions and performance capabilities. The consumer reads a technical specification — width, profile, rim size, load, speed — stated with engineering precision.

Actual channel: The designation is a palimpsest of four incompatible eras of measurement, frozen into a hybrid format by industrial competition. Width (225) is in millimeters because European manufacturers — led by Michelin, which patented the radial tire on June 4, 1946 — developed radial tires using metric dimensions. Rim diameter (17) is in inches because U.S. DOT regulations and the Tire and Rim Association (founded 1903 as the Clincher Tire Manufacturers' Association) had standardized rim sizes in inches and the infrastructure could not convert. Aspect ratio (45) is a dimensionless percentage — the sidewall height as a fraction of width — which was invisible until the 1960s because all tires had ratios near 90-100% and the property went unnamed. "R" means radial construction. The P-Metric system was introduced by TRA in 1976; ETRTO (est. 1964) developed the parallel Euro-Metric system. "91V" — load index and speed rating — encodes a lookup table (91 = 1,356 lbs) and an alphabetic speed code developed in 1960s Europe after Autobahn fatalities, where H sits out of alphabetical order "to maintain continuity with established practices" and X was excluded because Michelin already used "X" as a brand name. The UMTRI study (Sivak & Schoettle, 2017) found consumers treat the designation as an opaque code to match when replacing tires — they read the numbers without reading what the numbers mean. Earlier systems used inches throughout (30×3 high-pressure era, 4.50-21 balloon era, G78-15 alpha-numeric era). The modern format presents unified engineering specification; it delivers a negotiated settlement between American and European industrial standards, mixing two unit systems, a percentage, two letter codes, and two lookup tables in a single line.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (engineering notation performs technical authority while concealing the politically contingent origins of the hybrid format; see also #327, #315, #318) + convention-as-nature (the mixed metric/imperial format experienced as "how tires are specified" rather than as a frozen compromise between competing standards bodies; see also #329, #332, #326). First automotive metrology / tire standards entry.

Source: Michelin / FR patent 919,543 (1946). TRA P-Metric introduction (1976). ETRTO Data Book (first ed. 1969). Sivak & Schoettle / UMTRI Report SWT-2017-17 (2017). UNECE ECE Regulation No. 30 (1975). ISO 4000-1:2024.

Object: Wi-Fi generation naming and the 802.11 letter sequence (#334)

Assumed channel: A router labeled "Wi-Fi 6" tells the consumer which generation of wireless technology they are buying. The number communicates a technological step — newer generation, faster speed, better performance. The label reads as straightforward as a version number.

Actual channel: The Wi-Fi Alliance (originally WECA, founded 1999 by 3Com, Aironet/Cisco, Intersil, Lucent, Nokia, Symbol Technologies) introduced generational naming on October 3, 2018, led by CEO Edgar Figueroa. Before that date, consumers navigated an opaque letter sequence — 802.11a, b, g, n, ac, ax, be — whose apparent randomness reflects that consumer-relevant PHY amendments (speed improvements) are scattered among 20+ non-consumer-facing amendments (security, QoS, roaming, mesh) in a single sequential IEEE letter series. The letters skip l (looks like 1), o (looks like 0), q (confused with 802.1Q), and x (used as informal wildcard). 802.11b deployed before 802.11a despite simultaneous ratification (September 16, 1999) because 2.4 GHz DSSS chipsets were cheaper to manufacture than 5 GHz OFDM — the letter "a" came first in the alphabet but last to market. The generational numbers erase massive variance within each generation: "Wi-Fi 6" on a $50 router (2×2, dual-band) and "Wi-Fi 6" on a $1,200 enterprise AP (8×8, tri-band, 160 MHz channels) share a label while sharing almost nothing operationally. Theoretical speeds (Wi-Fi 5: "up to 1,300 Mbps") run 50-85% above real-world throughput (~200-400 Mbps). Marketing aggregate numbers (AC1750, AX5400) sum bands no single device uses simultaneously. The name "Wi-Fi" itself is meaningless — Phil Belanger (founding board member) confirmed it is not an acronym; the tagline "The Standard for Wireless Fidelity" was invented post-hoc by board members uncomfortable with a brand name that meant nothing, then dropped when professional marketers joined. The Alliance started at Wi-Fi 4 (=802.11n), skipping 1-3, partly because "WiFi3" was trademarked by Edgewater Wireless and partly to avoid the ambiguity of whether 802.11a or 802.11b deserved to be "1."

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the generation integer performs technological equivalence across devices with radically different capabilities; the aggregate marketing number performs speed no single device achieves; see also #319, #317, #327) + convention-as-nature (consumers experience "Wi-Fi" as meaning "Wireless Fidelity" and the generation numbers as meaningful progression when both are branding decisions retroactively performing technical authority; see also #326, #332). First wireless networking / telecommunications standards entry.

Source: Wi-Fi Alliance press release (Oct 3, 2018). Belanger / Boing Boing (2005). Salcedo et al. / Applied Mathematical Sciences (2017, 802.11n throughput). Sivak & Schoettle / UMTRI SWT-2017-17 (2017, cf. #333). UNECE ECE Regulation 30. IEEE 802.11 working group records.

Object: Egg size classification and USDA grading (#335)

Assumed channel: A carton labeled "Large Grade A" communicates that the eggs inside are large and high quality. "Large" means big. "Grade A" means good. The consumer reads a property of the eggs.

Actual channel: "Large" and "Grade A" are independent classification systems measuring different properties. Size is determined by minimum net weight per dozen — not per egg. A "Large" carton must weigh at least 24 ounces per dozen (established in 7 CFR Part 56, formally codified June 8, 1967, 32 FR 8232). Individual eggs within a Large carton can vary by up to half an ounce while the carton still meets the standard. Grade is determined by candling — holding eggs against a light source to assess interior quality: air cell depth (≤3/16" for Grade A, indicating freshness via moisture loss through porous shell), albumen clarity, yolk centering, and absence of blood/meat spots. Grade AA (≤1/8" air cell) exists above A, and Grade B (≤3/8", blood spots <1/8" permitted) below. "Large" is the middle of six sizes — Jumbo (30 oz/doz), Extra Large (27), Large (24), Medium (21), Small (18), Peewee (15) — but functions as the default because American recipes standardize on Large eggs (one Large egg ≈ 50g without shell). The word "Large" performs above-average when it denotes the midpoint. Consumers rarely encounter Medium or Small at retail; Jumbo and Extra Large command premiums. Brown eggs hold 62.8% market share (2025) despite no correlation with grade, size, or nutritional content — color reflects hen breed, not egg quality. Academic research confirms consumer decisions follow label cues (organic, free-range, brown) rather than the formal grading system most consumers cannot interpret.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the size word performs a property of the egg when it denotes a position on a weight scale; the grade letter performs quality assessment through a candling procedure consumers have never seen; see also #293, #322, #308) + convention-as-nature ("Large" experienced as a descriptive adjective rather than a technical classification occupying the middle of a six-point scale; brown experienced as quality rather than breed pigmentation; see also #328, #326). First poultry science / egg grading entry.

Source: USDA AMS / 7 CFR Part 56 (1967, codified). Egg Products Inspection Act / 21 USC §1031 (1970). USDA Egg Grading Manual (AMS). Federal Register 32 FR 8232 (Jun 8, 1967).

Object: USB version naming and the retroactive renaming scheme (#336)

Assumed channel: A cable or device labeled "USB 3.2" communicates a specific generation of Universal Serial Bus technology. Higher numbers mean newer, faster connections. The version number reads as a linear progression: 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 3.1, 3.2.

Actual channel: The USB Implementers Forum (USB-IF, incorporated 1995 in Portland, Ajay Bhatt of Intel credited as lead architect of the original specification) has retroactively renamed previous versions twice, making the version number unreliable as a speed indicator. USB 3.0 (November 2008, 5 Gbps "SuperSpeed") was retroactively renamed to USB 3.1 Gen 1 when USB 3.1 (July 2013, 10 Gbps "SuperSpeed+") was released — what was formerly "USB 3.0" became "USB 3.1 Gen 1" and the new 10 Gbps speed became "USB 3.1 Gen 2." Then both were renamed again when USB 3.2 (September 2017, ratified) was released: USB 3.0 became USB 3.2 Gen 1 (5 Gbps), USB 3.1 became USB 3.2 Gen 2 (10 Gbps), and the new 20 Gbps speed became USB 3.2 Gen 2×2. A device labeled "USB 3.2" could run at 5, 10, or 20 Gbps — a 4× range under one version number. In 2022, the USB-IF introduced yet another naming scheme: USB 5Gbps, USB 10Gbps, USB 20Gbps, USB 40Gbps (USB4) — finally using speed in the name. Meanwhile, connector type (Type-A, Type-B, Mini, Micro, Type-C) is independent of protocol version — a USB Type-C cable can carry USB 2.0 (480 Mbps) through USB4 (40 Gbps). The physical connector does not disclose the protocol. The version number does not disclose the speed. The consumer's only reliable information is on the packaging (if present), not the cable or port.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the version number performs linear technological progression while concealing retroactive renaming that makes the number meaningless as a speed indicator; "USB 3.2" is three different speeds; see also #334, #319, #317) + convention-as-nature (consumers experience version numbers as inherently forward-progressing, making retroactive renaming invisible — a device that was "USB 3.0" yesterday is "USB 3.2 Gen 1" today with no change to the hardware; see also #334, #332). First computer interface standards / connectivity metrology entry.

Source: USB-IF / USB 3.0 specification (Nov 2008). USB-IF / USB 3.1 specification (Jul 2013). USB-IF / USB 3.2 specification (Sep 2017). USB-IF / USB4 specification (2019). USB-IF naming convention update (2022).

Object: Mattress firmness scale and the absence of standards (#337)

Assumed channel: A mattress labeled "Medium Firm" or rated "6.5 out of 10" communicates a standardized measure of how hard or soft the sleep surface is. The consumer reads a property of the mattress, comparable across brands. "Medium Firm" means the same thing everywhere.

Actual channel: No regulatory body — not ASTM, ISO, CPSC, or FTC — defines mattress firmness categories. There is no standard for what "Medium," "Firm," or "Plush" means. Indentation Load Deflection (ILD, measured per ASTM D3574) quantifies foam hardness as the force in pounds required to compress a foam sample 25% of its thickness using a 50-square-inch circular indenter. An ILD of 25-31 is commonly called "medium" by manufacturers — but the translation from ILD to marketing word varies by brand. A "medium" from one manufacturer can correspond to a "firm" from another. The 1-10 firmness scale used by review sites (Sleepopolis, Mattress Clarity, Sleep Foundation) is subjective — each reviewer establishes their own reference points, and no cross-calibration exists between sites. The mattress-in-a-box revolution (Casper, founded 2014; Tuft & Needle, 2012; Purple, 2016) reduced consumer choice to one or two firmness options per brand, making the firmness word the primary differentiator despite its having no standardized referent. CertiPUR-US (Alliance for Flexible Polyurethane Foam, est. 2008) certifies foam composition (VOCs, formaldehyde, heavy metals) but does not certify firmness. Body weight, sleeping position, and personal preference alter subjective firmness experience of the same ILD rating by several scale points. The word performs standardization in an industry that has none.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the 1-10 scale and the firmness words perform standardized measurement in the absence of any standard; see also #308, #322, #293) + convention-as-nature (consumers experience "Medium Firm" as a property of the mattress rather than a manufacturer's unregulated marketing claim; see also #335, #326, #328). First consumer products / sleep industry metrology entry.

Source: ASTM D3574 (Standard Test Methods for Flexible Cellular Materials — Slab, Bonded, and Molded Urethane Foams). CertiPUR-US certification standards (2008). FTC enforcement actions on mattress labeling (16 CFR Part 260 — Guides for Environmental Marketing Claims, applied to foam certifications but not firmness).

Object: Diamond grading and the 4 Cs system (#338)

Assumed channel: A diamond graded "F color, VS2 clarity, 1.02 carats, Excellent cut" has been objectively measured by four independent criteria. The consumer reads properties of the stone. The four letters and numbers communicate quality with scientific precision.

Actual channel: The Gemological Institute of America (GIA, founded 1931 by Robert M. Shipley in Los Angeles) created the 4 Cs — Cut, Color, Clarity, Carat — and the grading scales now used globally. The D-to-Z color scale starts at D because previous informal systems (AA, A, B, C; I, II, III; Roman numerals) had degraded through inconsistent use. GIA chose D to signal a clean break. The scale measures absence of yellow body color: D is "colorless," Z is "light." But "fancy colored" diamonds — vivid yellows, pinks, blues — are graded on a separate scale where more color equals more value. The same property (body color) reverses its valuation at a threshold the consumer never sees. Clarity is assessed at 10× magnification using a loupe — a standard chosen by convention, not by physics. An inclusion invisible at 10× but visible at 20× does not affect the grade. What counts as a flaw is determined by the instrument's magnification, not by the flaw's existence. GIA defines eleven clarity grades (FL, IF, VVS1, VVS2, VS1, VS2, SI1, SI2, I1, I2, I3), each requiring judgment about inclusion type, position, number, and relief — subjective assessments despite the grading vocabulary performing objectivity. Carat (from the carob seed, standardized at 200 mg in 1907 by the Fourth General Conference on Weights and Measures) is weight, not size — a well-cut 0.90 ct diamond can appear larger than a poorly-cut 1.00 ct. The consumer reads carat as size. Same stone, resubmitted to GIA, has received different grades — reproducibility is imperfect, though GIA does not publish its internal consistency rates. Rapaport price list (Martin Rapaport, 1978) publishes wholesale prices per carat by color and clarity — a grid that creates price cliffs at grade boundaries (e.g., G vs. H color, SI1 vs. SI2) where the visual difference is imperceptible but the price difference is substantial.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the letter-grade system performs scientific measurement through vocabulary — D, VS2, Excellent — while concealing the subjective judgment inherent in each assessment; see also #308, #293, #335) + dimensional-truncation (four properties compressed to four symbols; the consumer reads each symbol as a fact about the stone, not as a judgment call within a convention; see also #327, #317, #320). First gemology / luxury goods metrology entry.

Source: GIA / Liddicoat & Crowningshield (1957, color grading system). Fourth General Conference on Weights and Measures (1907, metric carat). Rapaport Diamond Report (1978). Yarnell / C&EN 82(5): 26-31 (2004, diamond grading controversies).

Object: Gasoline pricing and the 9/10-cent fraction (#339)

Assumed channel: The gas station sign says $3.49⁹⁄₁₀. The consumer reads $3.49. The superscripted fraction — nine-tenths of a cent — is a formatting convention, visible but unprocessed. The price is $3.49.

Actual channel: The price is $3.499 per gallon — effectively $3.50. The 9/10-cent fraction originated in the 1930s when gasoline cost approximately 10-18 cents per gallon and the federal excise tax was 1 cent per gallon. At those prices, 9/10 of a cent represented roughly 1% of the total price — a meaningful competitive differentiator. Stations could undercut competitors by a fraction of a cent rather than a full cent. The Iowa State Tax Commission and other state revenue authorities levied fuel taxes in fractional cents (e.g., 1.5¢/gallon), making fractional pricing necessary for tax pass-through. As gasoline prices rose from cents to dollars, the fraction's competitive significance collapsed. At $3.50/gallon, 9/10 of a cent is 0.026% of the price — commercially meaningless. But the convention persists because it is universal: every station uses it, and unilaterally dropping it would make a station's posted price appear 1 cent higher than competitors. The fraction is a Nash equilibrium — no individual station benefits from changing, so no station changes. Consumers process $3.49⁹⁄₁₀ as $3.49, not $3.50 — the left-digit anchoring effect documented by Thomas & Morwitz (Marketing Science, 2005) applies to gasoline pricing, where the dollar figure and first digit dominate perception. The fraction exists in a perceptual blind spot: too small to read, too universal to remove, too precise to feel like marketing. Twenty gallons at $3.499 costs $69.98. Twenty gallons at $3.50 costs $70.00. The difference is two cents. The format performs twenty cents.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the fraction performs price precision while functioning as a perceptual exploitation — left-digit anchoring makes $3.49⁹⁄₁₀ read as $3.49 rather than $3.50; see also #331, #319, #317) + convention-as-nature (the fraction experienced as "how gas is priced" rather than as a 1930s competitive tactic frozen into universal practice by Nash equilibrium; see also #332, #326, #329). First petroleum retail / consumer pricing psychology entry.

Source: Thomas & Morwitz / Marketing Science 24(1): 4-14 (2005, left-digit effect). Iowa State Tax Commission (1930s, fractional fuel tax levies). Anderson / Atlantic (2014, history of gasoline pricing).

Object: Hotel star ratings and the absence of a global standard (#340)

Assumed channel: A "5-star hotel" is the best category of hotel worldwide. Stars communicate a standardized quality level — one star is basic, five is luxury. The consumer reads a universal grading system. Stars mean the same thing everywhere.

Actual channel: No global standard for hotel star ratings exists. The World Tourism Organization (UNWTO, est. 1975, Madrid) proposed harmonization but never achieved it. Different countries use different systems administered by different bodies: France uses a government-regulated 1-5 star system (Atout France, reformed 2009, 246 criteria across 3 categories); Germany uses the German Hotel and Restaurant Association (DEHOGA/Hotelstars Union, shared with 17 European countries, 270 criteria, voluntary); the UK uses AA (Automobile Association, est. 1908, independent assessment) and VisitBritain ratings (1-5 stars); the United States has no federal system — AAA uses diamonds (1-5, inspectors visit anonymously), Forbes Travel Guide (formerly Mobil Travel Guide, est. 1958, uses stars, only awards 4- and 5-star). In many countries — including large tourism markets in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa — hotels self-assign stars with no external verification. A "5-star hotel" in Dubai and a "5-star hotel" in Paris are evaluated by different organizations using different criteria with different cultural expectations. Online platforms (Booking.com, Expedia, Google) display stars on hotel listings but the source varies — sometimes from national classification, sometimes self-reported, sometimes inferred from amenity checklists. The consumer sees five stars and reads universality. The stars are local classifications presented in a format that performs global comparability.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (stars perform standardized quality assessment in the absence of a global standard; the same visual symbol — ★★★★★ — means different things in different countries but looks identical to the consumer; see also #337, #308, #293) + convention-as-nature (the consumer experiences "5-star" as a property of the hotel rather than as a classification assigned by a specific national body using criteria the consumer has never seen; see also #335, #338, #322). First hospitality industry / tourism classification entry.

Source: UNWTO (2015, hotel classification study). Atout France (2009 reform, Arrêté du 23 décembre 2009). Forbes Travel Guide (est. 1958 as Mobil Guide). AAA Diamond ratings (current criteria). DEHOGA / Hotelstars Union (17-country voluntary system).

Object: Lumber nominal sizing and the 2×4 that measures 1½″×3½″ (#341)

Assumed channel: A "2×4" is a piece of wood that measures 2 inches by 4 inches. The name is the dimension. When a builder or homeowner buys a 2×4 at a lumber yard, they are purchasing a board whose cross-section is two inches by four inches. The number on the label is the measurement of the object.

Actual channel: A standard 2×4 measures 1½ inches by 3½ inches — half an inch less in each dimension than the name states. This is not an error or a rounding. It is the consequence of a process — rough-sawing, kiln-drying, and planing — that has been standardized into a naming convention that retains the pre-process dimensions as the product's identity. The rough-sawn board starts at approximately 2″×4″. Kiln-drying from green (~30% moisture) to working moisture (6-12%) causes tangential shrinkage of 6-12% and radial shrinkage of 3-5%, removing approximately ¼ inch per dimension. Planing (surfacing to smooth faces) removes another ¼ inch per dimension. The result is 1½″×3½″. The first national lumber size standard was the American Lumber Standard of 1924, published by the Central Committee on Lumber Standards under the U.S. Department of Commerce. Successive revisions (1926, 1928, 1939, 1953) adjusted tolerances. In 1941, the National Lumber Manufacturers Association entered a consent decree with the U.S. District Court requiring creation of an impartial oversight agency — the American Lumber Standard Committee (ALSC, recognized 1953). The current dimensions were formally standardized in 1964 under what is now Voluntary Product Standard PS 20 (NIST/Department of Commerce). The standard applies to all softwood lumber sold in the United States. The naming convention is legal: PS 20 distinguishes "nominal" from "actual" dimensions and permits the nominal designation as the trade name. Lowe's settled a California class-action lawsuit in 2014 (five county district attorneys, $1.5 million in penalties) over labeling practices, but the court in a parallel Home Depot case (Northern District of Illinois, 2017) held that "2×4" is understood as nominal and is not misleading. Rough-sawn lumber — unplaned, unsurfaced — retains its full nominal dimensions: a rough 4×6 is actually 4″×6″. The divergence is entirely a product of the finishing process, but the name performs the pre-process state while the board embodies the post-process state. Metric lumber systems (European standard EN 336) exhibit parallel divergence: 47×100 mm dressed from 50×100 mm sawn.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the nominal dimension performs measurement — "2×4" reads as a specification — while describing a pre-process state the consumer never encounters; the number on the label is the dimension of a board that no longer exists; see also #327, #322, #320) + convention-as-nature (the consumer experiences "2×4" as a property of the wood rather than as a naming convention preserved from the rough-sawn era through industry standardization, consent decree, and voluntary product standard; see also #329, #326, #333). First construction materials / lumber standards entry.

Source: ALSC / American Lumber Standard Committee (est. 1953). NIST PS 20 (American Softwood Lumber Standard, current revision 2021). U.S. Department of Commerce / Central Committee on Lumber Standards (1924, first standard). Lowe's labeling settlement (California, 2014). Home Depot dismissal (N.D. Ill., 2017).

Object: American Wire Gauge and the inverted numbering of conductor size (#342)

Assumed channel: A wire's gauge number indicates its size. A higher gauge number means a bigger, thicker wire — the way a higher number means more of something in virtually every other consumer context. When an electrician or homeowner selects wire for a circuit, the gauge number communicates capacity.

Actual channel: The American Wire Gauge system is inverted: higher numbers mean thinner wire. A 22 AWG wire (0.025 inches diameter) is far thinner than a 10 AWG wire (0.102 inches diameter). The inversion originates from the manufacturing process. Wire was produced by drawing a thick copper rod through progressively smaller dies — hardened tools with precisely sized holes. Each pass through a die reduced the wire's diameter. The gauge number tracked the number of drawing operations: more draws meant thinner wire, hence a higher number. The system was formalized in 1857 by J.R. Brown and Lucien Sharpe of Providence, Rhode Island, at the request of the Association of Brass Wire and Sheet Manufacturers. It is also called the Brown & Sharpe (B&S) gauge. The mathematical structure is a geometric progression: the ratio between 0000 AWG (0.460 inches) and 36 AWG (0.005 inches) spans 39 steps with a constant multiplier of 92^(1/39) ≈ 1.1229 between successive gauges. Every 3 gauge steps doubles the cross-sectional area. Every 10 gauge steps multiplies the area by approximately 10. The formula is d_n = 0.005 × 92^((36−n)/39). The National Electrical Code (NEC §310.15) maps gauge to maximum amperage: 14 AWG for 15A circuits, 12 AWG for 20A, 10 AWG for 30A — using the gauge the consumer cannot intuitively read to specify the safety threshold the consumer must not exceed. The metric alternative (IEC 60228) specifies wire by cross-sectional area in mm² — larger numbers mean thicker wire, no inversion, no confusion. Sheet metal gauge uses the same inverted principle but with different actual thicknesses per gauge number depending on material (steel vs aluminum vs copper). The current standard is ASTM B258-18. For wires larger than 0000 AWG, the industry abandoned gauge numbers entirely and switched to circular mils — acknowledging that extending the inverted system further would be unworkable.

What it means: convention-as-nature (the consumer encounters gauge numbers as properties of the wire rather than as artifacts of an 1857 manufacturing process; the inversion — higher number = thinner wire — violates the intuitive expectation that bigger numbers mean bigger things; see also #341, #333, #329) + format-as-objectivity (the gauge number performs measurement while encoding a manufacturing step count that has been obsolete for over a century; modern wire is not drawn through numbered dies, but the numbering persists; see also #336, #327, #322). First electrical engineering / conductor standards entry.

Source: J.R. Brown & Lucien Sharpe (Providence, RI, 1857). ASTM B258-18 (Standard Specification for AWG Sizes). NEC §310.15(B)(16) (ampacity tables). IEC 60228 (metric conductor sizing). Association of Brass Wire and Sheet Manufacturers (1857, standardization request).

Object: Insulation R-value and the thermal resistance that describes the material, not the wall (#343)

Assumed channel: The R-value printed on a bag of insulation — R-13, R-19, R-30 — measures how well the insulation resists heat flow. A higher number means better insulation. An R-19 wall is insulated to R-19. The number on the bag is the number of the wall.

Actual channel: R-value (ft²·°F·h/BTU) measures the thermal resistance of the insulation material alone, tested under idealized laboratory conditions (ASTM C518, heat flux meter apparatus at 75°F mean temperature). The number describes a sample between two plates in a lab. It does not describe a wall. When R-13 fiberglass batts are installed in a 2×4 wood-framed wall (16 inches on center), thermal bridging through the studs — wood at R-1.25 per inch versus fiberglass at R-3.3 per inch — reduces the whole-wall R-value to approximately R-6 to R-10. The labeled R-13 becomes an effective R-10 or less because heat preferentially flows through the lower-resistance path (the studs). Upgrading from R-13 to R-19 in a 2×6 wall adds approximately R-1.1 of effective whole-wall performance, not R-6, because the additional insulation only improves the cavity path while the stud path remains unchanged. Everett C. Shuman at Penn State's Building Research Institute proposed R-value in 1945 as an intuitive consumer metric — higher is better, and values are additive in series. The FTC promulgated the R-value Rule (16 CFR Part 460) on August 29, 1979, effective September 30, 1980, requiring standardized labeling. The FTC has fined companies for false R-value claims — $350,000 against Thermalkool (2013) for "R-100 paint" claims, $104,257 against Northwestern Ohio Foam for overstating R-value by 600%. Closed-cell foam insulation (polyisocyanurate, XPS) experiences thermal drift: blowing agents escape over time and are replaced by air, permanently reducing R-value. The LTTR (Long-Term Thermal Resistance) methodology, developed by Oak Ridge National Laboratory and industry groups in the late 1990s, addresses this by requiring aged R-value reporting. Europe uses U-value (W/m²·K) — the reciprocal of R-value — where lower numbers mean less heat loss. U-value describes what crosses the barrier. R-value describes what doesn't. The format choice determines whether the consumer reads resistance or loss.
