What it means: format-as-objectivity (the number on the bag performs whole-wall thermal performance while measuring only cavity material in lab conditions; the consumer reads R-19 and believes the wall is R-19; see also #341, #330, #327) + dimensional-truncation (a three-dimensional wall system — studs, cavities, sheathing, cladding, air films, fasteners — is reduced to a single number derived from one component tested in isolation; see also #323, #308, #317). First building science / thermal insulation metrology entry.

Source: Shuman / Penn State Building Research Institute (1945, R-value concept). FTC 16 CFR Part 460 (1979/1980, R-value Rule). ASTM C518-23 (heat flux meter). ORNL/TM-2012/583 (closed-cell foam thermal drift). FTC v. Thermalkool (2013, $350,000). Energy Vanguard (four types of R-value).

Object: EnergyGuide label and the annual energy cost on household appliances (#344)

Assumed channel: The yellow EnergyGuide label on a refrigerator, dishwasher, or air conditioner displays the appliance's estimated annual energy cost in dollars and its estimated annual electricity consumption in kilowatt-hours. The number tells the consumer what the appliance will cost to run. The consumer compares labels and chooses the cheaper appliance.

Actual channel: The EnergyGuide label was mandated by the Energy Policy and Conservation Act of 1975 (EPCA, Pub. L. 94-163) and implemented by the Federal Trade Commission under 16 CFR Part 305 (Appliance Labeling Rule, effective 1980). The annual cost estimate is derived from a Department of Energy test procedure (10 CFR Part 430) that measures energy consumption under standardized laboratory conditions. Refrigerators are tested in a controlled room at 90°F ambient temperature with doors opened a prescribed number of times. Dishwashers are tested with a standardized soil load and water temperature. The test procedure captures a specific usage scenario — one the consumer may or may not replicate. A family of six opening the refrigerator thirty times a day consumes more energy than the DOE's test protocol assumes. The electricity price used to calculate the annual cost is a national average published annually by DOE — currently approximately $0.16/kWh — which bears no relation to the consumer's actual utility rate (ranging from $0.10 in Louisiana to $0.40+ in Hawaii). The dollar figure on the label is the product of a standardized test and a national average price applied to a hypothetical consumer in a hypothetical home. The label's comparison scale — a horizontal bar showing where the model falls relative to similar models — compares the appliance to others tested under the same artificial conditions. The comparison is internally consistent. Its relationship to the consumer's kitchen is not. Energy Star certification (EPA/DOE, est. 1992) adds a binary yes/no above the continuous EnergyGuide scale, creating a threshold effect where appliances just above and just below the cutoff may differ by less than the test procedure's margin of error. The label is revised periodically — the scale's range is updated when the most and least efficient models in a category change — so the same appliance's position on the bar can shift without any change to the appliance itself.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the dollar figure performs a consumer-specific prediction — "this will cost you $67 per year" — using a national average electricity rate and a laboratory usage scenario that describes no actual consumer; see also #343, #331, #330) + population-as-individual (a national average price and a standardized test protocol are presented as an individual consumer's expected experience; see also #305, #306, #324). First consumer appliance regulation / energy labeling entry.

Source: Energy Policy and Conservation Act (1975, Pub. L. 94-163). FTC 16 CFR Part 305 (Appliance Labeling Rule, 1980). DOE 10 CFR Part 430 (test procedures). EPA/DOE Energy Star (est. 1992). EIA average retail electricity prices (annual).

Object: Typographic point size and the measurement of text (#345)

Assumed channel: A font set at "12 point" produces text of a specific physical size. Twelve-point text is the same size regardless of the font. The number measures the height of the letters on the page or screen. A 72-point headline is exactly one inch tall.

Actual channel: The typographic point originated with Pierre Simon Fournier (Modèles des caractères de l'imprimerie, Paris, 1737), who proposed a standardized unit for type bodies. François-Ambroise Didot refined it circa 1783, defining the Didot point as 1/72 of the French royal inch (pouce du roi) — approximately 0.376 mm. The American point, standardized by the United States Type Founders Association in 1886 at a conference in Niagara Falls, defined the point as 0.013837 inches — approximately 0.3514 mm, intentionally close to but not identical to the Didot point. Nelson Hawks proposed this value by averaging existing foundry picas. In 1985, Apple and Adobe adopted the PostScript point: exactly 1/72 of an inch (0.3528 mm), slightly larger than the American foundry point, chosen for computational convenience in digital typesetting. Three "points" coexist: Didot (European, approximately 0.376 mm), American foundry (0.3514 mm), and PostScript (0.3528 mm). The point does not measure the height of the letters — it measures the body: the metal block on which the letter was cast in the era of movable type. The body includes internal leading (space above and below the character). Different fonts at the same point size produce letters of visibly different heights because the proportion of the body occupied by the letter varies by typeface design. Twelve-point Times New Roman and 12-point Garamond produce letters of different apparent sizes. The x-height (the height of lowercase letters without ascenders or descenders) varies from roughly 40% to 70% of the body size across common typefaces. The consumer selecting "12 pt" in a word processor is selecting a body size from the era of metal type, rendered in a digital approximation of a standard that approximated an earlier standard, applied to a typeface whose internal proportions the point system does not control.

What it means: convention-as-nature (the consumer experiences "12 point" as a measurement of letter size rather than as a body-size convention inherited from metal typecasting; the point is the block, not the letter; see also #341, #342, #329) + format-as-objectivity (the number performs precision — "12 pt" sounds exact — while different typefaces at the same point size produce visibly different letter heights; see also #337, #340, #322). First typography / print metrology entry.

Source: Fournier (Modèles des caractères, Paris, 1737). Didot (c. 1783, French royal inch). USTFA / Nelson Hawks (Niagara Falls, 1886, American point). Adobe / PostScript Language Reference (1985, 1/72 inch). Bringhurst (The Elements of Typographic Style, 4th ed., 2012).

Object: The cooking cup and the three volumes called "one cup" (#346)

Assumed channel: A recipe says "one cup of flour." The cook measures one cup. The amount is standardized — a cup is a cup. The word "cup" names a specific volume the way "inch" names a specific length. Recipes written in cups are portable: the same recipe produces the same result in any kitchen.

Actual channel: Three volumes are called "one cup." The US customary cup is 236.588 mL (8 US fluid ounces), defined by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST Handbook 44). The metric cup, used in Australia, New Zealand, and increasingly in international recipes, is 250 mL. The imperial cup, used in pre-1970s British and Canadian recipes, is 284.131 mL (10 imperial fluid ounces). The ratio between the smallest (US) and the largest (imperial) is approximately 1:1.20 — a 20% difference named by the same word. A recipe calling for "2 cups of liquid" produces 473 mL in a US kitchen and 568 mL in an imperial kitchen. The difference — 95 mL, nearly half a US cup — can alter the outcome of baked goods, where hydration ratios are critical. The US fluid ounce (29.5735 mL) and the imperial fluid ounce (28.4131 mL) are themselves different volumes — the same word, two definitions. Eight US fluid ounces and ten imperial fluid ounces both equal "one cup" in their respective systems, but the imperial ounce is smaller, so ten of them yield a larger cup. The word "cup" performs universality. The volumes underneath it diverge by 20%. The metric system offers milliliters — a single, unambiguous unit — but US recipes resist metrication for the same infrastructural reason Fahrenheit persists: the measuring cups, the cookbooks, the generational memory are all calibrated to the US customary cup. The measuring cup in the kitchen drawer is the infrastructure.

What it means: convention-as-nature (the cook experiences "one cup" as a natural fact about volume rather than as one of three competing definitions inherited from different national metrology traditions; see also #332, #329, #326) + format-as-objectivity (the word "cup" performs a single, standardized volume while naming three different quantities; the format — a common English word — makes the plurality invisible; see also #341, #345, #340). First culinary metrology / recipe measurement entry.

Source: NIST Handbook 44 (US customary units). Weights and Measures Act 1985 (UK, imperial units). Australian National Measurement Regulations (1999, metric cup = 250 mL).

Object: Paint coverage rate on consumer paint cans (#347)

Assumed channel: The label on a gallon of paint says "covers approximately 400 sq ft per gallon." The number tells the consumer how much wall area one gallon will cover. Dividing the room's square footage by 400 gives the number of gallons needed. The number is the plan.

Actual channel: The stated coverage rate is measured under ideal laboratory conditions: a smooth, primed, sealed surface of uniform color, applied at the manufacturer's recommended thickness (typically 4 mils wet, 1.5-2 mils dry for latex) using a standardized roller. ASTM D5150 (Standard Test Method for Hiding Power of Architectural Paints) measures hiding power — the paint's ability to obscure the substrate — using a contrast ratio over black and white substrates. Coverage is derived from this: the spread rate at which the paint achieves acceptable hiding. But hiding power and coverage rate are not the same measurement — hiding describes opacity, coverage describes area. The label conflates them into a single number. Actual coverage depends on surface texture (smooth drywall = more coverage; textured stucco = less, potentially 50% less), porosity (bare wood or unprimed drywall absorbs paint, reducing effective coverage by 25-40%), color change (painting over a dark color with a light one may require 2-3 coats, effectively halving or thirding the stated rate), application method (brush vs roller vs sprayer, each depositing different thicknesses), and the paint's own formulation (higher solids content = better coverage; economy paints with lower solids cover less per gallon). A gallon rated at "400 sq ft" covering a textured, unprimed surface over a dark color in a single coat may actually cover 150-200 sq ft. The consumer who buys two gallons for an 800 sq ft room may need four. The label's number is the coverage under conditions the consumer's wall will almost never replicate.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the coverage number performs a consumer-specific prediction — "you need this many gallons" — while measuring a laboratory condition; see also #343, #344, #330) + population-as-individual (the single stated coverage rate is a best-case scenario presented as a typical outcome, the way the EnergyGuide label presents a national average as an individual prediction; see also #306, #305). First architectural coatings / paint standards entry.

Source: ASTM D5150 (hiding power test). ASTM D344 (relative hiding power). Sherwin-Williams / Benjamin Moore / PPG technical data sheets (manufacturer-specific coverage claims). PDCA (Painting and Decorating Contractors of America, coverage guidelines).

Object: NPK fertilizer analysis on consumer fertilizer bags (#348)

Assumed channel: A bag of fertilizer displays three numbers separated by hyphens — 10-10-10, 5-10-5, 46-0-0. The numbers represent the percentages of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium in the product. A 50-pound bag of 10-10-10 contains 5 pounds of nitrogen, 5 pounds of phosphorus, and 5 pounds of potassium. The rest is filler. The three numbers are the recipe.

Actual channel: The three numbers do not measure the same thing. The first number (N) is the percentage of elemental nitrogen by weight — straightforward. The second number (P) is not the percentage of phosphorus. It is the percentage of phosphorus pentoxide (P₂O₅), an oxide form that phosphorus does not exist as in the bag. To convert to elemental phosphorus, multiply by 0.4364. A "10" in the P position means 4.4% actual phosphorus. The third number (K) is not the percentage of potassium. It is the percentage of potassium oxide (K₂O), another oxide form that potassium does not exist as in the product. To convert to elemental potassium, multiply by 0.8302. A "10" in the K position means 8.3% actual potassium. The convention dates to early-nineteenth-century analytical chemistry, when Justus von Liebig and others analyzed fertilizers by igniting samples and weighing the oxide residues — the oxide form was the form the laboratory could measure. AOAC (Association of Official Analytical Chemists, now AOAC International) standardized this convention, and US federal law (administered through AAPFCO — Association of American Plant Food Control Officials) requires the guaranteed analysis to be expressed in the oxide form for P and K. The consumer reads three parallel numbers and assumes three parallel measurements. One measures an element. Two measure oxides of elements. The label presents uniformity. The chemistry behind the label is not uniform. A 10-10-10 fertilizer contains 10% nitrogen, 4.4% phosphorus, and 8.3% potassium. The three "tens" are not equal. Canada, Australia, and some European countries have adopted or recommended elemental reporting, but the US system persists because the regulatory framework — state fertilizer laws, AAPFCO model rules, AOAC methods — is calibrated to the oxide convention. The format survived the chemistry that created it.

What it means: convention-as-nature (the oxide reporting convention, born from nineteenth-century gravimetric analysis, persists as the "natural" way to express nutrient content despite being an artifact of a superseded laboratory method; see also #318, #341, #342) + format-as-objectivity (the three-number format — N-P₂O₅-K₂O — performs a parallel structure that implies parallel measurement, concealing that one number is elemental and two are oxides; see also #320, #345, #347). First agricultural chemistry / fertilizer regulation entry.

Source: Liebig, Chemistry in its Application to Agriculture and Physiology (1840). AOAC Official Methods of Analysis (fertilizer analysis). AAPFCO Official Publication (model fertilizer bill, guaranteed analysis requirements). Havlin et al., Soil Fertility and Fertilizers (8th ed., 2013). IFA (International Fertilizer Association) reporting standards.

Object: MERV rating on residential HVAC air filters (#349)

Assumed channel: A furnace filter has a MERV rating — MERV 8, MERV 11, MERV 13. Higher numbers mean better filtration. The consumer selects the highest MERV rating available, reasoning that the filter that catches the most particles protects the household the most. The number is the quality.

Actual channel: MERV (Minimum Efficiency Reporting Value) was established by ASHRAE Standard 52.2-1999 (updated 2007, 2017). The test measures a filter's ability to capture particles in three size ranges: E1 (0.3-1.0 µm), E2 (1.0-3.0 µm), and E3 (3.0-10.0 µm). The MERV rating is determined by the worst-performing size range — the minimum efficiency. A MERV 8 filter captures less than 20% of E1 particles, 70% or more of E3 particles, and is classified by its poorest performance. But the consumer reads "MERV 8" as a single quality number, not a composite minimum. The higher-is-better logic encourages purchasing MERV 13 or higher, but residential HVAC systems are designed for a specific pressure drop range. A MERV 13 filter restricts airflow significantly more than a MERV 8. If the blower motor cannot compensate — and most residential systems cannot — the reduced airflow causes the evaporator coil to freeze (in cooling mode), the heat exchanger to overheat (in heating mode), and overall system efficiency to drop. The filter catches more particles and damages the system that moves the air. The consumer who installs a MERV 13 filter in a system designed for MERV 8 gets better filtration and worse air circulation — meaning some rooms receive less filtered air overall, because the volume of air being filtered has decreased. The MERV rating measures the filter. The consumer needs to measure the system. The rating is a property of the media. The outcome is a property of the interaction between the media and the blower. The label reports the filter's capability. The ductwork determines the filter's effect.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the single MERV number performs a quality assessment — higher = better — while measuring minimum efficiency across particle size ranges, concealing that the "better" filter may reduce system performance; see also #347, #344, #343) + dimensional-truncation (the MERV rating collapses a multi-dimensional performance profile — three particle size ranges, pressure drop, loading capacity, system compatibility — into a single ordinal number; see also #320, #317, #237). First HVAC engineering / indoor air quality entry.

Source: ASHRAE Standard 52.2-1999 (Method of Testing General Ventilation Air-Cleaning Devices for Removal Efficiency by Particle Size). ASHRAE Standard 52.2-2017 (revised, added Appendix J for fine particle performance). EPA guidance on residential air filtration. ACCA (Air Conditioning Contractors of America) Manual D (ductwork design and pressure drop).

Object: Smoke detector labeling and the ionization/photoelectric distinction (#350)

Assumed channel: A device labeled "smoke detector" detects smoke. The consumer installs it, and when smoke is present, the alarm sounds. The label — "smoke detector" or "smoke alarm" — is a binary promise: smoke present, alarm sounds. The consumer's model is simple: the device detects smoke.

Actual channel: Two fundamentally different detection technologies are sold under the single label "smoke detector." Ionization detectors contain a small amount of americium-241, which ionizes the air in a sensing chamber, creating a steady current between two electrodes. When smoke particles enter the chamber, they attach to the ions, reducing the current, and the alarm triggers. These detectors respond quickly to fast-flaming fires (paper, grease) that produce small, light particles. Photoelectric detectors use a light source and a photosensor arranged so that the light does not normally hit the sensor. When smoke particles enter the chamber, they scatter the light onto the sensor, triggering the alarm. These detectors respond quickly to slow-smoldering fires (upholstery, electrical wiring) that produce large, visible smoke particles. The two types have dramatically different response times to different fire types. In NIST and UL tests, ionization detectors can be 15 to 50 minutes faster than photoelectric detectors for flaming fires. Photoelectric detectors can be 15 to 50 minutes faster than ionization detectors for smoldering fires. The majority of residential fire deaths occur in smoldering fires (NFPA data: 60-70% of home fire deaths involve fires where the victim was asleep and the fire smoldered before spreading). The most commonly sold consumer smoke detectors are ionization type, which are cheaper to manufacture ($5-10 retail vs $15-25 for photoelectric). The consumer who buys a "smoke detector" at the hardware store overwhelmingly gets the type that is slower to respond to the type of fire most likely to kill a sleeping occupant. The label "smoke detector" performs universality — it detects smoke — while the technology inside responds to one particle size range faster than another. The label does not distinguish because the consumer does not ask. The consumer's question is binary: "Does it detect smoke?" The answer is yes. The question the consumer should ask — "Which kind of smoke?" — does not fit the binary format of the label.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the label "smoke detector" performs universal smoke detection while naming a technology-specific, particle-size-dependent response; see also #349, #347, #343) + dimensional-truncation (the binary label — smoke detector / not smoke detector — collapses the multi-dimensional detection profile of particle size, fire type, response time into a single categorical claim; see also #349, #317, #237). 350th entry milestone. First fire safety / life safety systems entry.

Source: NIST Technical Note 1455-1 (Performance of Home Smoke Alarms). UL 217 (Standard for Smoke Alarms). NFPA 72 (National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code). Bukowski et al., Performance of Home Smoke Alarms: Analysis of the Response of Several Available Technologies (NIST, 2007). IAFC (International Association of Fire Chiefs) position statements on photoelectric smoke alarms.

Object: Laundry detergent load count on consumer bottles (#351)

Assumed channel: A bottle of laundry detergent says "64 loads." The consumer divides the price by 64 and gets a cost per load. Lower cost per load means better value. The load count is the comparison tool. The number is the value.

Actual channel: The "64 loads" claim is calculated by dividing the total volume of detergent by the recommended dose for a "medium" or "regular" load in a "standard" washing machine using "average" soil level. But the recommended dose itself varies by manufacturer, and the definition of a "load" is not standardized. The FTC requires that load claims be based on the manufacturer's recommended usage, but the manufacturer sets its own recommended usage. A manufacturer that recommends a smaller dose per load can claim more loads per bottle. The consumer comparing a "64-load" bottle to a "32-load" bottle may be comparing different recommended doses, not different amounts of detergent. Furthermore, modern HE (high-efficiency) washing machines use less water and require less detergent — typically half the dose of a standard top-loader. A bottle that claims "64 loads" for a standard machine may yield 128 loads in an HE machine, but the label's count is based on the standard dose. Most consumers overdose: Consumer Reports and detergent manufacturers' own studies consistently find that consumers use 2× to 4× the recommended amount, often filling the cap to the top rather than to the measurement line. The cap design contributes — the fill line is small, hard to read, and sits inside a dark cap, while the cap itself is much larger than the recommended dose. A "64-load" bottle used at the consumer's actual dosing rate may last 16-32 loads. The load count on the label measures the bottle divided by the recommendation. The consumer's actual load count is the bottle divided by the consumer's pour. These are different numbers, and the label reports neither the consumer's pour nor the consumer's actual load count. It reports the manufacturer's arithmetic.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the load count performs a consumer-specific prediction — "this bottle will last you 64 loads" — while calculating from a manufacturer-defined dose that few consumers actually use; see also #347, #344, #330) + population-as-individual (a single load count derived from one dosing scenario is presented as the universal load count for all machines, soil levels, and water hardness conditions; see also #347, #306, #305). First consumer product dosing / household chemistry entry.

Source: FTC Green Guides (16 CFR Part 260, environmental marketing claims). Consumer Reports (2010, 2015 detergent dosing studies). Procter & Gamble, Henkel, Church & Dwight product labels and dosing guidelines. ASTM D4265 (Standard Guide for Evaluating Stain Removal Performance in Home Laundering).

Object: Paper towel roll equivalence claims on consumer packaging (#352)

Assumed channel: A package of paper towels says "6 Double Rolls = 12 Regular Rolls." The consumer reads this as getting twice the product — the double roll is two regular rolls in one. More rolls would take up more space. The packaging solves this by making each roll larger. The number of "regular roll equivalents" is the value claim.

Actual channel: The "regular roll" in the equivalence claim is the manufacturer's own internal reference — not an industry standard, not a regulatory definition, not a fixed quantity. Each manufacturer defines its own "regular roll" differently: Bounty's regular roll contains approximately 40 sheets; Brawny's contains approximately 60; store brands vary from 50 to 80. The "double roll = 2 regular rolls" means the double roll contains twice as many sheets as that manufacturer's regular roll. But the double roll of one brand may contain fewer sheets than the regular roll of another brand. Furthermore, manufacturers have introduced "Big," "Huge," "Mega," and "Super Mega" designations — each defined as a multiple of the manufacturer's own regular roll. A Bounty "Super Mega" roll claims to equal 5 regular rolls, meaning 5 × 40 = 200 sheets. A Brawny "Pick-a-Size XL" roll with 130 sheets claims to be a "double roll." The equivalence language proliferates because no external standard constrains it. The FTC has not defined "regular roll." There is no ASTM standard for paper towel roll size. The consumer comparing a "6 Double Rolls = 12 Regular Rolls" package to a "4 Mega Rolls = 10 Regular Rolls" package is comparing two manufacturers' internal arithmetic, neither of which references the other. The sheet itself is not standardized: select-a-size sheets are smaller than full sheets, so a roll with 150 select-a-size sheets may contain less total paper area than a roll with 80 full-size sheets. The comparison unit — the roll — is a cylinder, not a quantity. The equivalence claim performs unit conversion without a fixed unit.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the equivalence claim "6 = 12" performs a mathematical conversion that implies a fixed reference unit, while the reference unit is manufacturer-defined and non-standardized; see also #351, #347, #330) + convention-as-nature (the word "regular" performs a natural baseline — the standard roll, the normal amount — while naming a manufacturer's marketing decision; see also #348, #341, #342). First consumer paper products / packaging standards entry.

Source: FTC packaging and labeling guidance. Procter & Gamble (Bounty), Georgia-Pacific (Brawny), Kimberly-Clark (Viva) product labels and sheet count specifications. Consumer Reports (2018, paper towel roll size comparison). NIST Handbook 130 (Uniform Packaging and Labeling Regulation).

Object: Water hardness classification and measurement scales (#353)

Assumed channel: Water has a "hardness" level — a physical property, like temperature or pH, that can be measured and expressed as a number. A water utility report says 210 ppm. A water softener salesman says 12.3 grains per gallon. These are different units for the same measurement. Hard water leaves scale deposits and doesn't lather soap well. The number tells you how hard your water is.

Actual channel: "Hardness" is not a physical property of water. It is a behavioral property of water when it encounters soap. Thomas Clark, a Scottish chemist, patented the soap test for water hardness in 1841: add a standard soap solution to a water sample until the lather persists for five minutes. The more soap required, the harder the water. The word "hardness" entered water chemistry through soap — not through mineralogy, not through physics, but through the difficulty of getting clean. Clark also devised a scale: one degree of hardness equaled one grain of chalk held in solution per Imperial gallon (4.546 liters), approximately 14.254 ppm. The measurement was later rationalized by chemistry. "Hardness" is now defined as the total concentration of divalent cations — primarily calcium (Ca²⁺) and magnesium (Mg²⁺) — expressed as the equivalent concentration of calcium carbonate (CaCO₃). But the water may contain no calcium carbonate at all. The hardness may come from magnesium sulfate, calcium chloride, or other dissolved salts. "210 ppm as CaCO₃" means the mineral content has the same effect as if 210 mg of calcium carbonate were dissolved in each liter — but the actual dissolved minerals may be different in species, proportion, and behavior. The CaCO₃ equivalent is a translation into a reference compound, not a description of what's in the water. Multiple scales coexist: the Clark degree (1 grain per Imperial gallon = 14.254 ppm), the French degree (10 mg/L CaCO₃ = 10 ppm), the German degree (10 mg/L CaO ≈ 17.848 ppm as CaCO₃ — measured in calcium oxide, not carbonate, adding a chemical conversion within the unit conversion), the grain per gallon (1 grain per US gallon = 17.118 ppm — a different gallon, producing a 20% discrepancy from the Clark degree), and mg/L as CaCO₃ (the municipal standard). The USGS classifies water as soft (0-60 mg/L), moderately hard (61-120), hard (121-180), or very hard (>180). The water softener industry uses grains per gallon with lower thresholds — classifying water as "hard" at levels the USGS would call "moderately hard." The single number also conceals two chemically distinct categories: temporary hardness (calcium and magnesium bicarbonates, removable by boiling — the source of kettle scale) and permanent hardness (sulfates and chlorides, requiring ion exchange or reverse osmosis). The utility report does not distinguish between them. The WHO publishes no guideline value for hardness; Catling et al. (2008) found possible cardiovascular benefit from hard water, particularly the magnesium component. Ion-exchange water softeners replace Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ with Na⁺ — removing minerals the body may benefit from while adding sodium. The consumer is sold a solution to a soap problem framed as a water quality problem, treating a number that was originally defined by how difficult it was to produce lather.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (a single number — gpg, ppm, or degrees — performs comprehensive water quality assessment while collapsing mineral species, temporary/permanent chemistry, health implications, and soap-era origins into one scalar; see also #351, #349, #347) + convention-as-nature (the word "hardness" and the CaCO₃ equivalent reporting convention normalize a soap-lathering measurement from 1841 as an intrinsic property of water; the water is "hard" because soap doesn't work, not because the water has changed; see also #348, #341, #342). First water chemistry / consumer water quality entry.

Source: Clark, On the Examination of Water, for Towns, &c. (1841, patent and soap-test methodology). USGS Water-Supply Paper 1473 (hardness classification). AWWA, Water Quality & Treatment (6th ed., 2011). Catling et al., "A Systematic Review of Analytical Observational Studies Investigating the Association Between Cardiovascular Disease and Drinking Water Hardness" (J Water Health, 2008). WHO, Hardness in Drinking-water: Background Document for Development of WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality (2011).

Object: Motor oil viscosity grade and SAE J300 classification (#354)

Assumed channel: Motor oil has a viscosity grade — 5W-30, 10W-40 — printed large on the bottle. The W stands for "weight." Lower first numbers mean thinner, lighter oil; higher second numbers mean thicker, heavier oil. The owner's manual specifies a grade. The consumer matches the grade. The number is the specification.

Actual channel: The Society of Automotive Engineers created the J300 viscosity classification in 1911 with five numbered grades (SAE 10, 20, 30, 40, 50). The numbers were grades — bins into which oils fell depending on viscosity range — not measurements. By 1933, the W grades appeared, designating oils tested at sub-zero temperatures for cold-weather engine starting. The W stands for Winter, not Weight — a misreading that has persisted for ninety years because "weight" fits the consumer's intuition (thin = light weight, thick = heavy weight) better than the fact (winter = cold test, non-W = hot test). The two numbers in a multigrade designation like "5W-30" are not a range. They are two separate tests at two separate temperatures: the 5W means the oil passes the Cold Cranking Simulator (ASTM D5293) at minus thirty degrees Celsius; the 30 means its kinematic viscosity at one hundred degrees Celsius (ASTM D445) falls between 9.3 and 12.5 centistokes. That range — 34 percent — is the width of a single grade. Two oils can both be SAE 30 while differing by a third in actual viscosity. Multigrade oils were enabled in the 1940s-50s by viscosity index improvers (VII) — long-chain polymer additives that coil tightly when cold and expand when hot, allowing a thin base oil to behave like a thicker oil at operating temperature. The number 30 is not what the oil is; it is what the oil becomes through polymer engineering. But those polymers can break under sustained shear stress inside bearings and cam followers. An oil that enters the engine as 5W-30 can shear down to 5W-20 over the course of an oil change interval — the grade on the bottle describing the oil's virgin state, not its aged state. HTHS viscosity (High Temperature High Shear, ASTM D4683, 150°C at one million reciprocal seconds) was added to SAE J300 to capture this dimension, but HTHS does not appear on the consumer bottle. Behind the grade sits the API service category — SP, SN, SM, SL — the actual performance specification governing wear protection, deposit control, oxidation resistance, and emissions compatibility. A 5W-30 meeting only API SJ is a fundamentally different product from a 5W-30 meeting API SP, despite the identical grade. The grade is printed large. The API category is printed small. The consumer who matches by grade has matched a viscosity bin to the shelf. The consumer who matches by category has matched chemistry to the engine. Font size on the bottle is proportional to consumer attention and inversely proportional to engineering significance.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the alphanumeric string "5W-30" performs a specification while naming two temperature-specific grade bins, each covering a range, neither describing behavior at the intermediate temperatures where most driving occurs; see also #353, #351, #349) + convention-as-nature (the SAE grade system, designed for single-grade classification in 1911 and adapted for multigrade in the 1950s, persists as the primary consumer identifier despite the performance specification having migrated to API service categories and OEM-specific requirements; see also #348, #341, #342). First automotive lubrication / tribology entry.

Source: SAE J300 (Engine Oil Viscosity Classification, current revision 2021). SAE International history (founded 1905). ASTM D5293 (Cold Cranking Simulator), ASTM D445 (kinematic viscosity), ASTM D4683 (HTHS viscosity). API 1509 (Engine Oil Licensing and Certification System, current edition). Mortier et al., Chemistry and Technology of Lubricants (3rd ed., Springer, 2010).

Object: FDA serving size and Reference Amount Customarily Consumed (RACC) (#355)

Assumed channel: A food label says "Serving Size: 2/3 cup." This is the recommended portion — how much the consumer should eat. The nutrition information below it — 230 calories, 12g fat, 28g sugar — describes what the consumer will ingest per serving. The serving size is a portion guide.

Actual channel: The serving size on a nutrition label is not a recommendation. It is a backward-looking survey statistic. The Nutrition Labeling and Education Act (NLEA) of 1990 required standardized serving sizes. The FDA implemented this in 1993 by establishing Reference Amounts Customarily Consumed (RACCs) for approximately 150 food categories, based on the USDA's Nationwide Food Consumption Surveys from 1977-78 and 1987-88. The RACC for ice cream was set at 1/2 cup, the RACC for beverages at 8 fluid ounces, the RACC for bagels at 55 grams — amounts that reflected what Americans reported eating per occasion in the late 1970s and 1980s. The RACC was designed to standardize comparison, not to guide consumption: so that two ice cream brands could be compared per equal portion. But on the label, in the format of the Nutrition Facts panel, "Serving Size" reads as instruction. The format converts a survey result into a dietary norm. The consumer does not think "this is what Americans reported eating in 1977." The consumer thinks "this is what I should eat." Meanwhile, portions grew. A bagel in 1977 weighed 55 grams; by 2000, the average bakery bagel weighed 100-110 grams. A 20-ounce bottle of soda — designed, sold, and consumed as a single product — was labeled as 2.5 servings. The per-serving calories looked moderate. The per-container calories required multiplication. In 2016, the FDA updated RACCs using 2003-2008 NHANES data (effective 2020): ice cream moved to 2/3 cup, beverages to 12 fluid ounces. The rule also required single-serving labeling for packages "reasonably consumed at one eating occasion" and dual-column labels showing both per-serving and per-package values. But the structural issue persists: the serving size is a comparison tool that the consumer reads as a consumption guide. The word "serving" means one thing in ordinary language (what someone puts on a plate) and another in regulatory language (a statistical artifact from survey data, converted to a household measure, assigned to a category). The gap between these meanings is where the format does its work.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the serving size — a household measure derived from decades-old survey data — performs neutral portioning while shaping the per-serving nutritional values that consumers use for comparison and dietary planning; see also #354, #351, #344) + context-migration (the RACC was designed for label-to-label comparison but migrated to a consumption recommendation through the visual grammar of the Nutrition Facts panel; see also #304, #313, #321). First food labeling regulation / nutrition communication entry.

Source: NLEA (Pub. L. 101-535, Nov. 8, 1990). 21 CFR 101.12 (Reference Amounts Customarily Consumed). FDA Final Rule, 81 FR 33742 (May 27, 2016, serving size updates). USDA Nationwide Food Consumption Survey (1977-78, 1987-88). NHANES (2003-2008 consumption data). Young & Nestle, "The Contribution of Expanding Portion Sizes to the US Obesity Epidemic" (Am J Public Health, 2002).

Object: Television refresh rate and proprietary motion rate marketing (#356)

Assumed channel: A television's refresh rate is printed on the price tag — Motion Rate 240, TruMotion 240, MotionFlow XR 960. Higher numbers mean smoother motion. A 960 television is four times smoother than a 240 television. The number is hertz — cycles per second — a physical measurement of display performance.

Actual channel: The native refresh rate of a television panel is the number of times per second the liquid crystal pixels physically change state. Consumer LCD panels are either 60Hz or 120Hz. There are no 240Hz, 480Hz, or 960Hz consumer television panels. The numbers on the price tag are proprietary composites. Samsung uses "Motion Rate," typically doubling the native rate: Motion Rate 240 = native 120Hz. LG uses "TruMotion" with similar doubling: TruMotion 240 = native 120Hz. Sony uses "MotionFlow XR" with up to eight-times multiplication: MotionFlow XR 960 = native 120Hz. Vizio uses "Effective Refresh Rate" at double the native rate. These composites are assembled from real processing techniques: frame interpolation (motion estimation/motion compensation, generating synthetic frames between originals — the soap opera effect that filmmakers ask viewers to disable), backlight scanning (briefly turning off the backlight between frames to reduce persistence blur — no new image data, but some manufacturers count each dark interval as a "refresh event"), and proprietary image processing. A "240 Hz effective" number may represent 120 image refreshes plus 120 darkness intervals. Half the count is darkness. The content bottleneck makes most of these numbers academic: film is 24 fps (since the late 1920s), broadcast TV is 30 fps, most streaming is 24-30 fps. A 120Hz panel displaying 24 fps content repeats each frame five times. The panel's capability exceeds the content's frame rate by a factor of five. Gaming via HDMI 2.1 (4K at 120 fps) is essentially the only current consumer use case where native 120Hz delivers content at matching speed. The native refresh rate — the one specification describing the panel's physical capability — appears in the technical specifications. The marketing composite is printed on the price tag.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the proprietary number — 240, 480, 960 — performs a hertz measurement while naming a composite of native refresh, backlight manipulation, frame interpolation, and processing algorithms; the consumer reads hertz and receives marketing arithmetic; see also #354, #353, #351) + convention-as-nature (the unit "Hz" implies physical cycles per second; proprietary terms like "Motion Rate" and "MotionFlow XR" appropriate the physical unit while redefining what counts as a cycle to include darkness intervals and synthetic frames; see also #336, #334, #327). First consumer display technology / motion processing entry.

Source: RTINGS.com, "Fake Refresh Rates: Samsung Clear Motion Rate vs Sony Motionflow vs LG TruMotion" (comprehensive comparison of marketing vs native rates). VESA DisplayHDR and HDMI 2.1 specifications. Tom's Guide, "The Best TV Refresh Rate Is 120Hz (and Anything Higher Is a Lie)." Samsung, LG, Sony, Vizio product specification sheets.

Object: Tire pressure — sidewall maximum versus vehicle placard recommendation (#357)

Assumed channel: The tire says "Max Press 44 PSI." The driver inflates to 44 or near it. Higher pressure means firmer tires, better fuel economy, and safer driving. The number on the tire is the correct pressure for the tire.

Actual channel: Two numbers govern tire inflation, printed in two locations by two manufacturers. The sidewall number (e.g., "Max Press 44 PSI") is the tire manufacturer's maximum cold inflation pressure — the highest pressure the casing can safely contain at its rated load capacity, a structural limit defined by the tire's materials and construction. The door jamb placard (e.g., "32 PSI") is the vehicle manufacturer's recommendation — the pressure that balances handling, traction, ride comfort, tread wear, and fuel economy for that specific vehicle's weight, suspension, and center of gravity. The tire does not know what vehicle it is mounted on. The vehicle manufacturer specifies the pressure for the vehicle, not the tire. Overinflation to the sidewall maximum (a common consumer behavior) reduces the contact patch — the tire crowns, pressing tread center into pavement and lifting shoulders — decreasing wet traction, accelerating center wear, and reducing impact absorption. The consumer who inflates to the maximum perceived it as the optimum. The TPMS (Tire Pressure Monitoring System), mandated by the TREAD Act of 2000 and required on all US vehicles since 2007, warns the driver when any tire drops 25% below the placard pressure. If the placard says 32 PSI, TPMS activates at 24. A tire at 26 PSI — significantly underinflated for handling and tire life — triggers no warning. The system was calibrated for catastrophic loss (the Firestone/Explorer failures killed 271 people), not gradual degradation. Temperature adds a variable the placard does not address: tire pressure changes approximately 1 PSI per 10°F. A tire at 32 PSI in 70°F October reads 28 in 30°F December — a drop that can trigger TPMS without any leak. The placard specifies "cold" inflation (ambient temperature, before driving), but the consumer typically checks tires after driving to a gas station, where friction heating has already added 2-4 PSI. The measurement conditions are violated by the act of reaching the measurement location.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (two authoritative numbers — 44 on the tire, 32 on the door — perform pressure recommendations while naming different things: a structural maximum and a vehicle-specific optimum; the consumer reads the tire's number because it's on the tire, the way a patient reads the medication bottle, not the prescription; see also #356, #354, #349) + convention-as-nature (the sidewall number is read as the tire's "correct" pressure because it is physically printed on the tire, as if the tire knows what pressure it should be at; the location performs authority the number's meaning does not support; see also #333, #341, #342). First automotive safety / tire inflation metrology entry.

Source: TREAD Act (Transportation Recall Enhancement, Accountability, and Documentation Act, Pub. L. 106-414, Nov. 1, 2000). FMVSS 138 (Tire Pressure Monitoring Systems). TRA (Tire and Rim Association) standards. NHTSA tire pressure guidance. Rubber Manufacturers Association consumer education materials.

Object: Percent Daily Value (%DV) and the 2,000-calorie reference on nutrition labels (#358)

Assumed channel: The nutrition label says "Sodium: 460 mg, 20% DV." This means the food provides twenty percent of the consumer's daily sodium. The percentage is personal — a fraction of what this consumer needs per day.

Actual channel: The "%DV" is a fraction of a fixed reference, not the consumer's actual need. The FDA established Daily Values in 1993 under the NLEA, based on a 2,000-calorie daily diet. Two thousand calories was a political compromise: the median caloric intake for American adults at the time was approximately 2,350. The FDA initially proposed 2,350 as the reference. The food industry lobbied for a lower number (smaller percentages look better on labels). Consumer advocacy groups pushed for ranges or demographic-specific values. The FDA settled on 2,000 — a round number below the median, unlikely to be seen as encouraging overconsumption. It is neither the average intake nor the recommended intake for any specific age, sex, weight, or activity level. Every %DV on every nutrition label is calibrated to this number. A 25-year-old male athlete eating 3,500 calories and a 65-year-old sedentary woman eating 1,600 calories both see the same "20% DV" for sodium — the athlete's actual fraction is roughly 11%, the woman's roughly 25%. The FDA considered demographic-specific DVs (separate columns for children, adult women, adult men) and rejected them for complexity — prioritizing comparability over precision. The FDA's consumer guidance adds another layer: 5% DV or less is "low," 20% or more is "high." The consumer reads 20% sodium, thinks "high," and makes a purchasing decision — having passed through three compressions: milligrams → percentage of a political number → binary judgment → action. The 2016 label update revealed the panel's population-level curation: Vitamins A and C were removed as required nutrients (deficiency no longer common in the US population), while Potassium and Vitamin D were added. The label tracks the population's nutritional gaps, not the individual's. The label says "Your Daily Value." The "your" is a statistical person eating a negotiated number of calories.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the percentage — the most personal of mathematical expressions, a fraction of a whole — performs individual dietary assessment while calculating from a fixed political reference that matches no specific consumer; see also #355, #351, #344) + population-as-individual (a single Daily Value derived from a political compromise about a statistical population is presented as "your" daily value on every label for every consumer; see also #355, #306, #305). First nutrition regulation / dietary reference communication entry.

Source: NLEA (Pub. L. 101-535, Nov. 8, 1990). 21 CFR 101.9 (Nutrition labeling of food). FDA Final Rule, 81 FR 33742 (May 27, 2016, updated DVs). Nestle & Ludwig, "Front-of-Package Food Labels: Public Health or Propaganda?" (JAMA, 2010). Willett, Nutritional Epidemiology (3rd ed., Oxford, 2012).

Object: Vacuum cleaner amperage rating as performance metric (#359)

Assumed channel: The vacuum box says "12 AMP MOTOR." Twelve amps is more powerful than ten amps. More power means better cleaning. The consumer compares the amp numbers on adjacent boxes and selects the higher one.

Actual channel: An amp is a unit of electrical current — the amount of electricity the motor draws from the wall outlet. It measures consumption, not performance. A twelve-amp motor draws 1,440 watts from a 120-volt outlet. How much of that wattage converts to useful suction depends on the motor's efficiency, which is not printed on the box. A twelve-amp motor at 60% efficiency produces 840 watts of suction work and 560 watts of waste heat. A ten-amp motor at 80% efficiency produces 960 watts of suction work and 240 watts of waste heat. The ten-amp vacuum produces more suction from less current. The consumer picks the twelve-amp vacuum because twelve is larger than ten. What actually cleans carpet is airflow (cubic feet per minute — the volume of air moved through the carpet) and suction (inches of water lift — the sealed-vacuum force that lifts carpet nap and unseats particles). Air watts — the metric combining both, calculated as (airflow × water lift) / 8.5 — is the closest single number to actual cleaning performance. ASTM F558 formalizes the measurement. None of these numbers appear on consumer packaging. Amps appears because it is a bigger number: 12 amps is a more compelling shelf comparison than 200 air watts. Dyson's cyclonic technology disrupted this by necessity — bagless cyclones drew fewer amps than conventional vacuums but maintained constant airflow, so Dyson marketed air watts rather than amperage. The industry partially followed, but amps never left the box. The consumer now encounters amps, watts, air watts, and proprietary metrics on adjacent products — incommensurable numbers that cannot be compared at the shelf because the units describe different physical quantities.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the amperage rating performs a power assessment — larger number = more powerful = better cleaning — while measuring electrical draw, not suction, airflow, filtration, or cleaning effectiveness; see also #356, #354, #318) + dimensional-truncation (the amp rating collapses motor efficiency, airflow volume, suction force, filtration quality, brush agitation, and nozzle seal into a single electrical measurement; see also #317, #327, #330). First consumer appliance marketing / vacuum cleaner metrology entry.

Source: ASTM F558 (Standard Test Method for Measuring Air Performance Characteristics of Vacuum Cleaners). IEC 60312 (international vacuum cleaner performance standard). Consumer Reports vacuum cleaner testing methodology. Dyson Ltd. marketing materials (air watts specification shift).

Object: Air conditioner BTU rating and tonnage classification (#360)

Assumed channel: The air conditioner is rated at 36,000 BTU/hr, or "3 tons." More BTUs means more cooling. A three-ton system is larger and more powerful than a two-ton system. The consumer buys the tonnage the contractor recommends.

Actual channel: A "ton" of cooling is 12,000 BTU per hour — the amount of heat required to melt a short ton (2,000 pounds) of ice at 32°F in 24 hours (288,000 BTU ÷ 24 hours = 12,000 BTU/hr). The unit descends from the ice-harvesting era, when commercial cooling meant literal blocks of ice delivered to buildings. Mechanical refrigeration inherited the metaphor. A three-ton system does not weigh three tons. It removes heat equivalent to melting three tons of ice per day. The BTU — British Thermal Unit — is itself a unit of heat (heat needed to raise one pound of water by one degree Fahrenheit) used to rate a machine that cools. The measurement is thermodynamically correct (cooling is heat removal) but experientially inverted (the consumer thinks about cold air, the rating measures heat subtracted). The rated capacity — 36,000 BTU/hr — is measured at standard test conditions: 95°F outdoor, 80°F indoor, 50% relative humidity. When outdoor temperature exceeds the test condition, capacity drops as the condenser's temperature differential narrows. A three-ton system may deliver only two and a half tons at 105°F — capacity decreasing when demand peaks. SEER (Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio) adds another averaging layer: total cooling divided by total electricity over a season (65-104°F), while EER (measured at a single 95°F condition) is typically lower. SEER 16 may correspond to EER 12 — the consumer expecting 16 BTU/Wh on the hottest day gets 12. Manual J load calculations (ACCA) determine actual cooling needs, but contractors commonly oversize by 20-50%. Oversized systems short-cycle: reaching the thermostat setpoint too quickly, shutting off before dehumidification completes. The homeowner feels clammy at 72°F, lowers the thermostat, and the oversized system runs continuously — the extra capacity making comfort worse because comfort is temperature and humidity together, not temperature alone.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the BTU rating performs cooling capacity while measured in heat units, derived from ice-melting equivalence, and tested at conditions that diverge from peak demand; SEER smooths efficiency into a seasonal average that conceals peak-day performance; see also #359, #356, #344) + convention-as-nature ("tonnage" normalizes a refrigeration-era metaphor as a natural measurement of air conditioning; the consumer accepts "3-ton AC" without connecting it to ice harvesting from frozen lakes; see also #353, #348, #341). First HVAC sizing / mechanical cooling metrology entry.

Source: ASHRAE Handbook — Fundamentals (capacity and efficiency standards). ACCA Manual J (residential load calculations). DOE 10 CFR Part 430 (test procedures for central air conditioners). AHRI Standard 210/240 (Unitary Air-conditioning and Air-source Heat Pump Equipment).

Object: Residential square footage in real estate listings (#361)

Assumed channel: The listing says "2,400 square feet." The consumer reads this as the size of the house — a single number that enables comparison, that divides into the price to yield a per-foot cost, that answers "how big" with four-digit precision.

Actual channel: The "2,400 square feet" may include or exclude: finished basement (below grade), enclosed sunporches (heated or not), bonus rooms above garages (ceiling height thresholds), attic conversions (permanent stairway required by some standards). ANSI Z765 — the American National Standard for Single-Family Residential Buildings — specifies "above-grade finished area" and excludes below-grade space regardless of finish quality. But ANSI Z765 is voluntary. Not all states require it. Not all agents or MLS databases enforce it. A listing that includes 600 square feet of finished basement in its total shows 2,400; a comparable listing following Z765 shows 1,800 for the same above-grade footprint. The "smaller" listing may have more daylit living space. Appraisers measure from exterior walls — the total includes 6-12 inches of framing, insulation, and drywall on each side that the occupant cannot use. A house with 12-inch walls loses approximately 8% of its measured area to structure. The occupant lives in ~2,200 square feet while the listing says 2,400. Four entities may measure the same house for four purposes: the county assessor (from permit records, for property tax), the appraiser (from exterior laser measurement, for mortgage lending), the real estate agent (from builder plans or prior appraisals, for listing), the contractor (from interior room-by-room measurement, for renovation). Four numbers from one house. Price per square foot — the standard comparison metric — divides total price by total area, blending above-grade with below-grade, exterior-measured with interior-lived, heated with unheated, daylit with windowless. Basement square feet are worth less per foot than main-floor feet. The blend presents heterogeneous space as a single value.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the square footage number — "2,400" — performs precise spatial quantification while concealing the composition of what's measured, the rules used to measure it, and the boundary between building envelope and occupiable space; see also #360, #359, #353) + population-as-individual (a single area number blends spaces of different utility, value, and character into one figure that the consumer compares across listings whose composition differs; see also #358, #355, #347). First real estate valuation / residential measurement entry.

Source: ANSI Z765-2021 (Square Footage — Method for Calculating). Appraisal Institute, The Appraisal of Real Estate (15th ed., 2020). FNMA Selling Guide (Fannie Mae property eligibility standards). NAR (National Association of Realtors) MLS data standards.

Object: Washing machine capacity in cubic feet (#362)

Assumed channel: The washing machine is rated at 5.0 cubic feet. This is the machine's laundry capacity — how much it can wash in one load. A larger number means more clothes per load. The consumer compares drum sizes and buys the largest.

Actual channel: The "5.0 cubic feet" is the total internal volume of the drum, measured by filling with water under DOE 10 CFR Part 430, Subpart B, Appendix J. The measurement is standardized, reproducible, and unrelated to the consumer's experience. Clothes are three-dimensional, compressible, and irregular. The manufacturer's recommended fill level for optimal cleaning — where clothes can tumble, detergent can circulate, and water can penetrate — is approximately 60 to 70 percent of drum volume. A 5.0-cubic-foot drum optimally loaded holds about 3.0 to 3.5 cubic feet of loosely placed clothes. The consumer who fills the drum to its rated capacity overpacks by approximately 40 percent. Overpacked loads cannot agitate properly — the machine delivers its worst cleaning performance at its rated capacity. No federal test measures "usable laundry capacity" — the volume or weight of clothes the machine can effectively clean. The word "capacity" on the spec sheet and the word "capacity" in the consumer's mind refer to different volumes: drum volume versus laundry volume. The gap is approximately 40 percent. European washing machines use kilogram ratings (e.g., "9 kg") measuring the weight of dry clothes the drum can wash — an input metric that describes what the consumer puts in, not what the drum contains. The American cubic-foot rating measures the container. The marketing race has pushed drum sizes from 3.5 cu ft (2010 average) to 5.0+ cu ft (2024), with Samsung, LG, and Maytag competing on the number printed on the spec sheet. The consumer compares the numbers. Larger numbers win. The usable-fill ratio has not changed.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the cubic-foot number performs laundry capacity assessment while measuring drum volume — the geometric interior of the cylinder, not the usable clothes space; the number is precise, standardized, and answers a different question than the consumer asks; see also #361, #360, #359) + dimensional-truncation (the single volume number collapses drum geometry, fill ratio, fabric type, agitation clearance, and water circulation into one scalar; see also #359, #330, #327). First laundry appliance / consumer appliance sizing entry.

Source: DOE 10 CFR Part 430, Subpart B, Appendix J (Uniform Test Method for Measuring the Energy Consumption of Automatic and Semi-Automatic Clothes Washers). IEC 60456 (international clothes-washing machine test methods, kg-based). Consumer Reports washing machine testing methodology. AHAM (Association of Home Appliance Manufacturers) product standards.

Object: Printer cartridge page yield and ISO/IEC 24711 (#363)

Assumed channel: The ink cartridge box says "200 pages." The consumer reads the number as a prediction: this cartridge will print 200 of my pages. A cartridge rated at 200 pages lasts twice as long as one rated at 100. Cost per page — price divided by yield — tells the consumer which cartridge is cheapest for their printing.

Actual channel: ISO/IEC 24711:2021 (color inkjet) and ISO/IEC 19752:2017 (monochrome laser) define "page" as one impression of a standardized test pattern covering approximately 5 percent of the printable area. Five percent is sparse — a few lines of text, a small graphic, mostly white space. The standard was designed to make cartridges comparable under controlled, repeatable conditions (23°C ± 2°C, 50% ± 10% RH, specific reference paper, five rotating test patterns from ISO/IEC 24712). It succeeds at comparison. The problem is context migration: the number moves from comparative tool to absolute prediction the moment it appears on a box in a retail aisle. A typical consumer business letter covers 12 to 15 percent of the page — roughly three times the standard's assumption. A 200-page cartridge yields approximately 70 to 100 of the consumer's pages. A full-coverage photograph at 60 to 100 percent yields 10 to 15 prints — the rated number and the actual number diverge by a factor of 13 to 20. ISO/IEC 19752 applies the same 5 percent coverage to monochrome laser cartridges: a 2,600-page rating yields perhaps 1,800 for a business user and 800 for a legal editor reviewing tracked-change manuscripts. The consumer whose printing most closely matches the test pattern is the consumer who prints least. Cost per page inherits the standard's denominator: a $25 cartridge at 200 ISO pages costs 12.5 cents per page, but at 10 percent consumer coverage (100 actual pages) costs 25 cents, and at photo coverage exceeds $1.50. The quotient presents itself as the consumer's cost while dividing a real price by an ISO yield. No prominent disclosure on the box specifies the 5 percent coverage assumption. Some manufacturers print "actual yield varies" in small type — acknowledging variability without explaining what the number approximates.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the yield number performs a prediction about the consumer's usage while measuring a standardized test condition; the number is precise, reproducible, and answers a question the consumer didn't ask; see also #362, #361, #355) + context-migration (the number was designed for inter-cartridge comparison under identical conditions but migrates to consumer prediction of cartridge lifespan and cost-per-page calculation; see also #355, #275). First printing technology / consumable yield metrology entry.

Source: ISO/IEC 24711:2021 (Determination of ink cartridge yield for colour inkjet printers and multi-function devices that contain printer components). ISO/IEC 19752:2017 (Determination of toner cartridge yield for monochromatic electrophotographic printers and multi-function devices that contain printer components). ISO/IEC 24712 (Colour test pages).

Object: Carry-on luggage sizing and the "carry-on size" label (#364)

Assumed channel: A suitcase tag says "carry-on size." This means the bag fits in the overhead bin. The consumer can board any flight with this bag and carry it on. "Carry-on size" is a standard, like "twin" or "queen" for bed dimensions — a fixed specification the entire industry agrees on.

Actual channel: No universal standard defines "carry-on size." IATA recommends 55 × 35 × 20 centimeters (approximately 21.7 × 13.8 × 7.9 inches), but no airline matches this exactly. United, American, and Delta converge on 22 × 14 × 9 inches including wheels and handles. Southwest allows 24 × 16 × 10. Spirit specifies 22 × 18 × 10 for overhead bin access (paid) and 18 × 14 × 8 for a free personal item. European carriers vary widely: Lufthansa 55 × 40 × 23 cm, British Airways 56 × 45 × 25 cm, EasyJet 45 × 36 × 20 cm, Ryanair 40 × 20 × 25 cm for the free tier. Each airline sets its own limit based on its own overhead bin dimensions, its own revenue model, and its own enforcement appetite. The luggage industry labels bags "carry-on size" when they approximately fit the most permissive major domestic carrier specification — typically the US Big Three's 22 × 14 × 9. But the industry often measures the shell excluding wheels and handles, while airlines measure including them. Wheels add approximately 2 inches of height; handle housing adds approximately 1 inch of depth. The bag sold as "carry-on size" may exceed the airline's specification by 2-3 inches. The metal sizer at the gate — a rectangular frame — is the final physical authority, but it tests a rectangular solid against an irregular, sometimes compressible object, and enforcement varies by load factor, gate agent discretion, and day of the week. No regulatory body certifies the phrase "carry-on size." No test standard defines it. The label communicates compliance with a universal specification that does not exist.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the phrase "carry-on size" performs a binary certainty — fit or unfit — while describing a probability that varies by carrier, country, fare class, enforcement mood, and load factor; see also #363, #362, #337) + convention-as-nature (the label reads as a fixed standard, like a paper size or a mattress size, when it is a marketing judgment about the most common permissive specification; see also #329, #337, #322). First air travel / luggage standards entry.

Source: IATA Cabin Baggage Guidelines. United Airlines, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Southwest Airlines, Spirit Airlines carry-on policies (airline websites). Ryanair, Lufthansa, British Airways, EasyJet cabin baggage specifications.

Object: Water heater tank capacity vs first-hour rating (#365)

Assumed channel: The water heater says "50 gallons." This means the heater provides 50 gallons of hot water. A 50-gallon heater provides 25% more hot water than a 40-gallon heater. The consumer compares tank sizes.

Actual channel: The "50 gallons" is the volume of the storage tank — how much water it contains, not how much hot water it delivers. When the consumer draws hot water, cold water enters through the dip tube at the bottom and mixes with the remaining hot water. Before the tank is half-drained, the outlet temperature drops below the bather's comfort threshold. A 50-gallon tank delivers approximately 35 gallons of usable hot water — about 70% of rated volume — before mixing degrades the output. The actual measure of consumer experience is the First-Hour Rating (FHR), defined by DOE 10 CFR Part 430, Subpart B, Appendix E: the total hot water a fully heated tank delivers in its first hour, including recovery — the heater's capacity to reheat incoming cold water during use. A 50-gallon gas water heater with a 40,000-BTU burner may deliver an FHR of 70 gallons; a 50-gallon electric heater with a standard 4,500-watt element may deliver only 58. Same tank volume, different usable output, because recovery rate differs dramatically: gas recovers 40-45 gallons per hour, electric 18-21. The consumer who switches from gas to electric at the same tank size loses more than half the recovery capacity while seeing the same "50 gallon" number. Geography compounds the gap: incoming groundwater temperature ranges from 37°F (Minnesota winter) to 77°F (Arizona summer), changing recovery rate by approximately 40% for the same heater, but the FHR is tested at a standard inlet temperature. The tank volume appears on the nameplate, in the plumber's catalog, and on the receipt. The FHR appears on the EnergyGuide label — smaller type, surrounded by annual cost estimates, on a yellow sticker the consumer often removes after installation. The number the consumer compares describes the container. The number that predicts the consumer's experience is on a removable sticker.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the tank-gallon number performs a hot-water capacity claim while measuring storage volume — the physical container, not the thermal experience; the number is prominent, permanent, and answers a question the consumer didn't ask; see also #362, #363, #360) + dimensional-truncation (the single volume number collapses recovery rate, fuel type, inlet temperature, mixing dynamics, and draw pattern into one scalar; see also #362, #359, #344). First residential plumbing / water heater sizing entry.

Source: DOE 10 CFR Part 430, Subpart B, Appendix E (Uniform Test Method for Measuring the Energy Consumption of Water Heaters). ENERGY STAR Water Heater specifications. ASHRAE Handbook — HVAC Applications, Chapter 50 (Service Water Heating).

Object: Pet food guaranteed analysis and AAFCO crude protein (#366)

Assumed channel: The dog food bag says "Crude Protein (min) 26%." The consumer reads: at least 26 percent of this food is protein — amino acids the dog can use for muscle, tissue repair, immune function. Higher crude protein means more nutritious food. Comparing two bags by crude protein percentage reveals which has more nutrition.

Actual channel: "Crude protein" is not protein. It is total nitrogen multiplied by 6.25 — the Kjeldahl method (1883), which measures nitrogen content and applies a conversion factor assuming all nitrogen derives from protein at 16% nitrogen by mass. The method counts all nitrogen sources: amino acids, but also melamine, urea, nucleic acids, and ammonia compounds. The 2007 pet food recall demonstrated the vulnerability: melamine (66.7% nitrogen by mass) from Xuzhou Anying was added to wheat gluten concentrate, raising the crude protein number without adding a single amino acid. The number rose; dogs died. "Crude" before protein, fat, and fiber denotes approximate analytical method, not colloquial meaning — crude fat includes waxes and pigments (ether extract); crude fiber captures some cellulose but misses most soluble and much insoluble fiber (total dietary fiber may be 2-3× crude fiber). The Guaranteed Analysis — required by AAFCO (Association of American Feed Control Officials) model regulations, adopted by state feed control agencies — reports these values as minimums and maximums, not specifications. A food guaranteed at 26% minimum may contain 30-35%. "Guaranteed" means floor/ceiling, not target. As-fed reporting compounds comparison problems: dry kibble at 26% crude protein / 10% moisture = ~29% dry-matter protein; wet food at 10% crude protein / 78% moisture = ~45% dry-matter protein. The wet food appears half as nutritious but is nearly twice as concentrated. No label converts to dry-matter basis. The ingredient list adds another layer: ingredients ranked by pre-processing weight, giving moisture-heavy ingredients (chicken at 70% water) first position despite contributing less dry matter than corn meal listed second.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the guaranteed analysis performs nutritional assessment through analytical chemistry — nitrogen proxies for protein, ether-extract proxies for fat, acid/alkali residue proxies for fiber — each number precise and reproducible but measuring a chemical property, not a nutritional one; see also #363, #355, #348) + proxy-as-direct-measurement (crude protein presents total nitrogen × 6.25 as protein content; the consumer reads the proxy as the property; melamine exploited the gap between proxy and referent; see also #348, #107). First pet nutrition / animal feed regulation entry.

Source: AAFCO Official Publication (Model Regulations for Pet Food and Specialty Pet Food). 21 CFR 501 (Animal Food Labeling). FDA Compliance Policy Guide Sec. 690.100 (Guaranteed Analysis). Kjeldahl (1883, Zeitschrift für analytische Chemie). FDA/USDA investigation of 2007 pet food recalls (melamine contamination).

Object: Microwave oven wattage and the input/output ambiguity (#367)

Assumed channel: The microwave box says "1100 watts." This is the cooking power — how much energy the microwave delivers to the food. More watts means faster cooking. A recipe that specifies "1100W, 3 minutes" will work correctly in this microwave.

Actual channel: Two wattages exist for every microwave oven: input power (what the magnetron draws from the wall outlet) and output power (the microwave energy actually delivered to the food). Output power is typically 60 to 65 percent of input. An "1100-watt" microwave marketed by input power cooks at approximately 700 watts. IEC 60705 defines output power measurement via a water-heating test (one liter, controlled start temperature, measured temperature rise), but no regulation mandates which wattage appears on the box. Some manufacturers label output, others input, others a nominal wattage from the magnetron's specification sheet. The consumer cannot determine which the box describes. Recipe developers typically test on output-rated microwaves, creating a systematic mismatch: the frozen dinner that specifies "1100W, 3 minutes" assumes 1100 watts reaching the food; the consumer's "1100-watt" (input) microwave delivers 700, undercooking by 30 to 40 percent. Power levels compound the gap: "Power level 5" on most microwaves does not halve the magnetron's output but cycles it on and off — full power for half the time, zero for the other half (duty cycling). Only inverter microwaves (Panasonic, 1988) actually reduce magnetron output, delivering true variable power, but the power-level display is identical. The watts-per-cubic-foot ratio — which determines how quickly a given oven heats a given volume of food — appears on no label, though it governs the consumer's experience more directly than either wattage alone.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the wattage number performs a cooking-power claim while potentially measuring electrical input — the energy drawn from the wall, not the energy delivered to the food; the number is precise, prominent, and ambiguous between three possible referents; see also #365, #362, #359) + convention-as-nature (the single number reads as a fixed property of the appliance, concealing the distinction between input, output, and nominal wattage — and the additional distinction between duty-cycled and true variable power at reduced settings; see also #359, #337). First kitchen appliance / microwave oven metrology entry.

Source: IEC 60705 (Household microwave ovens — Methods for measuring performance). DOE 10 CFR Part 430, Subpart B, Appendix I (Uniform Test Method for Measuring the Energy Consumption of Microwave Ovens). Panasonic inverter microwave technology documentation.

Object: Speaker and audio power ratings — PMPO vs RMS (#368)

Assumed channel: The speaker box says "1000W." This is the speaker's power — how loud it will play. More watts means louder, better sound. A 1000-watt speaker is ten times more powerful than a 100-watt receiver.

Actual channel: Multiple incompatible wattage measurements exist, ranging from honest to fabricated. RMS (root mean square) or continuous average power, measured per the FTC Amplifier Rule (16 CFR Part 432, 1974), represents the sustained power output across the full audio frequency range (20 Hz to 20,000 Hz) at rated distortion and impedance. Peak power is approximately 2× RMS for a sine wave. "Dynamic power" measures brief transient bursts under relaxed conditions. PMPO (Peak Music Power Output) is a theoretical instantaneous maximum — peak voltage squared divided by minimum impedance, held for a fraction of a millisecond — with no standard definition, no governing test procedure, and no regulatory enforcement. A "1000W PMPO" speaker typically delivers 25-50 watts continuous. The FTC rule requires RMS disclosure for amplifiers but does not clearly cover integrated speaker systems, Bluetooth speakers, or imported consumer electronics sold direct-to-consumer online. Impedance further inflates: the same amplifier rates 50W into 8Ω or ~80W into 4Ω — lower impedance yields a higher number. Impedance appears in specifications, not on the box. Behind all of this lies a logarithmic mismatch: perceived loudness doubles every ~10 dB, which requires 10× the power. Doubling from 50W to 100W is 3 dB — barely perceptible. The consumer compares watts linearly while the ear hears logarithmically. Marketing exploits the gap between the linear number and the logarithmic perception.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the wattage number performs a loudness/quality claim while measuring electrical capacity under conditions chosen to maximize the number; PMPO has no standard definition yet occupies the most prominent position on the box; see also #367, #359, #365) + convention-as-nature (the consumer reads watts as a linear property of loudness — twice the watts, twice as loud — when the relationship is logarithmic; the unit's apparent simplicity conceals a perceptual nonlinearity; see also #108, #359). First consumer audio / electroacoustic metrology entry.

Source: FTC Amplifier Rule, 16 CFR Part 432 (Power Output Claims for Amplifiers Utilized in Home Entertainment Products, 1974). IEC 60268-5 (Sound system equipment — Part 5: Loudspeakers). AES2-2012 (AES standard for acoustics — Methods of measuring and specifying the performance of loudspeakers).

Object: Garden hose sizing and the absent flow rate (#369)

Assumed channel: A garden hose labeled "5/8 inch, 100 feet, 6-ply, burst pressure 350 PSI" communicates the hose's capacity and quality. A 5/8-inch hose delivers more water than a 1/2-inch. A longer hose reaches farther. Higher burst pressure means a stronger hose. More plies mean more durability. These numbers predict the gardening experience.

Actual channel: Flow rate at the nozzle — the one number that predicts the consumer's experience — depends on three variables: inner diameter, hose length, and supply pressure. The label discloses the first two and omits the third. Friction loss increases with length: at 40 PSI municipal supply, a 100-foot 5/8-inch hose loses approximately 10 PSI (25% of supply pressure) to friction before water reaches the nozzle. A 100-foot 5/8-inch hose delivers approximately 14 GPM; a 50-foot 1/2-inch hose delivers approximately 12 GPM. The consumer who buys the larger diameter in the longer length gains less flow than expected because the length penalty partially offsets the diameter benefit. No label discloses GPM at rated length and supply pressure. Burst pressure (350 PSI) measures the destruction threshold — the pressure at which the hose physically ruptures. Municipal supply is 40-80 PSI. The hose operates at 10-20% of the labeled burst pressure. A hose rated at 200 PSI performs identically in residential use. The higher number wins comparison without improving experience. Ply count measures quantity of reinforcement layers, not quality — a 4-ply hose with brass couplings and quality mesh may outlast a 6-ply with plastic fittings and thinner mesh. Expandable hoses (latex or TPC inner tube, tripling in length under pressure) label the expanded length; the effective inner diameter under pressure is smaller than the cheapest conventional hose due to elastic restriction.
