What it means: format-as-objectivity (every number on the label — diameter, length, burst pressure, ply count — is accurate and none predicts the flow rate at the nozzle, which is the consumer's actual question; the label describes properties of the tube while the consumer needs a property of the water; see also #367, #365, #362) + dimensional-truncation (diameter alone cannot predict flow without length and supply pressure; the three-variable system is reduced to one displayed dimension; see also #365, #362, #359). First garden/lawn care / residential plumbing standards entry.

Source: Engineering ToolBox friction loss tables for garden hoses. ASTM D1130 (Standard Specification for Rubber and Rubber-Lined Industrial Hose). Municipal water supply pressure data (AWWA).

Object: Ceiling fan CFM rating and maximum-speed measurement (#370)

Assumed channel: The ceiling fan box says "5,200 CFM." This is the airflow the fan delivers to the room. More CFM means a cooler room. Five blades are better than three. A 52-inch fan moves more air than a 42-inch.

Actual channel: CFM (cubic feet per minute) is measured at maximum speed in a controlled test environment: specific mounting height, no obstructions, standardized conditions. The consumer runs the fan at medium (approximately 50-55% of rated CFM) or low (approximately 20-25%) because maximum speed is typically too loud for sustained use. The number on the box — the comparison metric — corresponds to the one speed the consumer rarely selects. ENERGY STAR rates fans by CFM per watt (airflow efficiency): a fan at 5,200 CFM / 60W = 87 CFM/W; a fan at 4,800 CFM / 35W = 137 CFM/W. The less powerful fan is 57% more efficient but loses the CFM comparison that drives the purchase. CFM/W appears on the ENERGY STAR label, not the store display. Blade count (five vs three) does not determine airflow — blade pitch (angle relative to horizontal) and blade area are the primary determinants. A 3-blade fan with 14° pitch may outperform a 5-blade at 10°. More blades increase drag without increasing airflow. Blade count is visible from the aisle; blade pitch requires a specification sheet. Fan-to-room sizing ratios appear in the owner's manual, not at the point of sale. Oversized fans create excessive wind-chill; undersized fans move insufficient air. The consumer attributes the result to motor quality rather than sizing mismatch. The reversible motor — counterclockwise for summer cooling, clockwise for winter warm-air redistribution — doubles the fan's seasonal utility, but the feature lives in the manual, and the manual enters the drawer before the consumer discovers it.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the CFM number performs a cooling-capacity claim while measuring maximum-speed airflow under test conditions the consumer never replicates; the number wins the comparison it was designed for rather than predicting the experience; see also #369, #367, #365) + dimensional-truncation (CFM at max speed collapses speed setting, room geometry, fan sizing, blade pitch, and mounting height into one number; the consumer's experience depends on all six; see also #369, #365, #362). First residential HVAC / ceiling fan metrology entry.

Source: ENERGY STAR Ceiling Fan specifications. DOE 10 CFR Part 430 (Ceiling fan test procedures). ANSI/AMCA Standard 230-12 (Laboratory Methods of Testing Air Circulating Fans for Rating and Certification).

Object: Swimming pool free chlorine and the FC/CYA ratio (#371)

Assumed channel: The pool test strip says "Free Chlorine: 3 ppm." The recommended range is 1-3 ppm. The pool is sanitized. The five colored pads — FC, TC, pH, alkalinity, CYA — each show "in range." The pool is safe to swim in.

Actual channel: Free chlorine alone does not determine sanitation when cyanuric acid (CYA) is present. CYA — added as stabilizer/conditioner or accumulated from trichlor/dichlor tablets — protects chlorine from UV degradation through a reversible equilibrium: hypochlorous acid (HOCl, the active sanitizer) binds with CYA to form chloroisocyanurate, releasing HOCl slowly as it is consumed. At 30 ppm CYA, approximately 3% of measured FC is in the active HOCl form at any instant. At 80 ppm CYA, the same percentage holds but the larger CYA pool binds more chlorine, reducing the effective sanitizing rate. The FC/CYA ratio determines sanitation: recommended ~0.075 (7.5%). At 3 ppm FC and 80 ppm CYA, the ratio is 0.038 — half the minimum — and the effective active chlorine is approximately 0.09 ppm. The strip says 3. The killing power is 0.09. The dominant residential sanitizer — trichlor tablets (trichloroisocyanuric acid) — adds FC and CYA simultaneously. Chlorine is consumed; CYA is not. Over a season, CYA accumulates from 30 to 80+ ppm while the owner adds more tablets to maintain FC, each tablet adding more CYA, creating a self-undermining cycle. The test strip measures five parameters on five independent pads with five independent range charts. Each passes individually. The system — which depends on the relationship between FC and CYA — fails. No consumer test strip computes the FC/CYA ratio. The fix — partial draining to dilute accumulated CYA — is prescribed by no strip, no range chart, and no product label.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (five independent test-strip pads perform comprehensive water-quality assessment while the consumer's question — is this pool safe? — depends on the ratio between two of them, which no pad addresses; each measurement passes its own test while the system fails; see also #370, #367, #365) + dimensional-truncation (free chlorine alone is presented as the sanitation metric, collapsing the CYA interaction, the FC/CYA ratio, temperature effects, and pH effects on HOCl dissociation into a single ppm number; see also #369, #362, #349). First recreational water chemistry / pool sanitation entry.

Source: CDC Model Aquatic Health Code (MAHC, 2018, cyanuric acid guidance). Ben Powell / Trouble Free Pool (FC/CYA guidelines). White (1999), Handbook of Chlorination and Alternative Disinfectants (5th ed.). APSP/PHTA pool water chemistry guidelines.

Object: Down fill power and the absent fill weight (#372)

Assumed channel: The jacket tag says "800 fill power." Higher fill power means a warmer jacket. An 800-fill jacket is warmer than a 650-fill jacket. Fill power is the measure of a down jacket's warmth.

Actual channel: Fill power measures loft — the volume of space one ounce of down occupies in a standardized cylinder test (IATA/IDFL method): a known weight of down in a graduated cylinder under a standardized compression weight. 800 means 800 cubic inches per ounce. Higher fill power means higher insulating efficiency per unit weight — the down traps more air per gram. But warmth depends on fill power multiplied by fill weight (total ounces of down in the garment). An 800-fill ultralight jacket with 3 ounces of down contains 2,400 cubic inches of loft. A 650-fill mountaineering parka with 10 ounces contains 6,500. The "inferior" fill power jacket is nearly three times warmer. Fill power appears on the tag; fill weight often appears only in technical specifications, if at all. The down-to-feather ratio (80/20, 90/10) further complicates: the fill-power rating applies to the down cluster fraction, not the blend. Feathers add weight without proportional insulation. An 80/20 blend at 800 fill and a 95/5 blend at 800 fill have different effective insulation per ounce of total fill. The deepest gap is environmental: down insulates by trapping still air. Water displaces that air. An 800-fill jacket soaked with rain or sweat insulates approximately as well as no jacket at all — loft collapses entirely. Hydrophobic treatments partially mitigate; synthetic insulations (PrimaLoft, Climashield) retain warmth when wet. Fill power assumes dry conditions, which is the condition the consumer hopes to maintain, not the condition the consumer will inevitably encounter.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (fill power performs a warmth assessment while measuring loft efficiency — one factor of a multi-factor equation; the number is precise, standardized, and provides one term where the consumer's question requires four; see also #370, #369, #367) + dimensional-truncation (the single number collapses fill weight, construction, blend ratio, and moisture conditions into one scalar that describes insulating efficiency per ounce, not total insulation per garment; see also #370, #369, #362). First outdoor apparel / insulation standards entry.

Source: IATA (International Down and Feather Testing Laboratory) fill-power test standards. IDFL (International Down and Feather Laboratory) testing protocols. EN 12130 (European standard for fill power measurement). USA Standard 2000 (American standard, 550-900+ range).

Object: Fabric denier and the thread-to-fabric gap (#373)

Assumed channel: The backpack tag says "600D nylon." Higher denier means a more durable fabric. A 1000D backpack is stronger than a 420D backpack. Denier measures how tough the material is.

Actual channel: Denier measures linear mass density — the weight in grams of 9,000 meters of a single fiber or yarn. The unit originates from the French denier, a medieval coin used to weigh silk in Lyon; one filament of raw silk weighs approximately one gram per 9,000 meters (hence 1 denier). The consumer reads denier as a durability ranking. The number measures thread thickness. Five variables determine the durability the consumer is actually shopping for: fiber type (Cordura 500D nylon outlasts standard 600D polyester by 2× in Taber abrasion testing), filament architecture (denier per filament, multifilament vs monofilament — same total denier, different fabric behavior), weave pattern (ripstop reinforces tear propagation resistance; plain weave does not — same denier, different tear strength), coating (polyurethane, silicone, DWR — zero percent of waterproofness resides in the denier number; 70D silicone-coated nylon repels water that uncoated 1000D nylon absorbs), and construction (seam type, reinforcement placement, stress distribution). Denier is not among the five. Denier is the proxy that stands for all five because it compresses to a single integer that fits on the tag. A further conflation: denier (linear density, g/9000m) ≠ GSM (areal density, g/m²). A 420D fabric with tight weave can weigh more per square meter than a 600D fabric with loose weave. Tex — the SI unit (grams per 1,000 meters) — is used in industrial contexts but not consumer-facing products, because 600 denier ≈ 67 tex, and the larger number survives in marketing.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (denier performs a durability assessment while measuring thread weight — one ingredient of the fabric the consumer is evaluating; the number is precise, standardized, and provides a ranking where the consumer's question requires five variables; see also #372, #370, #369) + dimensional-truncation (the single integer collapses fiber type, filament architecture, weave, coating, and construction into one scalar that describes thread thickness, not fabric durability; see also #372, #370, #365). First textile engineering / outdoor gear metrology entry.

Source: ASTM D1907 (standard test method for linear density of yarn). Invista/Cordura comparative testing data. ISO 2060 (textiles — yarn from packages — determination of linear density by skein method). Medieval silk trade etymology via Britannica.

Object: LED watt-equivalence and the ghost proxy (#374)

Assumed channel: The light bulb box says "60W equivalent." It replaces a 60-watt incandescent bulb. Higher watt-equivalent means brighter. Two bulbs labeled "60W equivalent" produce the same light.

Actual channel: For over a century, consumers shopped for light bulbs by wattage because incandescent technology converted electricity to light at roughly constant efficiency — more watts meant proportionally more light. Watts served as a proxy for brightness. LED technology broke that ratio: a 9-watt LED produces approximately 800 lumens, the same output as the old 60-watt incandescent. The proxy lost its referent but retained its consumer. "60W equivalent" is a transition label that translates from the dead unit (watts-as-brightness) to the living one (lumens), conceding that the correct unit hasn't arrived in consumer behavior. The FTC's 2011 Lighting Facts label (16 CFR Part 305, modeled on Nutrition Facts) places lumens at the top of a standardized back-panel, alongside energy cost, lifespan, color temperature, and actual wattage. EISA 2007 forced the technology transition by requiring minimum lumens per watt. Fifteen years later, the front of the package still carries "60W equivalent" in larger type than the lumen count, because the front sells and the back describes. The range for "60W equivalent" spans roughly 700-900 lumens across brands — a 29% spread under one label. Lumens per watt (the efficiency ratio) appears nowhere on any consumer label. A cheap 9W LED at 78 lm/W and a quality 9W LED at 100 lm/W carry the same watt-equivalent claim, same wattage, and the 20% efficiency gap is invisible in every number on the package. The consumer who learned to compare by watts, then by lumens, still cannot compare by efficiency without performing a division the label declines to perform.

What it means: format-as-objectivity ("60W equivalent" performs a brightness specification while providing a range-bound translation from a defunct proxy; the front label speaks the consumer's dead language while the back panel speaks the engineer's living one; two communication regimes on one package; see also #373, #372, #367) + convention-as-nature (the watt persists as brightness unit because a century of consumer behavior outlasts a decade of labeling reform; the ghost of a technology-specific proxy haunts the replacement technology's packaging; EISA 2007 changed the technology but not the purchasing vocabulary; see also #367, #364, #356). First consumer lighting / illumination metrology entry.

Source: FTC 16 CFR Part 305 (Lighting Facts label, 2011). EISA 2007 (Energy Independence and Security Act, Pub. L. 110-140). DOE Lighting Facts educational guidance. IES (Illuminating Engineering Society) lumen measurement standards.

Object: Air purifier CADR and the chamber-to-room gap (#375)

Assumed channel: The air purifier box says "CADR: Smoke 200, Dust 180, Pollen 220." Higher CADR means better air cleaning. A CADR 200 purifier cleans the air twice as well as a CADR 100 purifier. The numbers measure how well the purifier will clean the air in the room.

Actual channel: CADR — Clean Air Delivery Rate — is defined by AHAM AC-1 (ANSI/AHAM AC-1-2015). The number is cubic feet per minute of air in a 1,008-cubic-foot sealed test chamber from which particles of a specified size distribution have been removed, over and above the natural particle settling rate. Three separate CADR values are measured for three particle size ranges: smoke (0.09-1.0 μm), dust (0.5-3.0 μm), and pollen (5-11 μm). The measurement is at maximum fan speed. The consumer's room may be 2,500-5,000 cubic feet — two to five times the test volume. AHAM recommends choosing a purifier whose smoke CADR is at least two-thirds the room's floor area in square feet, but this sizing calculation appears nowhere on the box. Gas-phase pollutants — formaldehyde (off-gassing from manufactured wood products, a Group 1 carcinogen), benzene, toluene — are molecules, not particles. CADR measures zero about gases. An activated carbon filter that adsorbs VOCs has no CADR representation; a HEPA-only and HEPA-plus-carbon unit carry identical ratings. Ultrafine particles below 0.09 μm — the size range most associated with cardiovascular health effects — fall below the measurement window. Fan speed: the consumer runs medium or low (high is loud); CADR at medium is 50-60% of rated, at low 25-35%. No label pairs CADR with noise level at each speed. Filter degradation: the rating describes a new filter; six months of accumulation reduces effective CADR by 30-50%, and the replacement cost ($30-80 per cycle) appears nowhere in the CADR comparison.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (three CADR numbers perform a comprehensive air quality assessment while measuring particle removal rate at maximum speed in a specific chamber for a specific particle window; the number is standardized, third-party verified via AHAM Verifide, and provides chamber performance where the consumer needs room performance; see also #374, #370, #367) + dimensional-truncation (the particle size window excludes gas-phase VOCs and ultrafine particles; the single-speed measurement excludes the speed the consumer actually uses; the new-filter snapshot excludes the degradation curve the consumer actually experiences; see also #373, #372, #369). First indoor air quality / air purification metrology entry.

Source: ANSI/AHAM AC-1-2015 (Method for Measuring Performance of Portable Household Electric Room Air Cleaners). AHAM Verifide certification program. EPA Guide to Air Cleaners in the Home.

Object: Portable generator starting watts vs running watts (#376)

Assumed channel: The generator box says "9,500 watts." The number measures how much power the generator can produce. A 9,500-watt generator can run 9,500 watts of appliances.

Actual channel: The headline number — 9,500 watts — is starting watts (also called surge watts or peak watts): the power the generator can deliver for a few seconds during motor startup, when compressor motors draw 2-3× their running wattage. Running watts (also called rated watts or continuous watts) — the power the generator can sustain indefinitely — appears in smaller type: typically 75-85% of starting watts (here, 7,500W). The consumer adds running watts of appliances (e.g., refrigerator 700 + well pump 1,200 + window AC 1,400 = 3,300) and compares to the starting-watt headline with apparent headroom. But simultaneous compressor starts compound: 2,200 + 3,000 + 4,400 = 9,600 starting watts, exceeding the "9,500-watt" generator. Staggering (sequential motor startup) converts the spike into manageable sequential surges — explained in the manual's section 4, never on the box. Environmental derating: altitude (-3.5% per 1,000 feet; Denver = -17.5%), high temperature (reduced air density), propane fuel (-10% vs gasoline). Sea-level gasoline test conditions produce the label number. Runtime "12 hours at 50% load" is at optimal efficiency; at 75% load, runtime drops nonlinearly (engine works harder and less efficiently). THD (total harmonic distortion) — conventional generators 15-25%, inverter generators <3% — determines whether power damages sensitive electronics, but appears nowhere on the box. Most portable generators are purchased during or immediately before emergencies (hurricane season, ice storms), when the consumer reads the front of the box under duress and the manual remains in its plastic bag.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (starting watts headline performs a capacity specification while measuring a momentary surge capability; the consumer reads continuous capacity where the number describes peak transient; the box optimizes for the three-second purchasing decision, the manual addresses the three-hour operating reality; see also #375, #370, #367, #359) + dimensional-truncation (the single wattage number collapses the distinction between starting and running, the environmental derating, the fuel-type penalty, the THD quality dimension, and the runtime nonlinearity into one large integer; see also #375, #373, #372). First portable power / generator sizing entry.

Source: PGMA (Portable Generator Manufacturers' Association) safety and sizing guidelines. NFPA 110 (Standard for Emergency and Standby Power Systems). EPA emissions standards for small engines. CSA/UL 2201 (portable generator safety standard).

Object: Dishwasher noise rating and the dBA marketing race (#377)

Assumed channel: The dishwasher spec sheet says "44 dBA." The number measures how loud the dishwasher will sound in the kitchen. A 42 dBA dishwasher is noticeably quieter than a 44 dBA dishwasher. "Whisper quiet" means the machine sounds like a whisper.

Actual channel: The dBA number is a sound power level (acoustic energy radiated, in dB(A) re 1 pW) measured under IEC 60436/IEC 60704-2-3 in a controlled acoustic environment with standardized loading (rated capacity, mostly unsoiled items) during a specific cycle phase (EU mandates the eco programme; US has no mandatory test — AHAM DW-1 covers energy and water, not noise). Sound power level is not sound pressure level — what the ear hears depends on room acoustics, distance, and installation. In the US, dishwasher noise disclosure is entirely voluntary; no FTC, DOE, or ENERGY STAR requirement mandates the number or specifies the test method. The industry framework (developed through Owens Corning's third-party testing program circa early 2000s) references ISO 3744 sound power methodology, but participation is manufacturer-optional. The EU mandates dBA on the energy label (Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2017, effective March 2021) — a European 44 dBA and an American "44 dBA" are not necessarily equivalent. Bosch catalyzed the noise race (early 2000s, positioning against 60-65 dBA industry baseline), reframing quiet as a lifestyle proposition for open floor plans. The race compressed: 60+ dBA (1990s) → 50 dBA (mid-2000s) → 44 dBA (2010s) → 38 dBA (current floor, Bosch Benchmark/Miele Extra Quiet). At the premium end, marketing differentiates on 2 dBA increments (42 vs 44). The just-noticeable difference for broadband noise at moderate levels is ~3 dBA in everyday conditions (lab conditions ~1 dBA; Weber's law: JND worsens at lower levels — exactly the 40 dBA range where dishwashers are now marketed). A 2 dBA difference is below the practical perceptual threshold. "Whisper quiet" is applied to machines at 44 dBA; an actual whisper is 20-30 dBA — a 10-20 dB gap representing a 4× perceived loudness difference. The A-weighting filter (see #108) collapses spectral content: a 42 dBA machine with a tonal motor whine at 2 kHz and a 42 dBA machine with smooth broadband water noise are rated identically but experienced very differently — psychoacoustic research (Appliance Science, ScienceDirect 2021) finds sharpness and tonality predict annoyance independently of overall dBA. Installation variance: controlled tests in acoustic chambers produce the label number; actual kitchen installation introduces floor coupling (tile vs carpet: 2-3 dBA), cabinet resonance (particle board amplifies vibration), countertop mass (laminate vs stone), and leveling — documented discrepancies of 8-12 dBA between spec and in-situ measurement. A 44 dBA sound power level dishwasher in a 38 dBA ambient open-plan home is clearly audible, not masked — the marketing narrative that justified the quiet race (open floor plans) is the same context that makes the quiet claim inaudible only in the closed kitchens the design trend eliminated.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the dBA number performs precise, objective measurement while concealing the gap between sound power level and sound pressure level, between controlled test chamber and installed kitchen, between eco cycle and normal cycle, between standardized loading and actual dishes; in the US the entire number is voluntary and self-reported with no mandated methodology; see also #376, #375, #370, #359, #108) + dimensional-truncation (the single dBA figure collapses spectral content, installation variables, cycle phase, psychoacoustic annoyance profile, and the sound power/pressure distinction into one integer; 2 dBA marketing increments operate below the just-noticeable difference; "whisper quiet" applied to machines 4× louder than a whisper by perceived loudness; see also #376, #375, #373, #372). First consumer appliance noise marketing / dishwasher metrology entry.

Source: IEC 60436:2025 (5th ed., electric household dishwashers — performance). IEC 60704-2-3:2025 (4th ed., airborne acoustical noise — dishwashers). ISO 3744:2010/2025 (sound power levels). EU Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2017 (energy label, mandatory noise). FTC 16 CFR Part 305 (Appliance Labeling Rule — noise not required). AHAM DW-1-2020 (energy/water, not noise). ScienceDirect 2021 (psychoacoustic dishwasher annoyance study).

Object: Bicycle wheel and frame sizing and the three names for one rim (#378)

Assumed channel: A road bike tire says "700C." A mountain bike tire says "29 inch." A Dutch city bike tire says "28 inch." These are three different wheel sizes for three different kinds of bicycle. A road bike frame says "56cm." This measures the frame to centimeter precision. A larger number means a larger bike.

Actual channel: 700C, 29", and 28" are three names for the same bead seat diameter: 622mm (ISO 5775, ETRTO). The "700" in 700C is a surviving fragment of a defunct French sizing system (late 19th century) in which 700A, 700B, 700C, and 700D designated different tire widths on different rim diameters, all intended to produce approximately 700mm outer diameter when mounted. Only 700C survived — not because it was superior but because the industry converged on it when the other sizes fell out of production. With modern tires, the actual outer diameter of a "700C" wheel ranges from ~668mm (23mm road tire) to ~720mm (wide gravel tire). "700" measures nothing on a current bicycle. The "29er" mountain bike (Gary Fisher/WTB, ~1999, mass-produced by Trek 2002) was marketed as a wheel-size revolution; the rim was the same 622mm road rim with wider, knobby tires. Gary Fisher measured the outer diameter, said "let's call it a Twenty Nine," and a product category was born. Similarly, 27.5" = 650B = 584mm (French touring heritage, revived by Kirk Pacenti 2007 for MTB); 26" = 559mm. The perilous near-miss: 27" (630mm, dominant American road standard 1970s-80s) is 8mm larger than 700C (622mm) — completely incompatible rims with nearly identical names. Frame sizing: "56cm" nominally measures the seat tube, but center-to-center vs center-to-top measurement conventions differ by 1-2cm between manufacturers; one manufacturer changed conventions mid-production, producing identical frames labeled 2cm apart. Stack and reach (Dan Empfield, 2003) — the vertical and horizontal distances from bottom bracket to head tube top — are the two dimensions that unambiguously determine fit regardless of seat tube measurement convention. They appear in geometry charts. They do not appear in marketing. The bike is sold as "56cm" or "Large." Tire labeling carries three redundant systems: French (700x25C), ETRTO (25-622), imperial (1"). Sheldon Brown's Law of Tire Sizing: if two tires are marked with mathematically equal sizes expressed as decimal and fraction (1.75 vs 1¾), they are not interchangeable — the systems developed with different BSD assumptions.

What it means: convention-as-nature (three names — 700C, 29", 28" — perform categorical difference between road, mountain, and city cycling while describing the same 622mm physical object; the names carry identity, heritage, and brand positioning that the shared BSD would dissolve; 27" and 700C sound similar but are incompatible, while 700C and 29" sound different but are identical; the naming conventions were not corrected when ISO 5775 was developed because manufacturers had too much invested in category-specific branding; see also #333, #334, #336, #341) + format-as-objectivity (frame sizing in centimeters performs precision — "56cm" — while the measurement point is unstandardized and varies 1-2cm between manufacturers; stack and reach, the meaningful fit dimensions, remain in the geometry chart fine print; see also #377, #376, #333). First cycling standards / bicycle metrology entry.

Source: ISO 5775-1:2023 (bicycle tyre designations and dimensions). ISO 5775-2:2021 (bicycle rims). ETRTO (European Tyre and Rim Technical Organisation, constituted 1964 Montreux). Sheldon Brown tire sizing reference (sheldonbrown.com). Dan Empfield, stack and reach formalization (Slowtwitch, 2003). Gary Fisher/WTB 29er development (1999-2002).

Object: Window energy performance label and the NFRC four-number summary (#379)

Assumed channel: The window sticker shows four numbers: U-Factor 0.25, SHGC 0.22, VT 0.43, Air Leakage 0.30. Lower U-Factor means better insulation. The ENERGY STAR logo means the window is energy-efficient. The numbers describe how the window will perform in the house.

Actual channel: The NFRC (National Fenestration Rating Council, established 1989, Silver Spring MD) label reports four metrics — U-Factor (heat transfer rate, BTU/hr·ft²·°F), Solar Heat Gain Coefficient (fraction of solar radiation admitted, 0-1), Visible Transmittance (fraction of visible light admitted, 0-1), and Air Leakage (cfm/ft² of frame area) — each measured under NFRC standardized conditions (NFRC 100 for U-Factor, NFRC 200 for SHGC/VT, NFRC 400 for air leakage). The label reports whole-window values, which include the frame, edge-of-glass, and center-of-glass as area-weighted averages — a critical distinction because center-of-glass U-Factor for triple-pane low-E can be 0.10 while the whole-window value (including aluminum or vinyl frame thermal bridging) is 0.25. Some manufacturers cite center-of-glass values in marketing material. The NFRC label reports whole-window. The consumer comparing the two sees different numbers for the same product. Climate dependence: ENERGY STAR defines four climate zones (Northern, North-Central, South-Central, Southern) with different qualifying criteria. In the Northern zone, ENERGY STAR requires U-Factor ≤ 0.27 and SHGC ≥ 0.32 — wanting low heat loss AND high solar gain for passive winter heating. In the Southern zone: U-Factor ≤ 0.40 and SHGC ≤ 0.25 — wanting less solar gain to reduce cooling loads. The same window can qualify for ENERGY STAR in one zone and fail in another. A U-Factor 0.25 / SHGC 0.22 window is ENERGY STAR in the South but NOT in the North (SHGC too low — blocks the winter sun the heating system needs). The consumer sees the ENERGY STAR logo and reads "efficient." The logo means "efficient for this climate zone." The zone is in the fine print. The logo is not. R-value vs U-Factor: the insulation industry reports R-value (resistance, higher = better); the window industry reports U-Factor (conductance, lower = better). R = 1/U. A high-performance window at U = 0.25 has R-4. Adjacent wall insulation: R-13 to R-21. The window, displayed as a percentage of wall area, dominates heat loss while its resistance value (if translated) would read as inferior to the insulation on every side. The industries chose opposite conventions for the same physical quantity. Installation gap: NFRC testing measures the window unit. Installed performance depends on air sealing, flashing, thermal bridging through the rough opening, and integration with the wall's water-resistive barrier — variables absent from the label and contributing the majority of thermal performance loss in field studies (ORNL research, Lstiburek/Building Science Corporation). The label measures the component. The building experiences the installation.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (four numbers perform comprehensive assessment while each number is a lab value for a component, not a prediction of installed performance; whole-window vs center-of-glass values create two different numbers for the same product depending on whether marketing or NFRC labeling is referenced; see also #377, #376, #343) + population-as-individual (the ENERGY STAR logo performs universal efficiency while meaning zone-specific efficiency — the same window qualifies in one climate and fails in another; the logo reads as property of the window while being a property of the window-in-a-climate; see also #358, #344) + convention-as-nature (R-value and U-Factor are reciprocals of the same physical quantity, reported in opposite conventions by adjacent industries — insulation says R-13, the window next to it says U-0.25 = R-4, and the consumer cannot compare because the formats diverge; see also #343, #332). First fenestration / window energy performance entry.

Source: NFRC 100-2020 (U-Factor). NFRC 200-2020 (SHGC, VT). NFRC 400-2020 (Air Leakage). ENERGY STAR Residential Windows, Doors, and Skylights Version 7.0 (climate zone criteria). IECC (International Energy Conservation Code) climate zone map. ORNL Buildings Technology Research (installed window performance). Lstiburek, J. (Building Science Corporation) — field installation thermal bridging studies.

Object: Coffee roast labeling and the geographic names that describe process (#380)

Assumed channel: A bag of coffee says "French Roast." The coffee is from France or roasted in a French style. "Dark Roast" means strong, bold, and higher in caffeine. A darker roast is a premium product. The roast name tells the consumer what the coffee tastes like and where it comes from.

Actual channel: "French Roast," "Italian Roast," "Vienna Roast," and "City Roast" are processing descriptions, not origin descriptions. French Roast designates a very dark roast level (~Agtron 28-35 on the SCA/Agtron near-infrared reflectance scale, 0-100, lighter = higher); Italian Roast is darker still. The names attach geography to a temperature. No French regulatory body certifies French Roast. No Italian standard defines Italian Roast. The geographic names entered English-language coffee commerce in the 19th century as descriptions of roast preferences associated with regions — French consumers preferred darker roasts, Italian darker still — and survived as labels after the geographic association became invisible. The names perform origin while describing combustion. Darker roasting destroys origin character: the volatile aromatics, fruit acids, floral notes, and varietal characteristics that distinguish Ethiopian Yirgacheffe from Guatemalan Huehuetenango are progressively carbonized as roast temperature rises past first crack (~385°F/196°C) through second crack (~435°F/224°C) and into dark territory. Dark roast tastes like dark roast regardless of the bean's origin. This is the mechanism Starbucks exploits at scale: roasting dark enough to ensure consistency across a global supply chain. The consistency IS the erasure. The consumer reads "bold" and "strong" where the roaster achieved uniformity by burning away the variation that distinguishes one bean from another. The SCA cupping protocol (SCA, 2004/updated) grades specialty coffee on attributes — acidity, sweetness, body, flavor, aftertaste, balance — that dark roasting diminishes or eliminates. The grading system rewards what the roast level erases. Caffeine: the consumer believes dark roast = stronger = more caffeine. The relationship is directionally wrong. Caffeine is thermally stable through roasting temperatures; it degrades minimally. But dark-roasted beans expand (losing density), so a scoop of dark roast contains fewer beans and slightly less caffeine (~5-10%) than a scoop of light roast. By weight, the difference is negligible. "Strength" conflates caffeine content (similar across roast levels) with flavor intensity (bitterness from carbonization). No US regulatory definition of "light," "medium," or "dark" exists. FDA food labeling regulations do not define roast levels. The Agtron scale, the industry's objective colorimetric measurement, appears nowhere on consumer packaging. The third-wave movement (Counter Culture, Intelligentsia, Stumptown, ~2000s) inverted the value hierarchy — marketing origin and light roast to preserve the terroir the commodity market burned away — but the mass market (Folgers, Maxwell House, Starbucks, ~90% of US consumption) continues to position dark roast as premium.

What it means: convention-as-nature (geographic names — French, Italian, Vienna, City — perform origin while describing a processing step; the consumer reads provenance where the label encodes temperature; the names survived their geographic association and now attach national identity to degrees Fahrenheit; see also #378, #334, #332) + dimensional-truncation (the single roast-level axis — light to dark — collapses origin, variety, processing method, altitude, and soil into one quality dimension; darker roasting specifically destroys the multi-dimensional flavor complexity that distinguishes one coffee from another, and this erasure is marketed as "bold" and "strong"; see also #377, #370, #338). First coffee science / roast metrology entry.

Source: SCA (Specialty Coffee Association) cupping protocols and Agtron scale references. Rao, S., The Coffee Roaster's Companion (2014). Hoffmann, J., The World Atlas of Coffee (2014/2018). FDA 21 CFR food labeling (no roast level definitions). Counter Culture / Intelligentsia / Stumptown founding and third-wave positioning (~2000s).

Object: Oven temperature dial and the illusion of thermal precision (#381)

Assumed channel: The oven dial is set to 350°F. The oven is at 350°F. A recipe that says "350°F for 25 minutes" will produce the same result in every oven set to 350°F. The number on the dial is the temperature of the air inside the oven.

Actual channel: The oven does not hold a steady temperature. It cycles: the heating element activates until the thermostat (bimetallic strip or electronic sensor) registers above the setpoint, then deactivates until the temperature drops below a threshold, then reactivates. The actual air temperature follows a sawtooth wave — rising during the on-cycle, falling during the off-cycle. The "350°F" is the approximate midpoint of this oscillation. Typical cycling range: ±15-25°F for gas ovens, ±10-15°F for electric. The consumer who sets 350 is occupying a band from approximately 325 to 375. Calibration drift compounds: thermocouples and resistance temperature detectors age, losing accuracy over years. A 5-year-old oven commonly runs 25-50°F off its displayed setpoint. Most ovens have a hidden calibration offset adjustable through the control panel (typically ±35°F), documented in the manual, used by approximately nobody. Spatial variation: in a radiant oven, the temperature near the heating element differs from the center by 20-50°F. Rack position changes effective temperature — closer to the element means hotter. Convection (fan-assisted) improves uniformity but runs 25°F hotter at the same dial setting (hence "reduce by 25°F for convection" instructions). Opening the door drops temperature 25-75°F per opening. Gas ovens add moisture from combustion (affecting baking chemistry) and cycle more widely than electric. A standalone oven thermometer — a $5-15 correction tool available at every grocery store — is used by perhaps 10% of home cooks, because the dial already provided a number and the number was trusted. Recipe culture encodes the dial's precision ("350°F for 25 minutes"), not the oven's reality (325-375°F, cycling, drifting, varying by position, rack, convection setting, and gas/electric). The recipe that "failed" may be a recipe that worked in an oven 40°F off from the oven that tried to replicate it. Both dials said 350.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the dial displays a specific integer temperature — "350" — that performs precision while the oven delivers a cycling range, a drifting calibration, and spatial variation totaling ±50°F or more; the number on the dial is a setpoint for a control system, not a measurement of the cavity; recipe culture inherited the dial's precision and propagated it as specification; see also #377, #376, #367) + population-as-individual (the recipe assumes all ovens at "350" deliver the same thermal environment; the recipe is a population-level instruction applied to individual ovens whose actual temperatures vary by up to 100°F from each other; see also #379, #358, #344). First cooking appliance metrology / oven thermal performance entry.

Source: ASTM F1496-13 (standard test method for oven performance). Thermador, Bosch, GE owner's manuals (calibration offset instructions). Harold McGee, On Food and Cooking (2004, oven temperature variability). Cook's Illustrated oven testing (documented cycling and calibration drift). NIST temperature calibration references.

Object: Hi-res audio format specifications and the inaudible bandwidth (#382)

Assumed channel: A streaming service offers "Hi-Res Audio" at 96 kHz / 24-bit. The numbers are higher than CD quality (44.1 kHz / 16-bit). Higher numbers mean better sound. Hi-res audio sounds better than standard audio because it captures more of the music.

Actual channel: The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem (1928/1949) proves that a sample rate of 2× the maximum frequency of interest perfectly reconstructs the continuous signal — no information loss, no approximation, mathematically lossless. Human audible range: approximately 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (declining with age — most adults over 25 hear below 16-17 kHz). CD quality at 44.1 kHz captures frequencies up to 22,050 Hz — exceeding the audible ceiling. At 96 kHz, the system captures frequencies up to 48,000 Hz. At 192 kHz: up to 96,000 Hz. These frequencies are inaudible. The bandwidth extension is real; the audible benefit is contested. Meyer & Moran (AES, 2007): double-blind ABX testing of 554 trials found no statistically significant ability to distinguish SACD/DVD-Audio (hi-res) from CD downconversions among trained listeners. Reiss (JAES, 2016): meta-analysis found a small statistical effect (1.8% detection above chance) but attributed it to potential ultrasonic intermodulation distortion in playback equipment (creating audible artifacts from inaudible content) rather than direct perception of ultrasonic frequencies. Bit depth: 16-bit provides 96 dB dynamic range; 24-bit provides 144 dB. The threshold of pain is ~130 dB SPL. The noise floor of a quiet room is ~30 dB SPL. The 96 dB range of 16-bit exceeds the span from silence to pain. 24-bit's additional 48 dB of theoretical range is below the thermal noise floor of any playback electronics and below the noise floor of any recording microphone. The additional bits provide production headroom (useful in recording studios during mixing) but no additional audible resolution in playback. The hi-res marketing operates on the consumer's assumption that larger numbers = more information = better sound, when the additional information is either inaudible (ultrasonic frequencies) or below the noise floor (additional dynamic range). MQA (Master Quality Authenticated, 2014, Bob Stuart/Meridian) added a proprietary layer, packaging hi-res into smaller files with authentication — adding a third number-as-quality claim (authenticated vs non-authenticated) orthogonal to the original two. The consumer who pays for 192/24 is paying for frequencies they cannot hear and dynamic range their equipment cannot reproduce. The audible difference, when detected, is typically attributable to mastering differences (hi-res releases are often remastered with more care) rather than format specification.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (96 kHz and 24-bit perform superior fidelity through larger numbers while the additional information they encode is either above the audible frequency range or below the noise floor of playback equipment; the specification describes a mathematical property of the encoding, not an audible property of the sound; see also #377, #376, #368) + dimensional-truncation (sample rate and bit depth are two of dozens of factors determining perceived audio quality — recording technique, microphone placement, mixing, mastering, room acoustics, speaker quality, listener hearing — and are the two that appear on the product page while contributing the least marginal improvement at the consumer endpoint; see also #380, #377, #370). First digital audio / consumer audio format metrology entry.

Source: Nyquist, H. (1928), "Certain Topics in Telegraph Transmission Theory." Shannon, C. (1949), "Communication in the Presence of Noise." Meyer, E.B. & Moran, D.R. (AES Convention Paper 7057, 2007), "Audibility of a CD-Standard A/D/A Loop Inserted into High-Resolution Audio Playback." Reiss, J.D. (JAES 64(6), 2016), "A Meta-Analysis of High-Resolution Audio Perceptual Evaluation." AES (Audio Engineering Society) standards for PCM audio. Red Book CD standard (Philips/Sony, 1980, IEC 60908).

Object: Washing machine temperature labels and the variable behind the word (#383)

Assumed channel: The washing machine dial says "Hot," "Warm," or "Cold." Hot means a specific high temperature. Cold means a specific low temperature. The three settings deliver three distinct, consistent water temperatures. Hot cleans better than cold.

Actual channel: "Hot," "Warm," and "Cold" are not standardized temperatures. AHAM HLW-1 (test standard for residential clothes washers) defines Hot as 130°F (54°C), Warm as 100°F (38°C), and Cold as 80°F (27°C) — for testing purposes. Actual delivered temperatures vary by three independent factors: (1) Water heater setpoint: the DOE recommends 120°F for energy savings and scald prevention (down from the 140°F default of older installations); "Hot" on the machine cannot exceed what the water heater delivers, so "Hot" is often 120°F, not 130°F. (2) Inlet temperature: "Cold" means whatever temperature enters from the cold water supply pipe. In Minneapolis in January, cold tap water is approximately 37-40°F. In Phoenix in August, approximately 75-80°F. Same dial setting, 40°F range, determined by geography and season. (3) Mixing valve: "Warm" blends hot and cold supply. If hot is 120°F and cold is 40°F, warm is approximately 80°F. If cold is 75°F, warm is approximately 97°F. The word "Warm" performs constancy while the temperature varies by 17°F depending on when and where the machine runs. Fabric care labels (ASTM D5489) define "warm" as 105°F ± 15°F — a 30°F range — acknowledging the variability the consumer dial does not. Modern detergent chemistry inverts the assumed cleaning hierarchy: enzyme-based formulations (protease, lipase, amylase) are optimized for cold water (60-80°F); hot water above 140°F can denature enzymes, reducing effectiveness. The consumer hierarchy (hot cleans best) was accurate for soap-based washing; it is directionally wrong for enzyme-based detergent on most soil types. The "sanitize" cycle (marketed as killing bacteria) requires 150°F sustained for ≥7 minutes per NSF P172 — a temperature most residential water heaters cannot reach without raising the setpoint above scald-risk threshold. Many "sanitize" options use steam injection or extended agitation rather than achieving the NSF thermal threshold, but the label says "sanitize."

What it means: convention-as-nature (the three words — hot, warm, cold — perform categorical temperature control while the actual temperatures are functions of water heater setpoint, geographic cold-supply temperature, and seasonal variation; the consumer reads a thermostat where the machine delivers a mixture of variables the dial cannot represent; see also #381, #378, #332) + population-as-individual (the fabric care label defines "warm" as 105°F ± 15°F acknowledging population-level variation that the appliance dial erases; see also #381, #379, #358). First laundry appliance / wash temperature metrology entry.

Source: AHAM HLW-1-2010 (residential clothes washer testing). ASTM D5489 (care labeling of textile products). NSF/ANSI P172 (sanitization performance of residential clothes washers). DOE 10 CFR Part 430 Subpart B (energy conservation standards). ENERGY STAR cold wash guidance.

Object: Television peak brightness and contrast ratio specifications (#384)

Assumed channel: A TV spec sheet says "peak brightness: 2,000 nits" and "contrast ratio: 1,000,000:1." Higher brightness means a brighter picture. Higher contrast ratio means blacker blacks and whiter whites. A 2,000-nit TV is twice as bright as a 1,000-nit TV across the entire screen.

Actual channel: "Peak brightness" is measured in candelas per square meter (nits), but the measurement window matters. A 10% window test illuminates 10% of the screen to maximum brightness; a full-screen (100% APL) test illuminates the entire panel. LCD TVs with LED backlights can sustain near-peak brightness full-screen (backlight runs uniformly). OLED panels, which are self-emissive (each pixel is its own light source), have a thermal power budget — driving all pixels to maximum simultaneously would exceed the panel's thermal dissipation capacity. An OLED rated at 2,000 nits on a 10% window may deliver 200-400 nits full-screen (ABL — Automatic Brightness Limiter activates). The consumer reads "2,000 nits" as the brightness of the picture. The picture is rarely 10% white on black. For a daylight outdoor scene (high APL), the OLED delivers 20-50% of the headline figure. The spec sheet rarely discloses which window size produced the number. Contrast ratio has two definitions: static (sequential — brightest white divided by darkest black measured at the same moment on the same panel state) and dynamic (measured at different times, with backlight adjustment between measurements). An LCD with 1,000:1 static contrast can claim 1,000,000:1 dynamic contrast by dimming the backlight during the dark measurement and brightening it during the light measurement — a ratio of two different backlight states, not the panel's simultaneous capability. OLED achieves effectively infinite static contrast (each pixel turns off completely — true black = 0 nits, making any positive brightness divided by zero = infinite). This is OLED's genuine advantage. The marketing of LCD's "1,000,000:1 dynamic" against OLED's "infinite" makes the LCD appear comparable when the measurement methodologies are not comparable. HDR (High Dynamic Range) specifications — HDR10, HDR10+, Dolby Vision — define metadata and transfer functions, not display capability. An HDR10-compatible TV may have 400 nits peak brightness; HDR10 was designed for mastering at 1,000-4,000 nits. The label says "HDR10" — the label means "can decode the signal," not "can display the signal as intended." The consumer reads HDR as a display property. HDR is a signal property. The display's ability to reproduce the signal's intentions is a separate, undisclosed question.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (peak brightness at 10% window performs as the brightness of the picture while full-screen brightness may be 20-50% of the headline number; contrast ratio at dynamic measurement performs as the panel's capability while measuring two different backlight states; HDR compatibility performs display quality while describing signal decoding; see also #382, #377, #356) + dimensional-truncation (a single nit number collapses the window-size dependence, the ABL behavior, the APL-brightness relationship, and the ambient-light viewing conditions into one integer; a single contrast ratio collapses the static/dynamic distinction and the measurement methodology into one ratio; see also #382, #377, #368). First display metrology / television brightness-contrast entry.

Source: VESA DisplayHDR certification standard (version 1.1, peak luminance tiers). CTA-861-H (HDR static metadata). Dolby Vision specification. OLED ABL thermal management (LG Display technical documentation). rtings.com display measurement methodology. IEC 62087 (methods of measurement for power consumption of audio, video, and related equipment — includes screen luminance tests).

Object: Ice cream overrun and the volume that is air (#385)

Assumed channel: A pint of ice cream contains a pint of ice cream. The consumer compares prices per pint — $3.99 versus $6.99 — and calculates value by volume. A pint is a pint.

Actual channel: "Overrun" is the percentage of air incorporated into ice cream during the churning and freezing process. 100% overrun means the volume doubled — half the pint is air. Federal regulation 21 CFR 135.110 requires ice cream to weigh at least 4.5 pounds per gallon (approximately 540 grams per pint) and contain at least 10% milkfat by weight. The minimum weight is low enough to permit substantial overrun. Economy ice cream typically has 90-100% overrun: the consumer buys a pint container that weighs approximately 250-300 grams (barely above the federal minimum after accounting for packaging weight). Premium ice cream typically has 25-50% overrun: the same pint container weighs 400-450 grams. Same shelf, same container shape, same volume. The premium pint contains roughly 50-80% more ice cream by mass than the economy pint. The consumer shopping by price-per-pint is comparing different amounts of ice cream in identical containers. Overrun is not disclosed on the label. Net weight is printed (as required by law), but the consumer shops by container size, not by reading the fine-print weight and dividing price by grams. Gelato typically has 25-30% overrun, which is why it tastes denser — it is denser. The term "gelato-style" in the US market carries no regulatory binding on overrun percentage. The format — a pint container at a price — performs a comparison the content does not support.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (a standardized volume container performs equal quantity while air content varies 2:1 between economy and premium products; the pint performs as the unit of comparison when the actual ice cream mass per pint varies from ~250g to ~450g; see also #380, #355, #366) + dimensional-truncation (a single price-per-pint collapses the overrun percentage, the milkfat content, the total solids, and the density into a volume-based comparison that erases the mass variable; see also #355, #366, #362). First frozen dessert / dairy metrology entry.

Source: 21 CFR 135.110 (FDA, ice cream identity standard). IDFA (International Dairy Foods Association) manufacturing guidelines. Marshall, Goff, and Hartel, Ice Cream (7th ed., Springer, 2013), chapters on overrun measurement and air cell structure. USDA nutrient database entries for ice cream by fat content and brand.

Object: Potting soil labeling and the bag that contains no soil (#386)

Assumed channel: A bag in the garden center says "potting soil." It contains soil suitable for pots. "Topsoil" contains the top layer of soil. The volume printed on the bag — "1 cubic foot" — is the amount of material inside. The consumer buys soil by volume.

Actual channel: "Potting soil" (more accurately "potting mix") typically contains zero actual soil. The ingredients are peat moss or coconut coir (a mined or harvested organic fiber for moisture retention), perlite (expanded volcanic glass for aeration), vermiculite (expanded mica for moisture and nutrient retention), composted bark, and sometimes wetting agents or slow-release fertilizer. The industry moved to soilless media because actual soil in containers compacts, drains poorly, and harbors soil-borne pathogens (damping-off fungi, nematodes). The word "soil" on the bag describes a legacy category name, not the material. "Garden soil" is potting mix blended with some actual mineral soil, intended for amending garden beds — it is still mostly manufactured media. "Topsoil" has no federal definition and no enforceable standard for organic matter content, particle size distribution, or depth of origin. A bag labeled "topsoil" may be subsoil, screened fill dirt, or construction-site material with organic amendment added. The volume on the bag — "1 cubic foot" or "2 cubic feet" — is measured at the factory in a loosely filled state. Settling during shipping and storage can reduce the dispensed volume by 10-20%. Moisture content varies with storage conditions (a bag stored outdoors absorbs rainwater, increasing weight without increasing usable media). The consumer buying a "1 cubic foot" bag to fill a pot measured in gallons must convert (1 cu ft ≈ 7.48 US gallons) and account for drainage material and settling, calculations the label does not facilitate. The word performs the material. The volume performs the quantity. Neither is what the bag contains.

What it means: convention-as-nature (the word "soil" performs a natural material when the product is entirely manufactured media — peat, perlite, bark; "topsoil" performs a geographic origin that has no enforceable definition; see also #380, #383, #341) + format-as-objectivity (the volume measurement on the bag performs a quantity comparison while compaction, settling, moisture absorption, and factory fill conditions vary the actual dispensed amount; see also #362, #369, #355). First consumer horticulture / garden products entry.

Source: ASTM D5268 (standard specification for topsoil used for landscaping purposes — voluntary, not federally enforced). University extension services (Penn State, Cornell, Purdue) potting mix composition guides. Bunt, Media and Mixes for Container-Grown Plants (Springer, 1988). FTC packaging and labeling guidelines (Fair Packaging and Labeling Act, 15 U.S.C. §1451-1461).

Object: Humidifier output capacity — gallons per day at conditions the consumer does not control (#387)

Assumed channel: The humidifier box says "output: 4 gallons per day" and "covers rooms up to 500 square feet." The consumer reads: this machine will add 4 gallons of moisture per day to a 500-square-foot room.

Actual channel: Output capacity is tested under AHAM Standard 611 conditions: 70°F dry-bulb, 20% relative humidity. At 20% RH, the air is extremely dry — the vapor pressure deficit between the water surface and the air is at its maximum, driving maximum evaporation. As the room's humidity rises toward the consumer's target — typically 40-45% RH in winter — the vapor pressure deficit decreases and the evaporation rate drops proportionally. A humidifier rated at 4 gallons per day at 20% RH may deliver 2-2.5 gallons per day at 35% RH and less at 40%. The headline capacity describes the machine's output at the condition of maximum need, not the output at the condition the consumer is trying to achieve. The "room coverage" rating (500 sq ft) is calculated from the output capacity at the test condition, using assumed ceiling height (8 ft), assumed air exchange rate, and assumed starting humidity — assumptions that vary by home construction, HVAC operation, and climate. A leaky older home in Minneapolis (3 ACH natural) needs approximately 3× the output of a tight new-construction home (0.5 ACH) for the same square footage and target humidity. The room size on the box assumes a single air-change rate. The consumer's home provides another. Tank capacity (4 gallons) is container volume — it describes how often the consumer must refill, not how much moisture reaches the air. An evaporative humidifier's tank empties at the output rate; an ultrasonic humidifier's tank empties at a rate independent of humidity achieved (it aerosolizes water regardless of air conditions, potentially over-humidifying and producing mineral dust from hard water). The consumer reads one number — gallons per day — and inhabits a room with a different number.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the gallons-per-day rating at 20% RH performs as the machine's output when the consumer experiences 50-65% of that output at their target humidity; the room-size coverage claim performs certainty about applicability while assuming air-change and construction variables the label does not disclose; see also #375, #377, #360) + population-as-individual (the room-size recommendation assumes a standard home with standard air exchange, standard ceiling height, and standard starting humidity, when the consumer's home has its own construction quality and climate exposure; see also #361, #381, #379). First residential humidity control / humidifier sizing.

Source: AHAM Standard 611 (ANSI/AHAM HU-1, Humidifiers — test method for output capacity and energy input). EPA ENERGY STAR criteria for residential humidifiers. ASHRAE Handbook — HVAC Applications, chapter on residential dehumidification and humidification. Consumer Reports humidifier testing methodology.

Object: Water filter pitcher claims — "reduces" vs "removes" and the NSF certification gap (#388)

Assumed channel: The water filter pitcher box says "reduces chlorine, mercury, and lead." The NSF/ANSI certification mark appears on the packaging. The consumer reads: this filter removes these contaminants from the water. The water that comes out is clean.

Actual channel: "Reduces" is the legally operative word. NSF/ANSI Standard 42 (aesthetic effects) certifies reduction of chlorine taste and odor — typically 97%+ reduction, meaning 3% remains. NSF/ANSI Standard 53 (health effects) certifies reduction of specific health-related contaminants including lead, mercury, and certain VOCs. The reduction threshold varies by contaminant: lead reduction to below 10 ppb (from a challenge concentration of 150 ppb) per the standard, not to zero. Mercury reduction to below 2 ppb. The consumer reads "reduces lead" and may infer zero lead. The standard certifies a threshold, not elimination. NSF/ANSI Standard 401 (emerging contaminants) covers pharmaceuticals, pesticides, herbicides — but certification is voluntary and most pitcher filters are not certified to Standard 401. The box lists the standards it meets. It does not list the standards it does not meet. A filter certified to Standards 42 and 53 may not reduce pharmaceuticals, PFAS, microplastics, or bacteria. PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) require NSF/ANSI Standard P473 — a separate certification that most standard carbon filters do not achieve. The consumer reads the listed contaminants and may infer comprehensive protection. The filter protects against the listed contaminants. The unlisted contaminants pass through. Filter capacity — "40 gallons" or "2 months" — is tested with challenge water at specified contaminant concentrations. Actual capacity depends on the consumer's source water: higher contaminant loads or sediment exhaust the activated carbon faster. A filter rated for 40 gallons with test water may effectively filter 25 gallons with heavily contaminated source water, with declining performance that the consumer cannot detect by taste or appearance. The pitcher does not indicate when reduction falls below the certified threshold — it indicates when the manufacturer's recommended time or volume has elapsed, a usage-based proxy, not a performance-based measurement.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the word "reduces" performs removal; the listed standards perform comprehensiveness while the unlisted standards define the gaps; the "40-gallon" capacity performs a fixed endpoint when actual exhaustion depends on source water quality; see also #375, #384, #377) + dimensional-truncation (the certification compresses the performance question into a list of contaminant names while omitting the reduction threshold, the challenge concentration, the unlisted contaminants, the capacity degradation curve, and the absence of real-time performance monitoring; see also #375, #384, #371). First consumer water treatment / filtration metrology.

Source: NSF/ANSI Standard 42 (Drinking Water Treatment Units — Aesthetic Effects). NSF/ANSI Standard 53 (Health Effects). NSF/ANSI Standard 401 (Emerging Compounds/Incidental Contaminants). NSF/ANSI P473 (Drinking Water Treatment Units — PFAS). EPA Safe Drinking Water Act, 42 U.S.C. §300f et seq. Water Quality Association consumer guidance.

Object: Bagged concrete mix PSI rating and the strength that depends on the consumer (#389)

Assumed channel: The bag of concrete says "4,000 PSI." The consumer reads: this concrete achieves 4,000 PSI compressive strength. The concrete is strong.

Actual channel: The 4,000 PSI is the compressive strength at 28 days of cure under laboratory conditions: ASTM C39 testing of cylinders made with the manufacturer's specified water-to-cement (w/c) ratio, cured at 73°F ± 3°F and 95%+ relative humidity. Three variables the consumer controls poorly determine the actual strength. (1) Water ratio: the bag specifies approximately 3 quarts of water per 80-pound bag (w/c ≈ 0.45). The consumer adds water by eye until the mix is "workable." More water increases slump (flowability) but increases void content after evaporation. A w/c of 0.65 — common when consumers add extra water for easier pouring — can reduce strength to 2,500 PSI, a 37% loss from the same bag. (2) Temperature: Portland cement hydration slows dramatically below 50°F and essentially stops below 25°F. Concrete poured on a 40°F October afternoon may not achieve the rated strength for months. Concrete that freezes before achieving approximately 500 PSI (typically 24-48 hours) may be permanently weakened. Above 90°F, rapid hydration produces weaker crystal structure. (3) Cure time: the bag says "sets in 20-40 minutes" and "walkable in 24 hours." The consumer may load the concrete at 24 hours. At 24 hours, the concrete has achieved approximately 20-25% of its 28-day strength. At 7 days, approximately 65-70%. At 14 days, approximately 85-90%. The 4,000 PSI is the 28-day number. The consumer's timeline is typically days, not weeks. The headline strength is a property of the bag's chemistry under controlled conditions. The achieved strength is a property of the consumer's water, temperature, and patience. The bag describes one. The slab delivers the other.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (4,000 PSI performs as a property of the bagged product when it is a property of the product + water ratio + ambient temperature + humidity + cure duration; see also #381, #387, #360) + population-as-individual (the standard cure conditions assume laboratory temperature and humidity, while the consumer's driveway has its own October afternoon, its own water hose estimate, and its own loading schedule; see also #381, #387, #361). First construction materials / concrete metrology entry.

Source: ASTM C39/C39M (Standard Test Method for Compressive Strength of Cylindrical Concrete Specimens). ACI 308R (Guide to External Curing of Concrete). Portland Cement Association, Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures (16th ed.). Quikrete and Sakrete bag labeling and technical data sheets.

Object: USB charger wattage and the speed the device does not request (#390)

Assumed channel: The charger box says "65W USB-C charger." The consumer reads: this charger charges at 65 watts. A 65W charger is faster than a 30W charger. The consumer buys the higher number for faster charging.

Actual channel: The 65W is the charger's maximum output capability — the most power it can deliver if the connected device requests it through the USB Power Delivery (USB PD) negotiation protocol. The actual charging power depends on what the device supports and requests. A phone that supports only 25W PD will draw 25W from a 65W charger — the charger offers its power profiles, the device selects the one it can use, and the negotiation settles at the device's maximum, not the charger's. A phone supporting 18W Qualcomm Quick Charge but not USB PD may draw 18W or fall back to 5V/3A (15W) if the protocols don't match. The charger's headline wattage is a ceiling. The device's supported protocol and maximum draw determine the floor. The consumer comparing a 65W charger at $45 to a 30W charger at $25 may be buying headroom their phone cannot use. Proprietary fast-charging protocols compound the mismatch. Samsung Adaptive Fast Charging, OnePlus VOOC/Warp/Dash (now SUPERVOOC), Oppo SuperVOOC, and Xiaomi HyperCharge each use different voltage/current strategies. A 65W charger that supports USB PD but not VOOC will not fast-charge a OnePlus phone at its rated speed — it falls back to baseline USB PD or standard 5V charging. The watt number on the charger box and the watt number on the phone spec sheet may describe incompatible protocols. The charging curve adds the third variable. Lithium-ion batteries charge in two phases: constant current (CC) at the headline wattage, then constant voltage (CV) as the battery approaches full. A phone that charges at 65W does so for the first 15-20 minutes (from ~10% to ~60%); the remaining 40% takes as long as the first 60%. Thermal throttling reduces the charging rate further — the phone's battery management system lowers power intake if the battery temperature exceeds its thermal envelope. "0 to 50% in 15 minutes" (a common marketing claim) is not half of "0 to 100% in 30 minutes." The math is nonlinear, the curve is asymptotic, and the consumer's experience of "fast" applies to only the first portion of the charge.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the wattage on the charger box performs as the charging speed when it is the maximum theoretical ceiling that depends on device negotiation, protocol compatibility, charging phase, and thermal conditions; the consumer comparing charger wattages is comparing ceilings, not experiences; see also #376, #367, #368) + dimensional-truncation (a single watt number collapses the USB PD negotiation, the proprietary protocol compatibility, the CC/CV charging curve, and the thermal throttling into one headline; see also #376, #330, #334). First consumer electronics charging / power delivery metrology.

Source: USB Power Delivery Specification (Rev. 3.1, USB-IF). Qualcomm Quick Charge specifications. OnePlus/Oppo SUPERVOOC technical documentation. Battery University (Cadex Electronics), CC/CV charging curves for lithium-ion chemistry. ChargerLAB independent charger testing methodology.

Object: Consumer adhesive bond strength claims and the substrate the consumer does not prepare (#391)

Assumed channel: The tube says "bonds up to 4,000 PSI" or "super strong — holds 2,000 lbs." The consumer reads: this glue holds things together with enormous force. The higher the number, the stronger the repair.

Actual channel: Bond strength is tested under ASTM D1002 (Standard Test Method for Apparent Shear Strength of Single-Lap-Joint Adhesively Bonded Metal Specimens) or similar standards. The substrates are typically aluminum or steel coupons, degreased with solvent, abraded to a specified surface roughness, bonded with a controlled adhesive thickness (0.005-0.010 inches), cured at specified temperature and humidity for 24-72 hours, and tested to failure in a tensile testing machine. The consumer's repair involves: a ceramic mug handle (porous, curved, residue from previous adhesive), surfaces wiped with a paper towel (not degreased with acetone or MEK), applied in a thick bead (excessive thickness reduces shear strength in most adhesives), held together by hand for 30 seconds (not clamped for 24 hours), and loaded the next morning. Cyanoacrylate ("super glue") achieves rated strength on clean, close-fitting surfaces because it polymerizes in the thin film of moisture between tightly mated parts. On porous surfaces, it wicks into the substrate and fails to form a continuous bond line. On oily surfaces, the oil prevents moisture access. Epoxy achieves rated strength with proper mixing (the 1:1 or 2:1 ratio is not decorative — incorrect mixing produces incomplete cross-linking and dramatically reduced strength), proper cure time (full cure at room temperature is typically 24-72 hours; "sets in 5 minutes" describes handling strength, not rated strength), and appropriate substrate. Polyurethane adhesives achieve rated strength with moisture-activated curing that depends on ambient humidity. The "4,000 PSI" on the tube was tested on degreased aluminum at 0.005-inch bond line after 72 hours of cure. The consumer's ceramic-to-ceramic bond with finger oils at a 0.030-inch gap after 8 hours of cure may achieve 400 PSI — a tenth of the headline. The number on the tube describes the adhesive's potential. The consumer provides the conditions that determine the actual.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the PSI or pound-force number on the tube performs as the adhesive's strength when it is the adhesive's strength under laboratory preparation, substrate selection, bond-line thickness, and cure conditions that the consumer will not replicate; see also #389, #381, #387) + population-as-individual (the ASTM test assumes a specific substrate, specific preparation, and specific cure, while the consumer's repair has its own material, its own surface condition, its own thickness, and its own patience; see also #389, #381, #387). First consumer adhesive / bonding metrology entry.

Source: ASTM D1002 (Apparent Shear Strength of Single-Lap-Joint Adhesively Bonded Metal Specimens). ASTM D2651 (Surface Preparation for Adhesive Bonding). Petrie, Handbook of Adhesives and Sealants (3rd ed., McGraw-Hill, 2007). Henkel Loctite technical data sheets. 3M Scotch-Weld structural adhesive technical bulletins.

Object: Grass seed bag coverage rate and the square footage that depends on everything else (#392)

Assumed channel: A 5-pound bag of grass seed says "covers up to 2,000 square feet." The consumer measures the bare patch, buys the bag, spreads the seed, and expects grass. The number tells the consumer how many bags to buy.

Actual channel: The bag carries two coverage numbers: "new lawn" and "overseeding." New lawn rate: 2,000 sq ft per bag. Overseeding rate: 4,000 sq ft. The same bag claims two different areas, differing by 2:1, depending on whether the consumer is establishing grass where none exists or thickening an existing lawn. The consumer who reads the larger number and is establishing a new lawn will spread half the seed needed. The distinction between these use cases — printed on the back in smaller type — is the first variable. Seed size is the second. Kentucky bluegrass seeds are tiny: approximately 2.2 million seeds per pound. Tall fescue seeds are large: approximately 230,000 per pound. A 5-pound bag of Kentucky bluegrass contains approximately 11 million seeds. A 5-pound bag of tall fescue contains approximately 1.15 million seeds — ten times fewer. The "2,000 sq ft" coverage rate is calculated from the recommended seeding rate for the specific mix, which varies by species. A mix heavy in fine fescue covers more area per pound than a mix heavy in perennial ryegrass because the seeds are smaller and more numerous. The consumer comparing two bags by coverage-per-dollar may be comparing different seed sizes, not different values. Germination rate is printed on the bag (legally required by the Federal Seed Act): typically 80-85% for fresh seed. The "2,000 sq ft" coverage assumes all seeds germinate. At 80% germination, effective coverage is 1,600 sq ft. At the tag's expiration date, germination may have dropped further. Establishment — the percentage of germinated seeds that survive to produce mature plants — depends on soil preparation, watering frequency, soil temperature (most cool-season grasses germinate optimally between 50-65°F soil temperature), seed-to-soil contact (requires raking or rolling), and competition from weeds. The bag's coverage rate describes the seed's potential at the factory. The lawn describes the seed's survival in the consumer's soil. The two numbers are not the same number.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the square-footage coverage claim performs as a prediction of lawn area when it describes a factory seeding-rate calculation at 100% germination on prepared soil; the dual "new lawn / overseeding" numbers perform two specific use cases while the consumer may not distinguish which applies; see also #347, #386, #389) + dimensional-truncation (a single coverage number collapses the species-dependent seeding rate, seed size variation, germination percentage, soil preparation, soil temperature, watering regime, and establishment rate into one square-footage claim per bag; see also #386, #347, #389). First consumer lawn care / turfgrass seed metrology entry.

Source: Federal Seed Act (7 U.S.C. §1551-1611, truth-in-labeling for seed). AOSA (Association of Official Seed Analysts) Rules for Testing Seeds. Scotts/Pennington consumer lawn seed packaging. Turgeon, Turfgrass Management (10th ed., Pearson, 2017). University extension turfgrass seeding rate guides (Penn State, Purdue, Cornell).

Object: Pressure washer PSI rating and the absent flow variable (#393)

Assumed channel: The pressure washer box says "3,000 PSI." The consumer reads: this machine is powerful. Higher PSI means more cleaning power. A 3,000 PSI machine cleans better than a 2,000 PSI machine.

Actual channel: Cleaning effectiveness is the product of pressure (PSI) and flow rate (GPM — gallons per minute), often expressed as "cleaning units" (CU = PSI × GPM). A 3,000 PSI machine at 2.0 GPM produces 6,000 CU. A 2,000 PSI machine at 3.0 GPM also produces 6,000 CU — identical cleaning power. The consumer compares the headline PSI numbers and concludes the 3,000 PSI machine is 50 percent more powerful. The machines are equivalent. PSI determines how deep the water penetrates a surface (necessary for embedded grime in concrete pores). GPM determines how fast the water flushes loosened debris away (necessary for efficient cleaning of large areas like driveways). The box prints PSI in large type. GPM, if printed at all, appears in specifications on the back panel or in the manual. The nozzle tip changes the effective pressure at the surface: a 0-degree tip concentrates the stream; a 40-degree fan tip spreads it across a wider area, reducing pressure per unit area proportionally. Distance from the surface also reduces effective pressure — pressure drops with the square of the distance. The consumer spraying from 12 inches instead of 6 inches delivers approximately one-quarter the surface pressure. The "3,000 PSI" is the pump's maximum output pressure at zero flow (deadhead pressure) or at rated flow depending on the manufacturer — a condition that changes the instant the trigger is pulled and the nozzle geometry intervenes. Some consumer-grade machines advertise "max PSI" (peak, unloaded) rather than "rated PSI" (sustained, under load), further inflating the headline number by 10-20%.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (PSI printed large performs as the cleaning-power metric when the actual metric is PSI × GPM; the consumer comparing PSI alone is comparing half the equation; see also #369, #359, #376) + dimensional-truncation (a single PSI number collapses the flow rate, nozzle geometry, spray distance, max-vs-rated distinction, and the pressure-flow product into one integer on the box; see also #369, #359, #376). First outdoor power equipment / pressure washer metrology entry.

Source: PWMA (Pressure Washer Manufacturers' Association) testing standards. CETA (Cleaning Equipment Trade Association) performance rating guidelines. Simpson, Ryobi, and Karcher consumer pressure washer specifications and testing methodology documentation.

Object: Dehumidifier pint-per-day capacity and the DOE test condition that halved the numbers (#394)

Assumed channel: The dehumidifier box says "35 pints per day." The consumer reads: this machine removes 35 pints of moisture daily. A 35-pint machine is more powerful than a 22-pint machine. The consumer compares pint ratings across brands and selects by the number.

Actual channel: In 2019, the DOE changed the dehumidifier test condition from 80°F/60% RH (AHAM DH-1, the previous industry standard) to 65°F/60% RH (10 CFR 430, Appendix X). The new test temperature is closer to actual basement conditions but produces dramatically lower extraction rates — the same machine that rated at 70 pints under the old test rates at approximately 35 pints under the new test. The hardware did not change. The compressor did not change. The capacity did not change. The number changed because the test changed.
