A consumer reading old reviews or older product literature for a "70-pint" dehumidifier may compare it to a current "35-pint" model and conclude the old one was twice as powerful. It was the same machine measured at different temperatures. The pint-per-day rating depends on the temperature and humidity of the incoming air. At 80°F and 60% RH (the old test), the air holds more moisture; the dehumidifier's evaporator coil creates a larger dew-point gap, extracting more water per unit of air processed. At 65°F and 60% RH, the air holds less moisture; the gap narrows; extraction drops. At 55°F — a typical winter basement temperature — the dehumidifier may extract half the rated pints even under the new, more realistic test condition. The number on the box describes the machine's performance at 65°F. The basement provides whatever temperature the season and insulation deliver. The "room size" recommendation compounds the problem: "up to 1,500 sq ft" assumes standard moisture loading (from soil permeability, foundation sealing, occupant activity, and ventilation rate) and standard air leakage. A basement with a sump pump, exterior wall cracks, and a dryer vent produces more moisture than the recommendation assumed.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the pint-per-day number performs as the machine's extraction rate when it is the rate at a specific test temperature and humidity that the consumer's space may not match; the 2019 DOE test change halved the headline numbers overnight without changing any hardware; see also #387, #375, #360) + convention-as-nature (the "pints per day" label performs as a stable measurement when the number's meaning shifted by 2× with the test condition change; consumers comparing pre-2019 and post-2019 ratings are comparing different tests under the same unit; see also #387, #383, #341). First residential dehumidification / moisture control metrology.

Source: DOE 10 CFR Part 430, Appendix X (Uniform Test Method for Measuring the Energy Consumption of Dehumidifiers). AHAM DH-1 (Dehumidifiers test standard, pre-2019). ENERGY STAR Dehumidifier Key Product Criteria (version 5.0, reflecting 2019 test method). Consumer Reports dehumidifier testing methodology.

Object: Bagged mulch volume and the coverage that depends on depth, decomposition, and settling (#395)

Assumed channel: The bag of mulch says "2 cubic feet." The consumer reads: this bag contains 2 cubic feet of mulch. Dividing the total bed area by the per-bag coverage yields the number of bags needed.

Actual channel: The "2 cubic feet" is the volume at the time of packaging — measured when the bag is filled at the processing facility. During shipping, stacking on pallets, and storage on the retail shelf, the mulch compresses. The consumer who opens the bag and spreads it may recover less than 2 cubic feet of usable volume. Shredded hardwood compresses more than pine bark nuggets because the smaller, irregular particles nest more tightly under pressure. The volume on the bag describes the mulch before the supply chain sat on it. The coverage calculation introduces a second variable the bag does not specify uniformly: depth. At 2 inches of depth, one 2-cubic-foot bag covers approximately 12 square feet. At the commonly recommended 3 inches, the same bag covers approximately 8 square feet. At 4 inches — sometimes recommended for weed suppression — approximately 6 square feet. The difference between 2-inch and 4-inch depth is a 2:1 ratio in bags purchased. Some bags print a coverage chart on the back; many print only volume. The consumer who estimates "I need about 20 bags" without specifying depth may under-mulch or over-buy by 50 percent. Mulch type compounds the variance. Fine-shredded hardwood mulch settles 20-30 percent within the first growing season as the material decomposes and compacts under rain and foot traffic. Coarse pine bark nuggets settle less — perhaps 10-15 percent — but float and migrate in heavy rain. The 3-inch application becomes 2 inches by August. The consumer who mulched "correctly" in April needs to top-dress by July. Bulk mulch — sold by the cubic yard from landscape suppliers — introduces a different measurement problem. A cubic yard is 27 cubic feet, but the material is loaded by a front-end loader into a truck bed. The loader bucket's capacity is approximate, the material's moisture content varies (wet mulch is denser and measures differently from dry), and the "cubic yard" the consumer purchased may be 24 to 30 cubic feet depending on the loader operator, the material's moisture, and how high the pile is heaped.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the volume number on the bag performs as a fixed quantity of material when the actual volume depends on compression during shipping, moisture content, mulch particle size, and the difference between fill-line volume and opened-bag volume; see also #386, #389, #392) + dimensional-truncation (a cubic-feet number collapses the depth variable, decomposition rate, settling percentage, mulch-type particle geometry, and seasonal degradation into a single volume claim that does not predict coverage without a depth the consumer must choose; see also #386, #392, #262). First landscape horticulture / consumer mulch metrology entry.

Source: Mulch & Soil Council voluntary product certification standards. University extension mulch depth and coverage guides (Virginia Tech, Penn State, University of Florida IFAS). USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service mulch specifications. Retail packaging from Scotts, Vigoro, and Timberline bagged mulch products.

Object: Cordless power tool voltage and the peak-vs-nominal labeling that inflated the numbers (#396)

Assumed channel: The cordless drill box says "20V MAX." The consumer reads: this is a 20-volt tool. A 20V tool is more powerful than an 18V tool. The consumer compares the DeWalt 20V MAX to the Milwaukee 18V and chooses the higher number.

Actual channel: In 2011, DeWalt transitioned from nickel-cadmium (NiCd) to lithium-ion (Li-ion) battery cells and simultaneously rebranded their 18V platform as "20V MAX." The physics: a lithium-ion cell has a nominal voltage of 3.6V and a fully charged (open-circuit) voltage of 4.0V. A 5-cell pack — the standard configuration for this power class — has a nominal voltage of 18V (5 × 3.6V) and a peak voltage of 20V (5 × 4.0V). The "20V MAX" is the open-circuit voltage of a freshly charged battery with no load connected. The instant the trigger is pulled and current flows through the motor, voltage drops to the nominal range — approximately 18V under light load, lower under heavy load. A DeWalt "20V MAX" drill and a Milwaukee "18V" drill use the same cell count, the same voltage class, and the same nominal working voltage. The consumer who chose the 20V tool over the 18V tool chose a label, not a voltage difference. The Federal Trade Commission has not standardized which voltage measurement appears on consumer power tool packaging. Some manufacturers label by nominal voltage (the working voltage under typical load). Others label by maximum voltage (the peak voltage of a fully charged, unloaded battery). The "MAX" qualifier, when present, technically discloses the distinction — but in practice, consumers read the number and compare it to the competitor's number. The same pattern extends to higher voltage classes: DeWalt's "60V MAX" FlexVolt system uses 15 lithium-ion cells in series — 15 × 4.0V = 60V peak, but 15 × 3.6V = 54V nominal. The competition labels equivalent tools at 54V. The consumer sees a 60V tool and a 54V tool and infers a performance gap that describes a labeling convention.

What it means: convention-as-nature (the "20V MAX" label performs as the tool's operating voltage when it is the battery's peak open-circuit voltage under zero load — a condition that exists only before the trigger is pulled; the same voltage class is labeled 18V by other manufacturers, making the number a marketing convention, not a performance distinction; see also #341, #393, #383) + format-as-objectivity (the voltage number on the box performs as a power specification when it describes one point on the battery's discharge curve — the maximum, measured at no load — rather than the working voltage the motor sees under typical use; see also #330, #390, #367). First cordless power tool / battery voltage metrology entry.

Source: DeWalt 20V MAX product line documentation and battery specifications. FTC enforcement guidance on power tool labeling. Milwaukee M18 and Makita 18V LXT battery specifications. ANSI/CTA-2045-A (battery labeling standards). Lithium-ion cell manufacturer datasheets (Samsung, LG Chem) specifying nominal vs. maximum cell voltage.

Object: Sandpaper grit number and the particle-size distribution the integer conceals (#397)

Assumed channel: The sandpaper package says "220 grit." The consumer reads: this is 220-grit sandpaper. Higher grit means finer. 220 is finer than 120. The consumer selects by number, expecting the number to specify the finish.

Actual channel: The grit number refers to the mesh screen through which the abrasive particles were sieved — a 220-mesh screen has approximately 220 openings per linear inch. Particles that pass through the screen but are retained by the next-finer screen are classified as that grit. The resulting particles are not uniform. A "220 grit" sheet carries a distribution of particle sizes, from slightly larger than the mesh to slightly smaller. The largest particles in the distribution determine the deepest scratches. The consumer expects a uniform scratch depth from a uniform grit. The distribution produces a range. Two grading systems coexist in the consumer market. CAMI (Coated Abrasives Manufacturers Institute, now part of the Unified Abrasives Manufacturers' Association) is used primarily in North America. FEPA (Federation of European Producers of Abrasives) is used in Europe and internationally, prefixed with "P" (e.g., P220). At lower grits the systems approximately correspond: CAMI 120 and FEPA P120 have similar mean particle sizes (approximately 125 μm). At higher grits the systems diverge significantly: CAMI 400 has a mean particle size of approximately 23 μm; FEPA P400 has approximately 35 μm — a 50 percent difference. The consumer who buys "400 grit" without knowing which system is on the package may get a significantly different abrasive. Some consumer packaging does not specify CAMI or FEPA. The abrasive material adds another variable: aluminum oxide (standard brown/tan sheets for wood), silicon carbide (gray/black wet-dry sheets for metal and finishing), ceramic alumina (blue or purple, aggressive cut for heavy stock removal), and garnet (natural mineral, softer, for fine woodworking). The same grit number on different abrasive materials produces different surface finishes because the minerals have different hardness, friability, and cutting characteristics. A 220-grit aluminum oxide sheet and a 220-grit silicon carbide sheet, applied with the same pressure to the same wood, leave different surfaces.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the grit integer performs as a single specification of surface finish when the actual finish depends on the particle-size distribution within the grit range, the grading standard used (CAMI vs FEPA), the abrasive mineral, and the technique of application; see also #342, #341, #262) + convention-as-nature (two grading systems — CAMI and FEPA — share overlapping number ranges but diverge at higher grits, making "400 grit" mean different particle sizes depending on the standard the manufacturer used, while the consumer reads the number as universal; see also #341, #396, #383). First abrasive metrology / surface finishing entry.

Source: UAMA (Unified Abrasives Manufacturers' Association) grit size standards. FEPA Standard 43-1:2006 and 43-2:2006 (grain sizes for coated abrasives). ANSI B74.18 (CAMI grading). Norton/Saint-Gobain abrasives technical reference. Flexovit industrial abrasives particle-size comparison charts.

Object: Trash bag gallon capacity and the volume that describes the can, not the contents (#398)

Assumed channel: The box says "13 gallon tall kitchen bags." The consumer reads: each bag holds 13 gallons. The consumer matches the bag to the can: a 13-gallon can gets 13-gallon bags.

Actual channel: The "13 gallon" refers to the nominal capacity of the kitchen trash can the bag is designed to fit — not the usable volume of the bag when installed. When the bag is fitted over the can's rim, the top 3 to 5 inches of the bag fold over the outside of the can to hold the bag in place. This folded-over section reduces the usable interior height. A drawstring closure, if present, gathers the top of the bag inward, further reducing the effective opening and the fillable volume. The usable capacity of a "13-gallon" bag fitted in a standard can with the top folded over and the drawstring at rest is approximately 10 to 11 gallons. The consumer who fills the bag to the drawstring and ties it has used approximately 80 percent of the labeled capacity. The "gallon" measurement itself introduces a second variable. A gallon is a unit of liquid volume — 231 cubic inches. Household trash is not liquid. It is irregular solid objects — food packaging, paper towels, bottles, wrappers — with significant air gaps between items. The packing efficiency of household trash varies: loosely tossed items leave 40 to 60 percent air gaps; compressed items leave fewer. A bag that holds 13 gallons of water holds considerably less than 13 gallons of kitchen trash by mass and by effective material volume, because the trash contains air the gallon measurement does not discount. The bag's thickness ("0.9 mil," "1.2 mil") determines stretch and puncture resistance but does not change the labeled volume. A thinner bag stretches more under load, potentially exceeding the nominal volume but risking puncture. A thicker bag stretches less, holding closer to the nominal volume but with more margin against failure. The consumer who overfills the thin bag — stretching it beyond 13 gallons — has more volume but less structural integrity. The "13 gallon" is a can-fitting specification that the consumer reads as a capacity promise.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the gallon number performs as the bag's capacity when it is the nominal capacity of the can the bag is designed to fit; the usable bag volume with fold-over and drawstring is less than the labeled number; the gallon unit itself describes liquid volume applied to solid, irregular contents with variable packing efficiency; see also #395, #386, #262) + dimensional-truncation (a single gallon number collapses the fold-over reduction, drawstring closure, packing efficiency of irregular solid waste, bag thickness and stretch characteristics, and the gap between liquid-volume units and solid-waste contents into one integer on the box; see also #395, #262, #392). First consumer waste management / refuse bag metrology entry.

Source: ASTM D4635 (Standard Specification for Polyethylene Films Made from Low-Density Polyethylene for General Use and Packaging Applications). Consumer packaging from Glad, Hefty, and store-brand trash bag products. Plastics Industry Association packaging standards. Consumer Reports trash bag testing methodology.

Object: Leaf blower CFM and MPH ratings and the nozzle that trades one for the other (#399)

Assumed channel: The leaf blower box says "530 CFM" or "180 MPH" or both. The consumer reads: more CFM means more power. More MPH means more power. The consumer compares whichever number is printed largest and selects the biggest one.

Actual channel: CFM (cubic feet per minute) and MPH (miles per hour) measure different properties of the same air stream, and they are inversely related through nozzle geometry. CFM measures the volume of air the impeller moves. MPH measures the speed of that air at the nozzle exit. A wider nozzle opening delivers more volume (higher CFM) at lower speed (lower MPH). A narrower nozzle concentrates the same volume into a faster stream (higher MPH) but covers less area per second (effectively lower useful CFM at the work surface). The manufacturer can emphasize whichever metric the nozzle geometry favors. For clearing dry leaves from a flat lawn — a large-area, low-resistance task — air volume (CFM) matters more than air speed, because the job requires moving debris across a broad surface. For dislodging wet, matted leaves from cracks or gutters — a small-area, high-resistance task — air speed (MPH) matters more, because the job requires breaking adhesion at a point. The consumer comparing a 530 CFM blower to a 180 MPH blower is comparing two different dimensions of blowing performance, each optimized for a different task, using numbers that cannot be compared directly. The measurement point adds another variable. "CFM" may be measured in the blower housing (before the nozzle), at the nozzle exit, or at a specified distance from the nozzle — each yielding a different number. "MPH" may be measured at the nozzle exit or at a working distance. No uniform standard governs where the measurement is taken for consumer labeling. ANSI/OPEI B175.2 provides a test protocol, but compliance in marketing materials is voluntary. Some manufacturers report "MAX" values (peak instantaneous readings at the highest speed setting); others report sustained values at a representative speed. A blower labeled "530 CFM / 180 MPH" may be measuring each metric under different conditions — CFM at full throttle in the housing, MPH at the nozzle exit with the concentrator attached.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (CFM and MPH each perform as the measure of blowing power, but they describe different dimensions of a single air stream that are inversely coupled through nozzle geometry; the consumer comparing one metric across brands is comparing products optimized for different tasks; see also #393, #370, #369) + dimensional-truncation (printing one metric — CFM or MPH — without the other conceals the trade-off the nozzle geometry creates; the measurement point, test condition, and nozzle configuration collapse into a single integer; see also #393, #370, #369). First outdoor power equipment / leaf blower metrology entry.

Source: ANSI/OPEI B175.2 (Handheld and Backpack Blowers — Safety and Performance Standards). ECHO, Stihl, DeWalt, and EGO consumer leaf blower specifications. OPEI (Outdoor Power Equipment Institute) testing methodology documentation.

Object: Consumer tape measure accuracy and the sliding hook that compensates for itself (#400)

Assumed channel: The tape measure reads inches and feet. The marks are where they should be. The consumer measures a board, reads "48 inches," and cuts at 48 inches. The number is the dimension. The tool is precise.

Actual channel: The metal hook at the tip of a retractable tape measure is loose. It slides approximately 1/16 inch — the thickness of the hook itself. This is intentional, not a defect. When the consumer hooks the end over a board edge and pulls (an outside measurement), the hook slides outward by its own thickness, aligning the 0-inch mark with the true edge of the material. When the consumer pushes the hook against a wall (an inside measurement), the hook slides inward by the same amount, compensating for the metal's thickness being added to the measurement. The sliding hook is a mechanical correction for two opposing measurement modes. If the hook is bent, worn, or incorrectly riveted — which occurs with use, dropping, or manufacturing variation — the compensation becomes inaccurate. A hook that has been pulled and bent outward by 1/32 inch over-measures on inside readings by that amount. The consumer who checks the tape's accuracy by measuring from the 1-inch mark instead of the hook will get a correct reading — but will need to subtract 1 inch from every measurement, a mental arithmetic step the tape was designed to eliminate. Consumer tape measures conform to tolerance classes. In the EU, EC Accuracy Class II (the most common consumer grade) permits ±0.3mm per meter at 20°C — meaning a 5-meter tape can be off by ±1.5mm (approximately 1/16 inch). Temperature changes the tape's length: steel expands approximately 0.0065mm per meter per degree Celsius. A 25-foot tape in 95°F sunlight (vs 68°F calibration temperature) can expand by approximately 1/32 inch over its length. In the US, NIST Handbook 44 governs commercial measuring devices, but consumer tape measures sold at hardware stores are not individually calibrated or certified. Two consumer tapes of the same brand may disagree by 1/16 inch on a 10-foot measurement — within tolerance, but noticeable when the consumer cuts a board on one side of the shop with one tape and checks the fit on the other side with a different tape. The blade width — typically 1 inch or 3/4 inch — creates a parallax issue: the consumer marking at the blade's edge versus its center shifts the mark by half the blade width. Professional carpenters account for this by always marking on the same side of the blade. The consumer does not.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the tape's printed marks perform as exact positions when the tool's accuracy depends on hook condition, tolerance class, temperature, and the consumer's marking technique — the tape presents its measurements as precise while operating within a tolerance envelope the consumer does not see; the sliding hook performs as a fixed end while compensating for its own variable; see also #341, #342, #397) + population-as-individual (the tolerance class permits a range of accuracy across all tapes of a given grade; two tapes from the same shelf may disagree within their shared tolerance — the consumer treats each tape as definitive, but the tape is one instance from a distribution of acceptable accuracies; see also #397, #262, #392). First consumer hand tool / dimensional metrology entry. 400th entry.

Source: NIST Handbook 44 (Specifications, Tolerances, and Other Technical Requirements for Weighing and Measuring Devices). EC Directive 2014/32/EU (Measuring Instruments Directive). ISO 9002 (tape measure calibration standards). Stanley, Milwaukee, and DeWalt consumer tape measure specifications and tolerance documentation.

Object: Consumer space heater wattage and the circuit-breaker ceiling that makes every heater the same (#401)

Assumed channel: The consumer compares space heaters: a 1,500W ceramic tower, a 1,500W oil-filled radiator, a 1,500W infrared panel. Different technologies. Different prices — $30 to $200. The consumer infers that the more expensive heater produces more heat, or at least better heat.

Actual channel: A standard North American residential outlet is on a 15-amp circuit at 120 volts. Maximum continuous draw: 1,500 watts (15A × 120V × 80% continuous-duty derating per NEC Article 210.23). Every consumer space heater plugged into a standard outlet is capped at 1,500 watts. A 1,500-watt ceramic heater, a 1,500-watt oil-filled radiator, and a 1,500-watt infrared panel all convert the same 1,500 watts of electrical energy into the same approximately 5,120 BTU per hour of heat (1 watt ≈ 3.412 BTU/hr). Electric resistance heating is approximately 100 percent efficient at point of use — all the electrical energy becomes heat. The $30 ceramic heater and the $200 oil-filled radiator produce the same total heat output. The difference is distribution method, not quantity. The ceramic heater blows hot air from a concentrated point — fast warmth in a small zone, rapid cooling when the heater cycles off. The oil-filled radiator heats a large thermal mass (diathermic oil) that radiates heat broadly and retains warmth longer after cycling off. The infrared panel emits radiant energy that warms objects and skin directly without heating the intervening air — the room air stays cool while the person feels warm. Each method creates a different thermal experience in the room. None creates more heat. The consumer who pays $170 more for the oil-filled radiator has purchased a different heat distribution pattern, not more heating capacity. The wattage is identical because the circuit demands it. The room-size recommendation — "heats up to 300 square feet" — assumes standard ceiling height (8 feet), standard insulation, and a moderate outdoor temperature. An uninsulated room with 10-foot ceilings in a Minnesota winter requires more heat than any single consumer space heater on a standard circuit can provide. The consumer in that room needs a second heater on a separate circuit, not a more expensive heater on the same one.

What it means: convention-as-nature (the 1,500W maximum appears as a property of the heaters when it is a constraint of the 15-amp residential circuit per NEC; every consumer heater is the same wattage not because the engineering converged but because the electrical code caps the draw; the marketing creates apparent differentiation within an identical power envelope; see also #396, #367, #374) + dimensional-truncation (the thermal experience depends on the heat distribution method — convective vs radiant vs thermal-mass — but the box prints only wattage, collapsing the method that determines comfort into a number that is identical across all products; see also #370, #359, #376). First residential heating / consumer space heater metrology.

Source: NEC (National Electrical Code) Article 210.23 (permissible loads on branch circuits). UL 1278 (Movable and Wall- or Ceiling-Hung Electric Room Heaters). ENERGY STAR does not rate space heaters (no efficiency differentiation at ~100% conversion). Consumer Reports space heater testing methodology. Electrical energy-to-heat conversion: Conservation of Energy (First Law of Thermodynamics).

Object: Bathroom scale displayed weight and the precision that performs as accuracy (#402)

Assumed channel: The digital bathroom scale reads "154.2 lbs." The consumer reads: body weight is 154.2 pounds. The decimal communicates precision. The consumer tracks daily fluctuations — 154.2 yesterday, 153.8 today — and interprets the 0.4-pound change as weight loss.

Actual channel: Consumer bathroom scales display weight to 0.2-pound increments (some to 0.1). The display precision is not the measurement accuracy. Most consumer strain-gauge scales have an accuracy of ±1 to 2 pounds — meaning the "154.2" could represent a true weight anywhere from 152.2 to 156.2 pounds. The 0.4-pound daily change the consumer interprets as progress is within the instrument's error margin. The surface changes the reading. Strain-gauge load cells require a hard, flat surface to distribute force evenly. On carpet, the scale's feet sink, the platform flexes, and the load cells receive uneven force. A scale that reads 154.2 on tile may read 149 to 151 on carpet — a 3 to 5 pound difference attributable to the floor. Some scales include "carpet feet" — adjustable extensions that partially compensate — but the correction is approximate. The consumer who moves the scale from the bathroom tile to the bedroom carpet has changed weight by moving the scale. Position on the platform matters. Standing centered distributes weight evenly across the four load cells. Standing forward shifts weight to the front cells; standing back shifts it to the rear. The asymmetric loading can change the displayed reading by 0.5 to 1.5 pounds. The consumer who steps on differently each morning gets a different reading from the same body at the same weight. Daily body weight fluctuates 2 to 4 pounds due to hydration, food mass in the digestive tract, sodium-mediated water retention, and glycogen stores (each gram of glycogen binds approximately 3 grams of water). A 16-ounce glass of water adds 1 pound. A large meal adds 2 to 3 pounds until digestion and excretion complete. Morning weight after overnight fasting and urination is typically the day's lowest reading — which is why fitness protocols specify "first thing in the morning, after using the bathroom." The scale's displayed number is the sum of body tissue, water, food in transit, glycogen hydration, and instrument error — displayed to a decimal that suggests the sum is resolved to its components.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the decimal display — 154.2, not "approximately 154" — performs as precise measurement when the instrument's accuracy is ±1-2 pounds, the floor surface can shift the reading by 3-5 pounds, platform position varies by 0.5-1.5 pounds, and daily biological fluctuation spans 2-4 pounds; the consumer reads a decimal and infers a precision the system does not support; see also #400, #397, #342) + population-as-individual (the displayed weight is a composite of body tissue mass, water, food in transit, and instrument error — a population of variables presented as a single individual number; the consumer tracks "weight" but the number is a fluctuating aggregate that the decimal display treats as a resolved measurement; see also #241, #400, #112). First consumer health measurement / personal weighing metrology.

Source: NIST Handbook 44 (Specifications and Tolerances for Scales). OIML R76 (International Organization of Legal Metrology — Non-automatic Weighing Instruments). Consumer Reports bathroom scale testing methodology. Withings, Renpho, and EatSmart consumer scale accuracy specifications.

Object: Paper shredder sheet capacity and the run time the box does not display (#403)

Assumed channel: The shredder box says "12 sheets per pass." The consumer reads: this shredder handles 12 sheets at once. The consumer selects by sheet count, assuming higher count means faster shredding.

Actual channel: The "12 sheets" is tested with standard 20-pound bond paper (75 g/m²) — the lightest common office paper. Heavier paper reduces the count: 24-pound bond reduces effective capacity to approximately 9-10 sheets. Card stock or manila folders may allow only 2-3 sheets. Envelopes, with their doubled layers and adhesive strips, count as 2-3 sheets each. Staples and paper clips, while technically accepted by many cross-cut shredders, slow the motor and reduce throughput. The "12 sheets" describes the machine's capacity under the lightest, cleanest feed condition. The consumer's desk drawer contains a mix of bond paper, card stock, envelopes with windows, and stapled packets — material that feeds at varying fractions of the headline number. Run time is the concealed constraint. Consumer shredders are rated for continuous operation of 5 to 20 minutes (depending on model tier) before requiring a cooldown period of 30 to 60 minutes to prevent motor overheating. The consumer with a filing cabinet of documents to shred — perhaps 2,000 sheets — does not shred continuously. At 12 sheets per pass and approximately 3 seconds per pass, the theoretical throughput is 240 sheets per minute. In 10 minutes: 2,400 sheets. But the 10-minute run time followed by 45 minutes of cooling produces an effective throughput of approximately 2,400 sheets per 55 minutes — roughly 44 sheets per minute averaged over the duty cycle. The box prints 12 sheets per pass. The duty cycle determines the actual pace. Security level adds a dimension the consumer may not compare. DIN 66399 classifies shred particle size from P-1 (strip-cut, 12mm strips) through P-7 (high-security, 0.8 × 5mm particles). Most consumer shredders are P-3 or P-4 (cross-cut, particles ≤4 × 40mm). Higher security levels require smaller cuts, which means more cutting per pass, which reduces both sheet capacity and motor life. The consumer who wants both high throughput and high security faces a trade-off the sheet-count number does not reveal.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the sheet-per-pass number performs as the shredding speed when the effective throughput depends on paper weight, mixed materials, run-time limits, cooldown cycles, and security level — the consumer comparing 12-sheet to 8-sheet machines is comparing a peak-condition metric that both machines rarely achieve in actual use; see also #376, #393, #399) + dimensional-truncation (a single sheet count collapses the paper-weight range, run-time/cooldown duty cycle, security-level trade-off, and mixed-material feed into one number; see also #376, #393, #399). First office equipment / document shredder metrology entry.

Source: DIN 66399 (Paper shredder security levels). NSA/CSS EPL-02 (Evaluated Products List for classified document destruction). Fellowes, AmazonBasics, and Royal consumer shredder specifications. Consumer Reports shredder testing methodology.

Object: Surge protector joule rating and the protection that depletes with use (#404)

Assumed channel: The surge protector box says "2,100 joules." The consumer reads: this device protects electronics from power surges. Higher joules means more protection. A 2,100-joule protector is better than a 1,000-joule protector.

Actual channel: The joule rating describes the total energy the metal-oxide varistors (MOVs) inside the surge protector can absorb over the device's entire lifetime — not per surge. Each surge the MOVs absorb degrades them slightly. A 2,100-joule protector that absorbs a 500-joule surge has 1,600 joules of remaining protection. After four such surges, the joule budget is exhausted. The MOVs degrade progressively: after absorbing energy equal to their rating, they may provide little to no clamping protection. Many surge protectors do not visually indicate when the MOVs are depleted — the power strip continues to function as a power strip (passing electricity to the outlets) while no longer providing surge protection. The consumer whose protector survived a lightning season three years ago may be plugging a $2,000 computer into what is effectively a power strip. The clamping voltage adds a second variable. UL 1449 (the safety standard for surge protectors, third edition, 2009) specifies clamping voltage — the voltage level at which the protector begins diverting surge energy to ground. A lower clamping voltage means earlier intervention: a protector that clamps at 330V lets less surge voltage through to the connected equipment than one that clamps at 500V. The joule rating and the clamping voltage are independent specifications. A high-joule protector with a high clamping voltage may absorb a lot of energy but let damaging voltage through to the equipment before it begins clamping. The consumer who selects by joule rating alone has chosen the protector's total absorption capacity without specifying how much voltage reaches the equipment before the protection activates. Response time — the speed at which the MOVs begin clamping — adds a third variable, measured in nanoseconds. A protector with a 1-nanosecond response lets less of the surge's leading edge through than one with a 5-nanosecond response. The leading edge of a lightning-induced surge can peak in microseconds. The response time is rarely on the box.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the joule rating performs as the level of protection when it is the total lifetime energy budget that depletes with each surge, may be partially consumed without visible indication, and does not describe the clamping voltage or response time that determine how much of each surge reaches the equipment; see also #376, #401, #396) + dimensional-truncation (a single joule number collapses the lifetime depletion curve, the clamping voltage threshold, the response time, the number and severity of surges already absorbed, and the indicator-light reliability into one integer on the box; see also #376, #401, #399). First consumer electrical protection / surge suppression metrology.

Source: UL 1449 (Surge Protective Devices, 3rd edition, 2009; 4th edition, 2014). IEEE C62.45 (Recommended Practice on Surge Testing for Equipment Connected to Low-Voltage AC Power Circuits). NEMA LS-1 (Low Voltage Surge Protective Devices). Tripp Lite, APC, and Belkin consumer surge protector specifications. Consumer Reports surge protector testing methodology.

Object: Bluetooth wireless range and the open-air specification that meets a house full of walls (#405)

Assumed channel: The Bluetooth speaker box says "100-foot wireless range" or "Bluetooth 5.0 — up to 800 feet." The consumer reads: this speaker works from 100 feet (or 800 feet) away. The consumer envisions using the speaker on the patio while the phone sits in the kitchen.

Actual channel: The range specification is tested in open-air, line-of-sight conditions — no walls, no furniture, no interference from other wireless devices. Bluetooth operates in the 2.4 GHz ISM band, shared with Wi-Fi routers, microwave ovens, cordless phones, and neighboring Bluetooth devices. Each wall between the transmitter (phone) and the receiver (speaker) attenuates the signal. A standard interior drywall wall reduces range by 20 to 30 percent. A concrete or brick wall reduces it by 50 percent or more. A floor/ceiling (wood joists and drywall): 30 to 40 percent. The "100-foot" open-air range becomes 30 to 50 feet through two drywall walls and a floor — the typical distance from a kitchen to a patio in a house. Bluetooth 5.0 (released 2016) extended the theoretical maximum range to approximately 800 feet by quadrupling the broadcast power budget. The "800-foot" specification requires both the transmitting and receiving devices to support the extended range, the connection to use the LE Coded PHY (long-range mode) rather than standard LE 1M PHY, and an unobstructed path. Most consumer Bluetooth audio products use standard LE 1M PHY or Classic Bluetooth for audio streaming because Coded PHY sacrifices throughput for range — unsuitable for high-quality audio. The "Bluetooth 5.0" on the box does not mean the device uses the long-range mode. It means the chipset supports the standard, which includes many features the product may not implement. The range is also determined by the weakest link: the phone's Bluetooth transmitter and the speaker's receiver, or vice versa. A speaker with a strong antenna paired with a phone with a weak antenna achieves the phone's range, not the speaker's. The consumer's range experience is determined by the lower-powered device in the pair, not the specification on the box of the higher-powered one.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the range number performs as the usable distance when it is the open-air, line-of-sight maximum that walls, interference, protocol mode, and the paired device's antenna all reduce; "Bluetooth 5.0" performs as a capability when the audio product may not implement the long-range mode the specification defines; see also #334, #390, #399) + dimensional-truncation (a single range number collapses the wall count, wall material, interference density, Bluetooth protocol mode, paired-device transmit power, and the weakest-link pairing into one integer or one specification version; see also #334, #390, #399). First consumer wireless audio / Bluetooth connectivity metrology.

Source: Bluetooth SIG Core Specification v5.0 (2016), v5.4 (2023). FCC Part 15 (2.4 GHz ISM band power limits). JBL, Sony, and Bose consumer Bluetooth speaker specifications and range testing disclosures.

Object: Pump sprayer gallon capacity and the pressure decay that determines coverage (#406)

Assumed channel: The garden pump sprayer says "1 gallon" on the tank. The herbicide label says "mix 1 oz per gallon, apply at 1 gallon per 1,000 sq ft." The consumer reads: pump the sprayer, walk the lawn, apply one gallon over 1,000 square feet. The gallon marking, the mixing ratio, and the coverage rate appear to form a closed system.

Actual channel: The gallon marking on the tank is molded into the plastic at the factory. The actual volume may differ by 10 to 15 percent — a tank marked "1 gallon" that holds 1.15 gallons produces a 15 percent dilution error before the consumer measures the first ounce of concentrate. The Ohio State University extension program identifies inaccurate tank capacity as a common cause of under- and over-application. A Nebraska study found that two-thirds of applicators were applying pesticides at rates with errors greater than 5 percent. The pressure adds a second variable. A consumer hand-pump sprayer reaches 40 to 60 PSI at full pressurization. The moment the trigger opens, pressure begins to decay. At 40 PSI, the nozzle may deliver 0.4 gallons per minute with a certain spray pattern. At 20 PSI — half the strokes later — the flow rate drops, the droplet size increases, and the spray pattern narrows. The consumer who pumps thirty strokes and walks the lawn is applying a decreasing volume per square foot with every step. The beginning of the pass receives more herbicide than the end. The coverage rate — "1 gallon per 1,000 square feet" — assumes constant pressure, constant walking speed, and constant nozzle height. The consumer controls none of these precisely. Walking speed alone varies application rate: 2 mph delivers twice the volume per square foot as 4 mph over the same area. Nozzle height changes the swath width — higher means wider but thinner coverage. The label's application rate is the output of a calibration protocol (Colorado State University extension: measure output into a container over a timed pass at a marked distance, calculate gallons per 1,000 sq ft) that the consumer has almost certainly never performed. The gallon on the tank, the ounce in the measuring cup, and the square footage of the lawn are three numbers. The actual application rate is determined by pressure, walking speed, nozzle height, spray pattern, and their variation across the pass — five variables the three numbers do not capture.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the gallon marking, the mixing ratio, and the label's coverage rate perform as a complete application system when the actual delivery depends on tank volume accuracy, pressure decay, walking speed, nozzle height, and spray pattern uniformity — five uncontrolled variables that the three printed numbers do not address; see also #399, #395, #403) + dimensional-truncation (a single coverage rate collapses the pressure decay curve, the walking speed variation, the nozzle height, the spray pattern change with pressure, and the tank volume tolerance into one ratio on the label; see also #399, #395, #403). First consumer garden chemical application / sprayer metrology.

Source: Ohio State University Extension FABE-531 (Proper Calibration and Operation of Backpack and Hand Can Sprayers). Colorado State University Extension 5.003 (Sprayer Calibration Fundamentals). Penn State Extension (Backpack Sprayer Calibration for Spot Applications). University of Georgia Pesticide Handbook calibration chapter. Gordon's Professional Solutions sprayer calibration guide.

Object: Extension cord amp rating and the voltage drop the length conceals (#407)

Assumed channel: The extension cord package says "15 AMP" and "100 feet." The consumer reads: this cord delivers 15 amps of power over 100 feet. The consumer plugs a 1,500-watt space heater into the far end of the cord and expects full performance.

Actual channel: The amp rating describes the maximum current the cord can carry without exceeding the insulation's thermal limit — not the current it delivers without loss. Every foot of copper wire has resistance, and resistance converts electrical energy into heat. A 100-foot, 16-gauge extension cord (the most common lightweight cord) has a round-trip conductor length of 200 feet. At 12.5 amps (1,500 watts at 120 volts — a standard space heater), the voltage drop across 200 feet of 16-gauge copper is approximately 20 percent. The heater receives 96 volts instead of 120. At reduced voltage, a resistive heater produces proportionally less heat (power drops with the square of voltage: 96V/120V squared = 64 percent of rated output). The 1,500-watt heater delivers roughly 960 watts. The consumer feels less heat and assumes the heater is defective. The cord, meanwhile, dissipates the missing watts as heat along its own length — warm to the touch under a rug, hot at the plug connection, a fire ignition source if coiled. Extension cords cause over 3,300 home fires annually in the United States, resulting in approximately 50 deaths and 270 injuries. The amp rating is not the problem. A 16-gauge cord rated for 13 amps can physically carry 12.5 amps without tripping the breaker. The breaker protects the house wiring (14-gauge, rated for 15 amps). The breaker does not protect the extension cord. A cord rated for 13 amps carrying 12.5 amps is within its rating but generating significant heat at 100-foot length. The consumer who checks the amp rating against the appliance's draw has performed the recommended safety calculation and arrived at a dangerous result — because the calculation does not include length. The gauge-length-ampacity relationship (NEC Chapter 9, Table 9) is a three-variable equation. The package prints two variables. The third — the one that determines whether the cord overheats — is the one the consumer supplies by unspooling the cord across the house.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the amp rating on the package performs as the cord's capacity when the actual safe capacity depends on the interaction of gauge, length, and load — the amp rating without the length at which it applies is a thermal limit stripped of its most important condition; see also #342, #401, #404) + dimensional-truncation (the single amp number collapses the gauge-length-ampacity curve, the voltage drop at distance, the heat dissipation along the cord, and the fire risk of coiled or covered installation into one integer; see also #342, #401, #404). First consumer electrical distribution / extension cord metrology.

Source: NEC Chapter 9, Table 9 (AC Resistance and Reactance for 600-Volt Cables). UL 817 (Cord Sets and Power-Supply Cords). CPSC extension cord fire data. ESFI (Electrical Safety Foundation International) extension cord safety guidelines. Allstar Electrical extension cord sizing guide.

Object: Slow cooker quart capacity and the fill line that redefines the vessel (#408)

Assumed channel: The slow cooker box says "6 Quart." The consumer reads: this appliance holds six quarts of food. A family of four needs a six-quart model. Bigger number means more food.

Actual channel: The quart rating describes the total volume of the ceramic insert filled to the brim — the geometric capacity of the vessel, not the usable cooking capacity. Manufacturers uniformly recommend filling a slow cooker between one-half and two-thirds full. Below half, the food cooks too fast, dries out, or burns against the sides. Above two-thirds, the food does not reach safe temperature quickly enough (the USDA's danger zone: 40°F to 140°F; food must pass through this range within two hours), the lid does not seal properly from steam pressure, and the liquid may overflow. A "6-quart" slow cooker used according to manufacturer guidelines holds 3 to 4 quarts of food — 50 to 67 percent of the number on the box. The consumer who buys a 6-quart model expecting to cook 6 quarts of chili must either overfill the insert (risking food safety and overflow) or accept that the appliance's usable capacity is the number on the box minus the mandatory headroom. The serving count adds a second layer. Hamilton Beach markets its 6-quart model as "serves 7+." Seven servings from 4 quarts of usable capacity yields roughly 18 ounces per serving — plausible for brothy soup, optimistic for a one-pot meal with protein and vegetables. The quart on the box is the starting integer. The food in the bowl is two derivations removed from the integer: total volume minus headroom, then divided by serving size.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the quart number performs as the cooking capacity when it is the brim-to-brim geometric volume that the manufacturer's own safety and quality guidelines reduce by one-third to one-half; the serving count derives from the reduced volume, not the labeled volume; see also #398, #257, #401) + dimensional-truncation (a single quart integer collapses the fill-line constraint, the food-safety temperature requirement, the lid-seal threshold, and the serving-size derivation into one number on the box; see also #398, #257, #401). First consumer kitchen appliance / slow cooker metrology.

Source: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service (Slow Cooker Safety). FDA Food Code (Temperature Danger Zone, 40°F–140°F). Crock-Pot, Hamilton Beach, and Instant Pot user manuals and fill-line specifications. Smart Slow Cooker size guide. Kitchen Pearls slow cooker capacity analysis.

Object: Shop vacuum peak horsepower and the inrush current the consumer reads as sustained power (#409)

Assumed channel: The shop vacuum box says "6.5 Peak HP." The consumer reads: this is a 6.5-horsepower machine. Bigger horsepower means more suction. A 6.5 HP shop vac is more powerful than a 5.0 HP shop vac.

Actual channel: "Peak horsepower" is measured during the motor's startup inrush — the surge of current that flows for 8 to 12 milliseconds when the motor is first energized and the rotor is stationary. This momentary surge draws far more current than the motor's continuous operating draw. A standard household outlet provides 15 amps at 120 volts — 1,800 watts, or approximately 2.4 horsepower in mechanical terms. No shop vacuum plugged into a standard outlet can sustain more than approximately 2.4 HP, and the motor's continuous output is further reduced by electrical-to-mechanical conversion losses (typically 50 to 65 percent efficient), yielding roughly 1 to 1.5 HP of sustained mechanical output. An independent laboratory test cited in a consolidated class action lawsuit (Gair v. Shop-Vac Corporation, 2016) found that a vacuum marketed as "6.5 Peak HP" produced 1.93 HP in sustained operation — 30 percent of the labeled number. A "2.5 Peak HP" model produced 1.29 HP — 52 percent of the labeled number. The ratio of peak to sustained varies: bigger peak numbers require proportionally larger inrush surges but are constrained by the same 15-amp outlet. Shop-Vac Corporation settled the consolidated class action in 2016, agreeing to modify marketing language and extend motor warranties. The actual performance metrics — CFM (airflow volume), water lift (sealed suction in inches of water column), and air watts (the product of airflow and suction) — predict cleaning effectiveness. These numbers appear in the specification table, not on the front of the box. The tank capacity adds a second discrepancy: the same class action found that advertised tank sizes exceeded actual usable capacity by approximately 36 percent, because the drum tapers toward the motor housing and the filter assembly occupies internal volume.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the peak HP number performs as the machine's power when it is a 0.008-to-0.012-second inrush measurement that the outlet's amperage physically prevents from sustaining; the number was sufficiently misleading to generate a consolidated class action and settlement; see also #229, #396, #376) + dimensional-truncation (a single peak HP number collapses the distinction between inrush and continuous current, the outlet's amperage ceiling, the motor's electrical-to-mechanical efficiency, and the three actual performance metrics into one integer on the box; see also #229, #396, #376). First consumer workshop / wet-dry vacuum metrology.

Source: Gair v. Shop-Vac Corporation (4:21-cv-00976, consolidated 2016). Shop-Vac Corporation class action settlement (2016, extended motor warranty, $4.25M attorney fees, marketing language modification). ASTM F558 (Standard Test Method for Measuring Air Performance Characteristics of Vacuum Cleaners). Intervac Design analysis of shop vac horsepower claims. MetroVac suction power comparison methodology.

Object: Lawn mower deck size and the cutting width the consumer reads as machine width (#410)

Assumed channel: The push mower spec sheet says "22-inch deck." The consumer reads: this mower is 22 inches wide. A 36-inch gate will accommodate it. The consumer buys the mower based on the deck number and plans the mowing path through the yard.

Actual channel: The deck size refers to the cutting width — the distance across the blade tips, measuring the swath of grass cut in one pass. The actual mower width includes the deck shell extending beyond the blade tips, the discharge chute (adding 4 to 8 inches on one side), anti-scalp rollers, wheel housings, and any side-mounted controls. A "22-inch" push mower typically measures 24 to 26 inches at its widest point without the discharge chute, and 28 to 32 inches with the chute in the mowing position. The consumer who buys a "36-inch" riding mower expecting it to fit through a 36-inch gate discovers the machine is 42 to 48 inches wide. The engine specification adds a second comparison problem. Briggs & Stratton, the dominant small-engine manufacturer for walk-behind mowers, switched from horsepower to gross torque (ft-lbs at 2,600 RPM per SAE J1940) for push mowers. Competitors may list horsepower, displacement in cc, or net torque. The consumer comparing a "6.75 gross torque" Briggs engine to a "190cc" Honda engine to a "6.5 HP" generic engine is comparing three different measurements of three different properties: rotational force, volumetric displacement, and power output. None can be converted to the others without additional specifications (compression ratio, RPM, bore-to-stroke ratio) that do not appear on the mower. The number on the mower — whether it describes the deck or the engine — refers to the dimension most favorable for shelf comparison, not the dimension the consumer needs to plan the mow or predict the cut.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the deck size performs as the mower's width when it is the blade-tip-to-blade-tip cutting swath that does not include the shell, discharge chute, or wheels; the engine metric varies by manufacturer, making comparison across brands impossible without conversion factors absent from the spec sheet; see also #333, #396, #229) + dimensional-truncation (a single deck number collapses the cutting width, machine width, discharge width, and gate-clearance requirement into one integer; a single engine number collapses torque, power, displacement, and RPM into one figure denominated in whichever unit favors the comparison; see also #333, #396, #229). First consumer outdoor power equipment / mower sizing metrology.

Source: SAE J1940 (Small Engine Power and Torque Rating Procedure, 2012 revision). Briggs & Stratton consumer FAQ (gross torque vs. horsepower explanation). Tractor Supply Co. deck size and cutting width guides. Main Street Mower deck measurement methodology.

Object: Disinfectant "kills 99.9%" claim and the contact time the consumer does not observe (#411)

Assumed channel: The disinfectant spray bottle says "Kills 99.9% of Germs*." The consumer reads: spray the counter, wipe it, the surface is disinfected. The asterisk, if noticed, references fine print. The consumer sprays, wipes within seconds, and moves on.

Actual channel: The "99.9%" efficacy claim is achieved under EPA-registered test conditions that include a specific contact time — the duration the surface must remain visibly wet with the disinfectant for the product to achieve the claimed kill rate. For Lysol Disinfecting Wipes, the required contact time is 4 minutes. For Clorox Disinfecting Wipes, 4 minutes. For many spray disinfectants, 3 to 10 minutes. The surface must stay wet — not damp, not residual, but visibly wet — for the entire duration. The consumer who sprays and wipes within 10 seconds has achieved a fraction of the claimed efficacy. The fraction is not printed. The consumer has no way to know whether a 10-second wipe kills 50%, 80%, or 95% of the target organisms — only the full contact time achieves the labeled claim. The EPA requires that all disinfectant products list the contact time in the directions for use, and the product must name the specific organisms it has been tested against. But the front label says "Kills 99.9%" in large type, and the contact time appears in the directions on the back panel, in the use instructions, in regulatory-sized text. The front performs the conclusion. The back contains the condition. The consumer reads the front. The front of the bottle and the back of the bottle are different documents aimed at different readers — the purchaser and the applicator — but the purchaser and the applicator are the same person, and that person reads the front.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the "99.9%" performs as the outcome of normal use when it is the outcome of a specific protocol — full contact time, visibly wet surface, specific organism — that the consumer almost certainly does not follow; the claim and its condition are separated by the front and back of the same bottle; see also #241, #219, #375) + dimensional-truncation (a single percentage collapses the contact time, the surface wetness requirement, the organism-specific testing, and the consumer's actual spray-and-wipe behavior into one number on the front label; see also #241, #219, #375). First consumer cleaning product / surface disinfection metrology.

Source: EPA Pesticide Registration (40 CFR 152-180). AOAC Use Dilution Test (disinfectant efficacy method). SPICE UNC Health (Surface Disinfection: Treatment Time vs. Contact Time, 2018). PDI International (Contact Time and Its Importance). Clorox and Lysol product labels (EPA Reg. No. specifications). GDS Associates (Disinfectant Contact Time Is Not Zero).

Object: Bathroom exhaust fan CFM rating and the ductwork that halves the airflow (#412)

Assumed channel: The bathroom exhaust fan box says "80 CFM." The consumer reads: this fan moves 80 cubic feet of air per minute. An 80-square-foot bathroom needs an 80 CFM fan (the standard rule: 1 CFM per square foot). The consumer installs the fan and considers the ventilation problem solved.

Actual channel: The 80 CFM is measured at 0.1 inches of water gauge (in. w.g.) static pressure — the resistance the fan encounters when pushing air through its ductwork. This is the Home Ventilating Institute (HVI) default test condition. A typical residential installation imposes significantly higher static pressure: each 10 feet of 4-inch duct adds 0.1 to 0.3 in. w.g.; each 90-degree elbow adds 0.05 to 0.15 in. w.g.; the roof cap or wall termination adds 0.05 to 0.15 in. w.g. A typical bathroom installation — 15 feet of 4-inch flex duct with two elbows and a roof cap — produces 0.25 to 0.4 in. w.g. of static pressure. At 0.25 in. w.g., a fan rated at 50 CFM (at 0.1) delivers 23 to 31 CFM — 46 to 62 percent of the labeled number. The DOE's building science research confirms that installed airflow commonly falls to half or less of the rated specification. ENERGY STAR attempted to address this: ENERGY STAR–certified fans must deliver tested airflow at 0.25 in. w.g. that is at least 70 percent of the airflow at 0.1 in. w.g. But non-ENERGY STAR fans (the majority of the market) are still rated at 0.1 in. w.g. — the condition that maximizes the printed number. The sone rating (noise) adds a second comparison problem. The consumer who chooses between a "1.0 sone" fan and a "3.0 sone" fan expects the 1.0 to be one-third as loud. Sones are linear for loudness: 2 sones is perceived as twice as loud as 1 sone. But the sone rating is measured at the fan's rated CFM. A fan that achieves its rated CFM only at 0.1 in. w.g. may run at higher speed (and higher noise) in an actual installation to compensate for duct resistance — or, if it cannot compensate, it delivers less air at the rated noise level. The consumer who selected for quietness has selected a noise number tested at an airflow the installation does not achieve.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the CFM number performs as the installed airflow when it is the airflow at a static pressure that the typical installation doubles or triples; the sone rating performs as the noise level when it is measured at an airflow the ductwork may not permit; see also #240, #245, #375) + dimensional-truncation (a single CFM integer collapses the static-pressure curve, the duct length, the elbow count, the termination type, and the duct diameter into one number on the box; see also #240, #245, #375). First residential ventilation / bathroom exhaust fan metrology.

Source: HVI (Home Ventilating Institute) Publication 916 (Airflow Test Procedure). ASHRAE Standard 62.2-2019 (Ventilation and Acceptable Indoor Air Quality in Residential Buildings). ENERGY STAR Ventilation Fan Key Product Criteria. DOE Building America ventilation guide. Residential Energy Dynamics best practices for residential ventilation.

Object: Insect repellent DEET percentage and the duration the consumer reads as strength (#413)

Assumed channel: The insect repellent bottle says "30% DEET" or "98.11% DEET." The consumer reads: higher percentage means stronger protection. A 98% DEET product repels more mosquitoes than a 30% DEET product. Maximum percentage provides maximum protection.

Actual channel: The DEET percentage determines the duration of protection, not the intensity. A 10% DEET product and a 30% DEET product repel mosquitoes equally during the period both are active — the 10% lasts approximately 2 hours, the 30% lasts approximately 5 to 8 hours. Above approximately 50% concentration, the duration curve plateaus: a 50% DEET product and a 98% DEET product provide roughly the same protection time. The consumer who buys 98% DEET expecting dramatically better protection than 30% has purchased additional concentration past the plateau for negligible additional duration. The EPA's repellent database shows that products with 20 to 30% DEET typically provide protection for several hours and represent the concentration range recommended by both the EPA and CDC as the optimal balance between efficacy and duration. The percentage format invites linear comparison: 98 is more than 30, therefore 98 is better. The relationship is logarithmic, not linear — each doubling of concentration adds a diminishing increment of duration, and beyond 50%, the increment approaches zero. The consumer comparing products on the shelf compares percentages because percentages are the numbers on the bottles. The number that matters — hours of protection — is not on the front label of most consumer repellent products. Some products include "up to X hours" language, but the duration depends on activity level, sweating, water exposure, and ambient temperature, making the printed duration as conditional as the disinfectant's contact time.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the DEET percentage performs as the product's protective power when it describes only the concentration of active ingredient, which determines duration on a logarithmic curve that plateaus at approximately 50%; the consumer reads the percentage as a linear scale of efficacy; see also #185, #236, #411) + dimensional-truncation (a single percentage collapses the logarithmic duration curve, the activity-dependent reapplication interval, the plateau above 50%, and the distinction between repellent intensity and repellent duration into one number on the bottle; see also #185, #236, #411). First consumer personal care / insect repellent metrology.

Source: EPA Insect Repellent Registration and efficacy database. CDC Yellow Book (Mosquitoes, Ticks, and Other Arthropods). North Carolina DHHS DEET safety guide. Consumer Reports insect repellent testing methodology. EWG (Environmental Working Group) repellent guide. RepellentInfo.org concentration analysis.

Object: Gas grill BTU rating and the fuel consumption the consumer reads as heat output (#414)

Assumed channel: The gas grill box says "60,000 BTU." The consumer reads: this grill produces 60,000 BTU of heat. More BTU means a hotter grill. A 60,000 BTU grill sears better than a 40,000 BTU grill.

Actual channel: BTU (British Thermal Unit) per hour measures the rate of fuel consumption — how much propane or natural gas the burners burn in one hour, not how much heat reaches the cooking surface. A grill that consumes 60,000 BTU of fuel per hour may deliver far less to the food, depending on combustion efficiency, heat retention of the firebox, grate design, and wind exposure. The total BTU is often inflated by including side burners, rotisserie burners, and smoker boxes — auxiliary burners that do not contribute to the primary cooking surface. A grill marketed as "60,000 BTU" may have 40,000 BTU on the main burners and 20,000 on the side burner the consumer uses to warm sauce. The metric that predicts cooking performance is heat flux — BTU per square inch of primary cooking area. A 40,000 BTU grill with 400 square inches of cooking area delivers 100 BTU per square inch. A 60,000 BTU grill with 800 square inches delivers 75 BTU per square inch — less heat density despite the higher total number. The 80 to 100 BTU per square inch range is generally considered adequate for searing. Below 80, the grill struggles to achieve proper browning. The consumer who selects by total BTU has selected the grill's fuel consumption without specifying the heat that reaches the food per unit of cooking area. Construction quality inverts the relationship further: a well-insulated grill with ceramic briquettes or heat diffusers retains more of each BTU than a thin-walled grill that radiates heat to the air. A lower-BTU grill with better construction may deliver more cooking heat than a higher-BTU grill that loses heat through its walls.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the BTU number performs as the grill's heat output when it is the fuel consumption rate that includes non-cooking burners, does not account for cooking area, combustion efficiency, or heat retention, and whose relationship to actual cooking temperature depends on construction quality the number does not describe; see also #229, #376, #409) + dimensional-truncation (a single BTU integer collapses the fuel consumption rate, the auxiliary burner inclusion, the cooking area, the heat flux per square inch, the combustion efficiency, and the heat retention into one number on the box; see also #229, #376, #409). First consumer outdoor cooking / gas grill metrology.

Source: Char-Broil consumer BTU guide. Smoked BBQ Source (How Important Are BTUs When Buying a Gas Grill). AmazingRibs.com (Gas Grills Buying Guide, Meathead Goldwyn). Barbeques Galore BTU guide. ID Times gas grill BTU analysis.

Object: Oscillating lawn sprinkler coverage area and the water pressure the box assumes but the hose may not deliver (#415)

Assumed channel: The sprinkler box says "covers up to 3,600 square feet." The consumer reads: this sprinkler waters 3,600 square feet of lawn. A yard of that size or smaller needs one sprinkler. The number describes what the sprinkler does.

Actual channel: The "up to 3,600 square feet" is measured at a specific water pressure — typically 80 PSI — that many residential water systems do not deliver. Most homes provide 30 to 60 PSI at the outdoor spigot after accounting for the pressure drop through the house plumbing, the hose length, and the hose diameter. An oscillating sprinkler's coverage area is a function of water pressure: at 80 PSI it may throw water 40 feet in each direction, producing the advertised rectangle. At 40 PSI — common for a suburban home with a 100-foot 5/8-inch garden hose — the throw distance drops to 20 to 25 feet in each direction. The area drops to approximately 1,000 to 1,500 square feet — 28 to 42 percent of the labeled number. The "covers up to" language is technically accurate: the maximum is the labeled number, at the labeled pressure, which the label does not print. The consumer who buys a single sprinkler for a 3,000-square-foot yard based on the box discovers half the lawn stays dry. Hose diameter compounds the gap: a 5/8-inch hose at 60 PSI delivers approximately 10.5 GPM; a 1/2-inch hose at the same pressure delivers approximately 6.3 GPM. The sprinkler's nozzles need a minimum flow rate to achieve full oscillation and throw distance. Below that threshold, the sprinkler oscillates but barely reaches half its rated area. The coverage rectangle printed on the box is the rectangle at maximum pressure through minimum hose resistance — a condition the consumer achieves only by connecting the sprinkler directly to the spigot with a short, large-diameter hose. The 100-foot hose coiled in the garage has already shrunk the rectangle before the sprinkler turns on.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the square-foot coverage number performs as the sprinkler's watering capability when it is the maximum area at a test pressure and flow rate that most residential installations cannot deliver; the "up to" qualifier is technically present but functionally invisible in the purchasing comparison; see also #406, #412, #239) + dimensional-truncation (a single square-foot integer collapses the water pressure, hose diameter, hose length, flow rate, throw distance, oscillation arc, and the nonlinear relationship between pressure and coverage area into one number on the box; see also #406, #412, #239). First consumer lawn irrigation / sprinkler metrology.

Source: Gilmour lawn size calculator and sprinkler coverage guide. Rain Bird sprinkler math guide. Bob Vila oscillating sprinkler testing. This Old House best oscillating sprinklers review. Garden Counselor oscillating sprinkler tips.

Object: Garbage disposal horsepower rating and the grinding performance the consumer reads as power (#416)

Assumed channel: The garbage disposal box says "3/4 HP" or "1 HP." The consumer reads: higher horsepower means more grinding power. A 1 HP disposal handles tougher food waste than a 1/2 HP disposal. The number on the box describes how well the machine grinds.

Actual channel: The horsepower rating on consumer garbage disposals is typically a peak value — the maximum the motor achieves during startup or under momentary stall load, not the continuous operating horsepower during grinding. This mirrors the shop vacuum peak HP problem (#409): the motor produces its rated power for fractions of a second. Continuous operating horsepower is lower — often significantly so. The amperage draw is a more reliable indicator of the motor's sustained capability, but amperage is not printed on the front of the box. The comparison architecture between models — 1/2 HP vs 3/4 HP vs 1 HP — treats horsepower as a linear scale of grinding ability. But grinding performance depends on factors the HP number does not contain: the number of grind stages (basic models have one stage; premium models have two or three stages that progressively pulverize waste into finer particles), the grind chamber material (galvanized steel vs stainless steel), the presence of auto-reverse to prevent jams, the RPM of the grinding plate (1,725 to 2,800 RPM depending on motor type — induction vs permanent magnet), and the chamber capacity. A 3/4 HP disposal with multi-stage grinding and stainless steel components may outperform a 1 HP disposal with a single grind stage and galvanized internals. The consumer who upgrades from 1/2 HP to 1 HP expecting proportionally better grinding has purchased motor startup capacity without specifying grind stages, chamber quality, or the jam-prevention features that determine whether the food waste actually leaves the drain.

What it means: format-as-objectivity (the HP number performs as the disposal's grinding capability when it is a peak motor specification that does not describe grind stages, chamber material, RPM, jam-prevention features, or the distinction between peak and continuous power; the consumer compares HP integers expecting a linear scale of food waste processing; see also #409, #229, #396) + dimensional-truncation (a single HP integer collapses peak vs continuous power, grind stages, chamber material, motor type, RPM, auto-reverse capability, and chamber capacity into one number on the box; see also #409, #229, #396). First consumer kitchen appliance / waste disposal metrology.

Source: Consumer Reports garbage disposal buying guide. Lowe's garbage disposal buying guide. InSinkErator product specifications. Think Tank Home disposal horsepower guide. Sepura Home garbage disposal power analysis.

Object: The fMRI brain activation map and the blood flow the viewer reads as thought (#417)

Assumed channel: An fMRI scan shows which parts of the brain are active during a task. The colored blobs on the gray brain image indicate where thinking happens. A higher-resolution brain scan reveals finer details of cognition. The image is a photograph of thought in action.

Actual channel: Seiji Ogawa at AT&T Bell Labs demonstrated Blood-Oxygen-Level-Dependent (BOLD) contrast in 1990: active neurons consume oxygen, blood flow increases to compensate, the ratio of oxygenated to deoxygenated hemoglobin changes, and the MR signal shifts by 1-5%. The measurement chain is four links long — neural firing → metabolic demand → hemodynamic response → magnetic signal change — and the scanner captures only the last link. The hemodynamic response function peaks 5-6 seconds after the neural event. Neurons fire on millisecond timescales. The scan captures a blurred echo arriving several seconds late — like photographing a conversation by measuring the heat the speakers left on their chairs. Each voxel spans 2-3 millimeters on a side and averages activity across approximately 630,000 neurons with potentially opposing functions. The colored blobs are not photographs. They are statistical maps, thresholded at an arbitrary significance level. Below the threshold, activity may exist but is visually absent — the blob boundary marks the analyst's decision, not a boundary in the brain. Craig Bennett and colleagues placed a dead Atlantic salmon in an fMRI scanner and showed it photographs of humans in social situations. Without correction for multiple comparisons (130,000 voxels = 130,000 independent statistical tests), several voxels in the salmon's brain cavity showed "significant" activation at p < 0.001. With proper correction: nothing. Anders Eklund, Thomas Nichols, and Hans Knutsson (2016, PNAS) tested common fMRI cluster-based statistical methods and found false-positive rates of 60-70% against an expected 5%. Fifteen years of published studies used methods that found clusters of activation at rates twelve to fourteen times the assumed false-positive rate. The reverse inference problem compounds the statistical one: Russell Poldrack (2006) named the fallacy — activity in a brain region does not establish engagement of the cognitive process associated with that region, because regions participate in multiple functions and functions recruit multiple regions. The mapping is many-to-many, but the colored image implies one-to-one. Deena Weisberg and colleagues (2008) demonstrated that adding neuroscience information — even irrelevant neuroscience information — to explanations of psychological phenomena makes the explanations more satisfying to non-experts. The brain image creates what they called a "seductive allure."

What it means: proxy-as-direct-measurement (blood oxygenation change, arriving 5-6 seconds late and averaged across 630,000 neurons, reported as "brain activity" or "thought"; the measurement chain is four links long and the scanner captures only the last link; see also #116, #132, #112, #175) + format-as-objectivity (the color-mapped brain image performs spatial precision and certainty through visual authority that the thresholded statistical map does not warrant; the blob boundary is the analyst's decision rendered invisible by the image format; Weisberg's "seductive allure" demonstrates that the format itself alters the viewer's evaluation of the claim; see also #267, #172, #175). First neuroimaging / cognitive neuroscience methodology.

Source: Ogawa et al. (1990), PNAS. Kwong et al. (1992), PNAS. Bennett et al. (2010), NeuroImage / Journal of Serendipitous and Unexpected Results. Eklund, Nichols, Knutsson (2016), PNAS. Poldrack (2006), Trends in Cognitive Sciences. Weisberg et al. (2008), Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience.

Object: The Hubble tension and the two measurements that should agree but don't (#418)

Assumed channel: The universe is expanding. The rate of expansion — the Hubble constant, H₀ — is a single number measured in kilometers per second per megaparsec. Two independent methods of measuring this number should, when refined sufficiently, converge to the same value. The number describes a property of the universe. The universe has one expansion rate. Therefore there is one correct answer.

Actual channel: Two methods have reached sufficient precision to definitively disagree. The local distance-ladder measurement (Adam Riess and the SH0ES team, 2022): calibrate Cepheid variable stars using geometric parallax, use Cepheids to calibrate Type Ia supernovae, use supernovae to measure galaxies out to the Hubble flow. Result: 73.04 ± 1.04 km/s/Mpc. The early-universe measurement (Planck satellite, 2018): measure temperature anisotropies in the cosmic microwave background, fit them with the ΛCDM cosmological model (Lambda-Cold Dark Matter), infer the expansion rate at recombination, extrapolate forward. Result: 67.4 ± 0.5 km/s/Mpc. The disagreement is ~5σ — the probability of chance agreement is roughly one in 3.5 million. JWST has independently confirmed the distance-ladder value, ruling out many proposed systematic errors in the Cepheid calibration.

The two numbers answer different questions disguised as the same question. The distance ladder asks: how fast is the universe expanding now, measured directly? The CMB asks: how fast should the universe be expanding now, assuming the standard cosmological model correctly connects the early universe to the present? If the model is correct, both answers must agree. If the model is incomplete — if dark energy varies over time, or if there are additional relativistic species, or if early dark energy briefly accelerated expansion, or if the fundamental physics connecting the two epochs is slightly different from ΛCDM — the numbers will diverge by exactly the amount the model is wrong.

The error bars on each measurement are small enough that both cannot be right if the connecting model is correct. But the error bars do not include the possibility that the model is wrong, because the model is the framework through which the CMB measurement is interpreted. The model is not a source of error within the measurement; it is the lens through which the measurement becomes a measurement of H₀ at all.

What it means: framework-presumes-convergence (two independent measurement methods are expected to converge on the same value because a connecting theoretical framework — ΛCDM — predicts they should; the framework is the lens through which one measurement is translated into the other's units; when the measurements disagree at 5σ, the framework has no internal mechanism for adjudicating between itself and the data; the model's uncertainty is not included in either error bar because the model is not treated as a variable — it is treated as a given; see also #226, #116, #109). First observational cosmology / Hubble parameter measurement.

Source: Riess et al. (2022), Astrophysical Journal Letters. Planck Collaboration (2018), Astronomy & Astrophysics. Freedman et al. (2024), various. Di Valentino et al. (2021), Classical and Quantum Gravity ("In the Realm of the Hubble Tension — A Review of Solutions"). Abdalla et al. (2022), Journal of High Energy Astrophysics.

Object: Dissolved iron in seawater and the contamination that was the measurement (#419)
